Reassign one of the two activities to a less-experienced engineer to break the tie.
Delay both activities until the specialist is free from other commitments.
questions.explanation: Managing the resource conflict starts by analyzing it and weighing leveling, re-sequencing, or added capacity before committing. Overtime, an unreviewed substitution, or a blanket delay each pick a response before the options are understood. Closest distractor: (C) — substituting a resource is a legitimate option but should follow the analysis, not precede it.

questions.question: When planning team and physical resources, what should MOST drive the plan?
choices: The resources that happen to be available when planning begins.
The project's requirements and the actual work to be performed.
The largest team the approved budget is able to fund.
The staffing level used on the organization's most recent similar project.
questions.explanation: Resource planning is driven by the project's requirements and the actual work to be performed. Sizing to whatever is available, to the budget, or to prior headcount matches resources to something other than the need. Closest distractor: (D) — prior headcount is a tempting benchmark but reflects a different project's work, not this one's.

questions.question: A key team member becomes unexpectedly unavailable for two weeks. What is the BEST first action?
choices: Pause the affected work until the team member returns in two weeks.
Bring in a contractor at once to backfill the missing skill set.
Assess the impact and optimize the remaining resources through reassignment or cross-training.
Extend the project finish date by two weeks to absorb the gap.
questions.explanation: Optimizing resources means assessing the impact and adjusting through reassignment or cross-training first. Halting the work, backfilling before analysis, or auto-extending the schedule commit before the options are weighed. Closest distractor: (B) — a contractor may help, but hiring before assessing the impact is premature.

questions.question: How does resource management on an adaptive team MOST differ from a predictive one?
choices: Adaptive teams forgo resource planning because requirements are still emerging.
A central resource manager allocates each member to tasks as they arise.
The project manager personally assigns every task to individual members.
Stable, dedicated cross-functional teams are favored over specialists reassigned task by task.
questions.explanation: Adaptive delivery favors stable, dedicated cross-functional teams for continuity and predictable flow, rather than specialists reassigned task by task. It does not skip resource planning or centralize per-task assignment. Closest distractor: (B) — per-task allocation sounds efficient but is the matrixed pattern adaptive teams deliberately move away from.

questions.question: A construction deliverable depends on materials with a long procurement lead time. To plan resources effectively, what should the PM do?
choices: Plan and order the long-lead materials early, based on the schedule dependencies.
Order the materials just in time, as each site activity reaches them.
Rely on the vendor's ability to expedite delivery whenever it is requested.
Hand material planning entirely to the vendor and track only the site work.
questions.explanation: Long-lead materials are planned and ordered early against the schedule dependencies so they arrive when needed. Just-in-time ordering, assumed expediting, or delegating the planning to the vendor each risk a delay the schedule cannot absorb. Closest distractor: (B) — just-in-time is sound for short-lead items but courts delay for long-lead materials.

questions.question: A resource is over-allocated across several activities, exceeding available hours. Which technique resolves the over-allocation within resource limits, even if the finish date must move?
choices: Schedule crashing.
Resource leveling.
Fast tracking.
Scope reduction.
questions.explanation: Resource leveling reschedules demand to resolve an over-allocation within resource limits and may move the finish date. Crashing and fast tracking compress the schedule but do not relieve over-allocation, and scope reduction is a different lever. Closest distractor: (A) — crashing adds resources to shorten duration but does not resolve an over-allocated resource.

questions.question: The PM wants the team to have the competencies needed for upcoming work. What is the BEST action?
choices: Rely on the team's existing skills, treating them as sufficient for the upcoming work.
Respond to a competency gap only after it has actually caused a schedule delay.
Assess required competencies against the team and plan training or acquisition to close gaps.
Recruit senior specialists into every open role regardless of what the work needs.
questions.explanation: Competency planning means proactively assessing required skills against the team and closing gaps through training or acquisition. Relying on current skills, reacting only after a delay, or over-hiring into every role are not effective planning. Closest distractor: (B) — waiting for a gap to surface is common but reactive rather than planned.

questions.question: A buyer's scope is completely and clearly defined and unlikely to change, and the buyer wants the seller to carry the risk of any cost overrun. Which contract type is MOST appropriate?
choices: Cost-plus-incentive-fee.
Time and materials.
Fixed-price incentive fee.
Firm-fixed-price.
questions.explanation: With fully defined, stable scope and the buyer wanting the seller to bear overrun risk, firm-fixed-price places essentially all cost risk on the seller. Fixed-price incentive fee is the closest miss — it is also fixed-price but a sharing ratio splits overruns, so the buyer still carries some cost risk; cost-plus and T&M forms leave more cost risk with the buyer and suit uncertain scope. Closest distractor: (C) — a fixed-price family member that nonetheless shares, not fully transfers, the overrun risk.

questions.question: The scope of a contracted engagement is not yet well defined and is expected to evolve. Which contract approach BEST fits while limiting the buyer's open-ended exposure?
choices: Time and materials with a not-to-exceed cap.
Cost-plus-fixed-fee with no ceiling on total reimbursable cost.
Firm-fixed-price priced against the current best-guess scope.
Cost-plus-percentage-of-cost with no defined limit.
questions.explanation: T&M flexes with evolving scope while a not-to-exceed cap bounds the buyer's exposure. Cost-plus-fixed-fee is the closest miss — it also fits uncertain scope but, without a ceiling, leaves the buyer's cost exposure open-ended; a firm-fixed-price on guessed scope forces premature definition, and cost-plus-percentage-of-cost rewards higher spending. Closest distractor: (B) — right for uncertain scope, but uncapped exposure is exactly what the stem asks to limit.

questions.question: Before entering negotiations with a critical vendor, what should the PM do FIRST?
choices: Begin the discussion with the vendor and shape your position as their terms and constraints emerge.
Determine the negotiation strategy — objectives, priorities, and walk-away points.
Have procurement run the talks and step in yourself only if a sticking point arises.
Anchor on the pricing from the last comparable vendor contract and push to match those terms.
questions.explanation: A negotiation strategy with clear objectives, priorities, and walk-away points must be set before talks begin. Opening the discussion and improvising (A) is the closest miss — it feels responsive but leaves the buyer negotiating without a floor or defined targets; leaning on procurement without your input, or anchoring on an old contract, skips your own preparation. Closest distractor: (A) — engaging early looks efficient, but strategy precedes the conversation.

questions.question: A vendor's deliverables are consistently late and below the quality expected. What should the PM do FIRST?
choices: Issue a formal breach notice to the vendor and start the process to terminate the contract.
Withhold payment on the deliverables in dispute to press the vendor to correct the shortfall.
Evaluate the vendor's performance against the agreement and address the gaps through the contract's mechanisms.
Escalate the vendor's poor performance to the sponsor and let leadership decide the response.
questions.explanation: Managing the contract means first comparing the vendor's performance to the agreement, then using the contract's remedies to correct the gaps. Withholding payment on disputed items (B) is the closest miss — it invokes a contractual lever but acts before performance has been formally assessed and may itself breach the payment terms; a breach notice and termination is premature, and escalation hands off the PM's own contract-management responsibility. Closest distractor: (B) — a real remedy, but applied before diagnosing against the agreement.

questions.question: Before closing a contract, how should the PM confirm the vendor has fulfilled its obligations?
choices: Accept the vendor's written statement that all contracted work has been completed.
Treat the fact that every invoice has been paid in full as evidence of completion.
Confirm that the contract's scheduled period of performance has now ended.
Verify that the agreement's objectives have been met against the acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Fulfillment is confirmed by verifying the agreement's objectives against the agreed acceptance criteria. Accepting the vendor's self-certification (A) is the closest miss — it addresses completion but substitutes the seller's own assurance for the buyer's independent verification; paid invoices and a passed end date show payment or timing, not that the work meets the agreement. Closest distractor: (A) — a completion claim is not verified completion.

questions.question: During procurement planning, the PM must decide whether to build a component in-house or buy it. What BEST informs this decision?
choices: A make-or-buy analysis weighing cost, capability, risk, control, and schedule.
A cost comparison that selects whichever external vendor offers the lowest total price.
The sourcing approach used on the organization's most recent comparable project.
Whichever option keeps the component under the project team's direct, in-house control.
questions.explanation: A make-or-buy analysis compares in-house versus external sourcing across cost, capability, risk, control, and schedule together. A lowest-price comparison (B) is the closest miss — cost matters, but deciding on price alone ignores the other factors the decision must weigh; copying a prior project, or optimizing a single factor such as control, is equally partial. Closest distractor: (B) — decisive-looking, but one factor of several.

questions.question: Two parties dispute the interpretation of a clause in the statement of work. What should the PM do?
choices: Adopt the interpretation offered by the party the team would rather keep working with.
Refer to the agreement's terms and manage the contract to resolve the interpretation.
Revise the statement of work yourself to state the meaning you believe was intended.
Suspend the vendor's work and wait for legal counsel to rule on the clause.
questions.explanation: Contract disputes are resolved by reference to the agreement's terms and its resolution mechanisms. Suspending work for legal counsel (D) is the closest miss — legal review may eventually help, but stopping the vendor and skipping the contract's own interpretation and dispute provisions can breach the agreement and escalates too soon; favoring a party or rewriting the SOW unilaterally abandons the agreed terms. Closest distractor: (D) — prudent-sounding, but a premature halt before applying the contract.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. What are the cost variance (CV) and schedule variance (SV) at the data date?
choices: CV = +$50,000 and SV = +$50,000; the project is ahead and under budget.
CV = -$50,000 and SV = -$50,000; the project is over budget and behind schedule.
CV = -$50,000 and SV = $0; the project is over budget but on schedule.
CV = $0 and SV = -$50,000; the project is on budget but behind schedule.
questions.explanation: CV = EV - AC = 200,000 - 250,000 = -$50,000 (over budget); SV = EV - PV = 200,000 - 250,000 = -$50,000 (behind schedule). Both are negative, so the project is over budget and behind plan.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. If the project keeps performing at its current cost efficiency, what total cost is it now forecast to reach by completion?
questions.explanation: CPI = EV / AC = 200,000 / 250,000 = 0.80. Assuming that efficiency continues, EAC = BAC / CPI = 500,000 / 0.80 = $625,000 — a forecast $125,000 overrun. $550,000 and $450,000 do not follow from the CPI, and $500,000 is the original BAC, which ignores the cost performance to date.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. The sponsor wants delivery within the original $500,000 budget. What cost efficiency (TCPI) must the remaining work achieve, and is that reasonable?
choices: TCPI = 0.80; the team can simply continue at its current pace.
TCPI = 1.00; no change in performance is required.
TCPI = 1.20; the team must become markedly more efficient than its 0.80 to date, so re-baselining should be discussed.
TCPI cannot be determined from the data provided.
questions.explanation: TCPI to the BAC = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = (500,000 - 200,000) / (500,000 - 250,000) = 300,000 / 250,000 = 1.20. Having performed at CPI 0.80, the team would have to jump to 1.20 efficiency for all remaining work — rarely realistic, so the PM should surface a forecast/re-baseline conversation rather than promise the original budget. TCPI 0.80/1.00 misread the formula, and the data are sufficient to compute it.

questions.question: With EV = $45,000 and PV = $50,000, what is the schedule performance index (SPI), and how is it interpreted?
choices: 0.90; less work completed than planned — an EVM schedule-performance indicator of being behind plan.
1.11; dividing planned value by earned value suggests the project is running ahead of plan.
0.90; the ratio shows the project is over budget rather than behind on schedule.
1.00; earned and planned value are effectively balanced, so the project is on plan.
questions.explanation: SPI = EV/PV = 45,000/50,000 = 0.90, below 1, so less value was earned than planned — behind plan. Reading it as a cost indicator (C) is the closest miss — the 0.90 is right, but SPI reflects schedule performance in value terms, not budget; inverting the ratio yields the spurious 1.11, and 1.00 ignores the gap between EV and PV. Closest distractor: (C) — correct number, wrong dimension.

questions.question: A project has BAC = $200,000 and a current CPI = 0.80. If current cost performance is expected to continue, what is the estimate at completion (EAC)?
questions.explanation: When current variances are expected to continue, EAC = BAC/CPI = 200,000/0.80 = $250,000. Closest distractor: (A) $160,000 — multiplies BAC by CPI instead of dividing, turning an overrun into a saving; $200,000 is the untouched BAC, and $240,000 follows no standard EVM formula.

questions.question: A project has BAC = $400,000, AC = $150,000, and EV = $120,000. If the remaining work will proceed at the planned (budgeted) rate, what is the EAC?
questions.explanation: When the remaining work is expected at the budgeted rate, EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) = 150,000 + (400,000 - 120,000) = $430,000. Closest distractor: (C) $500,000 — that is EAC = BAC/CPI (CPI = 120/150 = 0.80), which assumes the current overrun continues; here the remaining work is expected at the budgeted rate, so the atypical-variance formula applies instead.

questions.question: A PM sets aside funds inside the cost baseline to cover identified risks that have planned responses, and can draw on them without executive approval. What are these funds?
choices: Contingency reserve.
Management reserve.
Budget at completion.
Cost baseline.
questions.explanation: Contingency reserve covers identified risks with planned responses, sits inside the cost baseline, and the PM can generally draw on it without executive approval. Management reserve (B) is the closest miss — it is also a reserve, but it covers unforeseen work, sits outside the cost baseline, and needs management approval to release; budget at completion and the cost baseline are total-budget containers, not the risk reserve. Closest distractor: (B) — the other reserve, distinguished by location and approval authority.

questions.question: Partway through a refinery upgrade, the team hits a subsurface condition no one had foreseen; the added work is within the project's scope but its cost was never part of the cost baseline. To fund it from the management reserve, what is normally required?
choices: The project manager may commit the funds directly as the accountable budget owner.
Management or governance approval to release the funds into the cost baseline.
The cost is first absorbed from the contingency reserve set aside for identified risks.
No approval is needed, since the added work still falls within the project's scope.
questions.explanation: Management reserve covers unforeseen but in-scope work and is controlled by management, so releasing it into the cost baseline normally requires management or governance approval. PM discretion (A) or spending without approval (D) misstate that control, and drawing from contingency (C) misapplies a reserve meant for identified, analyzed risks. Closest distractor: (C) — pulling from contingency looks convenient, but an unforeseen condition is exactly what management reserve, not contingency, exists to fund.

questions.question: The same defect keeps recurring in a deliverable. To improve quality at its source, what should the PM do?
choices: Strengthen final inspection so the recurring defect is caught before delivery.
Rework each failed unit and re-verify it against the quality specification.
Perform root-cause analysis and improve the process to prevent the defect.
Raise the recurring defect to the quality manager for a formal review.
questions.explanation: Building quality in means removing the cause so the defect stops recurring, not managing its symptoms downstream. Stronger inspection only detects it, reworking failed units fixes instances one at a time, and escalating reports the problem without correcting the process.

questions.question: The cost of preventing and appraising quality, plus the cost of internal and external failures, together represent what?
choices: The cost baseline.
The total cost of ownership.
The contingency reserve.
The cost of quality.
questions.explanation: Cost of quality sums the cost of conformance (prevention and appraisal) and the cost of nonconformance (internal and external failure). The cost baseline is the time-phased budget, contingency reserve funds known risks, and total cost of ownership spans the asset's whole lifecycle. Closest distractor: (B) — total cost of ownership also aggregates costs, but over the product's operational life rather than the prevention-appraisal-failure set defined here.

questions.question: A deliverable meets its internal specification, but a required regulation was overlooked in the quality plan. What should the PM do?
choices: Ensure the regulatory requirement is incorporated and the deliverable meets it before acceptance.
Accept the deliverable now since it satisfies the agreed internal specification.
Log the missed regulation as a lesson learned and proceed to acceptance.
Ask the customer to formally waive the regulation to protect the schedule.
questions.explanation: A required regulation is mandatory and must be built in and met before acceptance; compliance is not traded against schedule or waived by a customer. Meeting the internal spec does not satisfy the missed regulation, and merely logging a lesson leaves a noncompliant deliverable. Closest distractor: (B) — passing the internal specification feels like done, but an overlooked legal requirement still blocks acceptance.

questions.question: To drive ongoing quality improvement on an adaptive team, which practice is MOST effective?
choices: Conducting a thorough quality audit once the final release is delivered.
Using retrospectives to inspect and adapt the process each iteration.
Measuring quality metrics only at each formal release milestone.
Delegating all quality responsibility to a dedicated QA department.
questions.explanation: Retrospectives operationalize continuous improvement by inspecting and adapting the process every iteration, so problems are corrected while the work is still in flight. A final audit, release-only measurement, or an isolated QA department all delay learning and separate quality from the team that produces it.

questions.question: Which statement BEST distinguishes quality assurance from quality control?
choices: Quality assurance inspects finished deliverables; quality control refines the underlying processes.
Quality control prevents defects up front; quality assurance detects them afterward.
Quality assurance improves the processes that create quality; quality control inspects deliverables to detect defects.
Quality assurance and quality control are interchangeable labels for the same inspection.
questions.explanation: Quality assurance is process-focused and preventive; quality control is product-focused and detective through inspection. The reversed pairings swap those roles, and treating the two as identical erases the prevention-versus-detection distinction. Closest distractor: (A) — it keeps the correct parallel structure but reverses which discipline inspects and which improves processes.

questions.question: Stakeholders have not clearly stated their quality expectations for a deliverable. What should the PM do FIRST?
choices: Apply industry-standard quality levels and assume they will satisfy the stakeholders.
Set the highest achievable quality for the deliverable regardless of the need.
Postpone quality planning until the deliverable reaches the testing phase.
Gather quality requirements from stakeholders and standards, and translate them into measurable criteria.
questions.explanation: Fitness for purpose is defined by eliciting quality requirements from stakeholders and standards and making them measurable before design or testing. Assuming a default standard, maximizing quality beyond the need (gold-plating), or deferring the planning all risk building the wrong quality. Closest distractor: (A) — an industry standard sounds safe and efficient, but it substitutes an assumption for the stakeholders' actual quality needs.

questions.question: The team proposes adding several extra features beyond the requirements to 'exceed expectations.' How should the PM recognize this?
choices: As gold-plating, which adds cost and risk without agreed value.
As value-added delivery that should be encouraged and rewarded.
As continuous improvement that enhances the overall product quality.
As part of confirming the deliverable meets its acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Adding features nobody requested is gold-plating: it consumes effort and introduces risk without any agreed increase in value. Genuine value delivery is driven by prioritized stakeholder requirements, and acceptance is judged against agreed criteria, not extra scope. Closest distractor: (B) — 'exceeding expectations' is framed as value, but unrequested scope is cost and risk the customer never agreed to.

questions.question: An activity has ES = 5, EF = 10, LS = 8, and LF = 13 (in days). What is its total float, and what does it mean?
choices: 0 days; the activity lies on the critical path with no slack.
3 days; the activity can slip 3 days without delaying the project.
5 days; the activity's duration equals its available slack.
8 days; the difference between LF and ES gives the float.
questions.explanation: Total float = LS − ES = 8 − 5 = 3 days (equivalently LF − EF = 13 − 10 = 3), so the activity can slip three days without moving the project finish. Zero would mean it is critical, while 5 and 8 come from subtracting the wrong pair of dates. Closest distractor: (C) — 5 equals EF − ES, the activity's duration, which is easily mistaken for its float.

questions.question: Using a three-point (PERT beta) estimate with Optimistic = 10, Most Likely = 15, and Pessimistic = 26 days, what is the expected duration?
choices: 15 days.
17 days.
16 days.
18 days.
questions.explanation: Expected duration = (O + 4M + P)/6 = (10 + 60 + 26)/6 = 96/6 = 16 days, weighting the most likely value four times. The simple average of the three points gives 17, the most likely alone gives 15, and the optimistic-pessimistic midpoint gives 18. Closest distractor: (B) — 17 is the plain three-number average, which drops the beta weighting on the most likely estimate.

questions.question: A hospital's IT team is three weeks behind on a system rollout tied to an immovable go-live date. To recover, the PM funds weekend overtime and assigns extra developers to the longest tasks on the critical path, absorbing the added labor cost. Which schedule-compression technique has the PM applied?
choices: Fast tracking, overlapping activities that were planned to run in sequence.
Resource leveling, rescheduling work to resolve resource over-allocation.
Resource smoothing, adjusting activities within their available float.
Crashing, adding resources to critical activities at higher cost.
questions.explanation: Crashing shortens the schedule by adding resources to critical-path work, accepting higher cost for a faster finish. Fast tracking compresses by overlapping activities rather than spending more, and leveling and smoothing rearrange resource use without buying speed. Closest distractor: (A) — fast tracking is the other compression technique, but it overlaps sequential work instead of adding resources at higher cost.

questions.question: To pull a product launch forward, a PM directs the team to begin production coding for a module while its interface design is still under review, rather than waiting for design sign-off. What is the MAIN risk this fast-tracking introduces?
choices: It guarantees a larger direct-cost increase than any other compression method.
Rework rises because dependent work starts before its predecessor finishes.
It reduces the delivered scope by dropping planned features.
It has little downside provided enough resources are made available.
questions.explanation: Fast tracking overlaps work that was meant to be sequential, so the successor starts before its predecessor is finalized and later changes force rework and added coordination. Crashing, not fast tracking, is the cost-heavy technique; fast tracking neither reduces scope nor is risk-free. Closest distractor: (A) — added cost is a real concern, but that is crashing's signature, and 'always more than any other option' overstates it.

questions.question: An adaptive team wants to estimate upcoming work by relative sizing rather than fixed hours. What BEST supports this?
choices: Story points reflecting relative effort, complexity, and uncertainty.
Fixed hour estimates assigned to each individual task.
Deadlines imposed by management for every backlog item.
A fully baselined predictive schedule for the release.
questions.explanation: Story points express size as relative effort, complexity, and uncertainty, which suits adaptive estimating and team-based relative sizing. Fixed hours and a baselined schedule are absolute, predictive constructs, and imposed deadlines are targets rather than estimates. Closest distractor: (B) — fixed hours are also an estimate, but they are absolute rather than the relative sizing the team wants.

questions.question: After the schedule baseline is set, analysis shows the critical path has shifted because an activity slipped. What should the PM do?
choices: Disregard the shift as long as float still remains elsewhere in the network.
Rebaseline the schedule right away without seeking formal change approval.
Analyze the schedule variation and take corrective action to protect the finish date.
Extend every activity's duration to build in a safety buffer.
questions.explanation: A shifted critical path is a schedule variance to analyze so corrective action can protect the completion date. Ignoring it because float exists elsewhere misses that the critical path drives the finish; rebaselining without approval bypasses change control, and padding every activity inflates the schedule. Closest distractor: (A) — float elsewhere is reassuring, but slack off the critical path does not protect the finish date the slipped activity now threatens.

questions.question: A new project has limited detail, but records from several similar past projects are available. Which estimating technique fits BEST for an early schedule estimate?
choices: Bottom-up estimating built from a full work decomposition.
Three-point estimating applied to the still-undefined work.
Parametric modeling without any reliable rate data.
Analogous estimating using historical data from the similar projects.
questions.explanation: Analogous estimating uses historical data from similar past projects to produce an early, high-level estimate when little detail exists. Bottom-up needs a full decomposition and parametric needs reliable rate data, neither of which is available this early. Closest distractor: (A) — bottom-up is more accurate, but it cannot be built without the detailed decomposition the project does not yet have.

questions.question: While developing the schedule, the PM finds the project depends on a deliverable from another program. What is the BEST action?
choices: Coordinate with the other program to align the dependency and integrate its milestone into the schedule.
Assume the other program will hit its date and plan around it.
Remove the external dependency from the schedule to keep it clean.
Escalate the dependency to the sponsor before attempting any coordination.
questions.explanation: A dependency on another program's deliverable is coordinated across the programs and its milestone integrated into the schedule so the interface is planned, not assumed. Assuming the other program's date, deleting the dependency, or escalating before any coordination all ignore a real external constraint. Closest distractor: (D) — escalation may follow, but the PM coordinates the interface first rather than handing it up unexamined.

questions.question: To assess progress objectively on a predictive project, on what should the PM rely?
choices: The percentage of scheduled tasks the team reports as finished so far.
Earned value and other agreed metrics compared against the baseline.
The count of activities currently shown as in progress on the board.
The team's and sponsor's shared sense of how far along the work feels.
questions.explanation: Objective progress on a predictive project relies on agreed metrics such as earned value measured against the baseline. Percent-complete self-reports, in-progress counts, and shared impressions capture perception or activity rather than verified progress against plan.

questions.question: An adaptive team wants a simple visual to forecast whether the remaining work will finish by the target date. Which is MOST useful?
choices: A Gantt chart laying out the planned activities and their dependencies.
A velocity chart of story points the team completed in each past iteration.
A burndown or burnup chart showing remaining work against time.
A defect trend chart of issues found and resolved over time.
questions.explanation: A burndown or burnup chart plots remaining or completed work against time, giving a simple forecast of completion. A Gantt suits predictive scheduling, a defect trend tracks quality, and velocity shows past throughput as an input rather than remaining work against the target date. Closest distractor: (B) — velocity feeds the forecast but is not itself the completion-versus-date visual.

questions.question: The PM realizes different stakeholders need different artifacts to understand status. What is the BEST action?
choices: Produce a single standard status artifact and distribute it to everyone.
Generate the full set of possible artifacts so no audience is left out.
Replace the written artifacts with regular live briefings for all groups.
Identify each audience's information needs and tailor the artifacts to them.
questions.explanation: Matching artifacts to each audience's information needs is both efficient and effective. A single standard artifact under- or over-informs some audiences, producing every possible artifact wastes effort, and live briefings alone leave no shared record.

questions.question: To keep project artifacts useful throughout delivery, what should the PM ensure?
choices: Artifacts are created, reviewed, updated, and kept accessible as the project evolves.
Artifacts are finalized during planning and then kept stable to avoid churn.
Artifacts are archived soon after creation to keep the workspace uncluttered.
Artifact access is limited to the PM to protect version control.
questions.explanation: Useful artifacts are living — created, reviewed, updated, and kept accessible so they support decisions as the project changes. Freezing them at planning, archiving them early, or restricting access all erode their value.

questions.question: Metrics show the team's velocity declining over three iterations. What should the PM do FIRST?
choices: Encourage the team to raise their pace so the velocity number recovers quickly.
Measure and analyze the trend, investigate causes with the team, and adjust the approach.
Treat the three-iteration dip as normal variation and keep the current plan unchanged.
Adjust the team's composition, swapping in stronger members to lift the velocity numbers.
questions.explanation: A declining trend is a signal to measure, analyze, and diagnose the cause with the team before acting. Pushing for a faster pace or changing membership treats a symptom, and dismissing it as normal variation ignores real information. Closest distractor: (A) — urging faster work feels responsive but skips the diagnosis the trend calls for.

questions.question: To communicate status effectively to a busy executive sponsor, what should the PM provide?
choices: A complete export of every project metric for full transparency.
The full detailed technical report so that nothing is left out.
A concise summary of status, key risks, and decisions needed.
A carefully framed update that emphasizes progress to keep confidence high.
questions.explanation: Executive reporting is concise and decision-focused — status, key risks, and decisions needed. A full metric export or detailed technical report overwhelms a busy sponsor, and framing that filters to good news misleads them.

questions.question: The PM finds that the current reporting produces artifacts almost no one reads. What should the PM do?
choices: Continue producing the reports to satisfy the standing reporting requirement.
Discontinue the reporting entirely to free up the team's time.
Add further reports to broaden coverage and improve transparency.
Assess the effectiveness of the artifacts and adjust what is produced.
questions.explanation: Continually assessing artifact effectiveness lets the PM prune low-value reporting while preserving needed transparency. Producing unread reports for compliance wastes effort, stopping all reporting loses visibility, and adding more compounds the overload. Closest distractor: (A) — meeting a standing requirement feels safe but keeps generating artifacts no one uses.

questions.question: A project's deliverables are complete and have been verified against their requirements. What is required to formally close the project?
choices: Reassign the team to the next project now that deliverables are accepted.
Obtain formal stakeholder approval of completion and complete the closure activities.
Archive the project files and records without a lessons-learned review.
Hold closure open until finance formally closes out the project budget.
questions.explanation: Formal closure requires the authorized stakeholders' acceptance of completion plus the closure activities such as lessons learned and handover; verified deliverables are not the same as a formally closed project. Reassigning the team first, skipping the lessons review, or holding closure for finance all leave the project improperly closed. Closest distractor: (A) — verified deliverables invite moving on, but closure is not complete without formal acceptance of completion and the closure activities.

questions.question: Before closing a phase, what should the PM confirm?
choices: The criteria defined to close the phase have been met.
The budget allocated to the phase has been fully spent.
Every risk logged against the phase has been fully closed.
The team is available and ready to start the next phase.
questions.explanation: Confirming that the defined phase-closure (exit) criteria have been met is what verifies the phase is genuinely complete. Full budget spend, an empty risk register, and team availability are not phase-closure criteria.

questions.question: At closure, the product must be handed to the operations team. What is the BEST action?
choices: Transfer the product to operations and let them establish their own support.
Keep the project team in place to run the product for operations.
Validate transition readiness — documentation, training, and support handover — before closing.
Postpone the handover until every foreseeable operational issue is resolved.
questions.explanation: Validating transition readiness — documentation, training, and support handover — ensures operations can sustain the product before the project closes. A hand-off without support, indefinite project-team ownership, or waiting for zero residual risk are all inappropriate. Closest distractor: (A) — transferring and letting operations build their own support completes the handover but skips the readiness check that makes it sustainable.

questions.question: Several closure activities are on the checklist. Which one BEST helps future projects benefit from this project's experience?
choices: Filing the final status report and formally closing out the budget.
Settling all outstanding vendor invoices and contract payments.
Releasing the team members promptly to their next assignments.
Conducting a final lessons-learned review and updating organizational process assets.
questions.explanation: Conducting a final lessons-learned review and updating organizational process assets carries this project's knowledge to future projects. Final reporting, vendor settlement, and resource release are legitimate closure tasks but transfer no learning.

questions.question: A sponsor terminates a project early, before completion. What should the PM do?
choices: Still perform proper closure — document status, capture lessons, and release resources in an orderly way.
Skip the closure steps entirely, since a canceled project will never deliver its intended product.
Keep the team working to finish the original deliverables despite the sponsor's termination.
Use the final report primarily to document who was responsible for the cancellation.
questions.explanation: Even a terminated project needs proper closure — documented status, captured lessons, and orderly resource release. Skipping closure loses value, continuing after termination wastes effort, and using the report to assign blame is inappropriate.

questions.question: To confirm the project delivered its intended benefits, what should closure include?
choices: A financial reconciliation of actual costs against the approved project budget.
Confirming acceptance and establishing how benefits will be measured and owned after handover, verifying any already realized against the objectives.
A team retrospective and celebration to formally mark the project's ending.
Prompt archiving of all project records without a closure review.
questions.explanation: Many benefits accrue after the project ends, so closure verifies the benefits realized so far and hands off the metrics and ownership for measuring the rest against the objectives. A purely financial reconciliation, a celebration, or archiving without review each omit that benefits handoff. Closest distractor: (A) — cost reconciliation is a real closure task but measures spend, not benefit realization or its post-project ownership.

questions.question: A project manager takes over a cross-functional initiative where routine decisions stall for days because no one is sure who has authority to approve what. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Approve the stalled decisions yourself for the moment so delivery keeps moving, then work out separately who actually holds the authority to decide.
Work with the sponsor and PMO to establish a governance structure — decision rights, thresholds, escalation paths, and reporting — drawing on applicable organizational process assets.
Route each stalled decision to the sponsor as it comes up so that a person with clear delegated authority makes the call.
Ask the cross-functional team to agree among themselves on which individual member should own and approve each type of routine decision.
questions.explanation: The gap is missing governance, so establishing decision rights, thresholds, escalation paths, and reporting (tailored from OPAs) with the sponsor and PMO removes the cause. Approving personally or sending every item to the sponsor treats the symptom, and an informal team agreement lacks organizational authority. Closest distractor: (C) — routing each decision to the sponsor yields authoritative answers but institutionalizes the bottleneck instead of fixing the structure.

questions.question: During planning, a steering committee asks how the project's success will be judged. The project already has schedule and cost baselines. What should the project manager ensure is defined?
choices: Schedule and cost performance targets, since meeting the funded baselines is what the committee will use to judge success.
The final acceptance criteria for each deliverable, so conformance to the agreed specification can be formally confirmed at handover.
Customer satisfaction survey results gathered at closeout, taken as the overall measure of whether the project succeeded.
A balanced set of success measures spanning delivery, product/quality, and business benefits, agreed with stakeholders and tied to the objectives.
questions.explanation: Governance judges success against objectives, outcomes, benefits, and value, so a balanced set of measures spanning delivery, product quality, and business benefits should be agreed up front. Schedule and cost targets are a real but partial view, deliverable acceptance criteria address conformance, and a single closeout survey measures only one facet. Closest distractor: (A) — schedule and cost targets are genuine success measures but capture only delivery, missing product quality and business value.

questions.question: A funding decision on the project exceeds the cost threshold delegated to the project manager under the governance framework. Stakeholders are pressing for a fast answer. What is the BEST action?
choices: Route the decision through the defined escalation path to the authority holding the delegated approval rights.
Approve the funding within the project team so the work can keep pace with the stakeholders' pressure.
Break the funding into smaller tranches that each stay under your own delegated approval threshold.
Hold the decision for the next scheduled steering-committee meeting to keep it on the agenda.
questions.explanation: A funding decision above the delegated threshold belongs to the authorized decision-maker and is routed through the governance escalation path, which can carry an expedited route for urgency. Approving it within the team or splitting the amount to stay under the limit circumvents governance, and holding it for the next meeting ignores the pressing timeline. Closest distractor: (C) — tranching keeps the work moving but is deliberate threshold-dodging.

questions.question: At a phase-gate review, the project is on schedule and on budget, but market data now shows the business case that justified the project no longer holds. What is the MOST appropriate outcome to support?
choices: Continue the project as planned, since it is on schedule and on budget and meeting all approved baselines at this gate.
Rebaseline the schedule and cost estimates to reflect the new market data, then continue delivering the original scope as approved.
Present the changed business case at the gate so decision-makers can choose to continue, continue with modification, or end the project.
Pause the project and hold all remaining work until the market recovers enough to restore the original business case.
questions.explanation: A phase gate weighs the project against its business case and can decide continue, continue-with-modification, or end — so a project meeting cost and schedule can still be stopped when its value has evaporated. Staying on baseline performance ignores the lost justification, rebaselining fixes numbers that are no longer the problem, and an open-ended pause is not the gate body's call to make unilaterally. Closest distractor: (A) — on-baseline performance feels like success, but value, not variance, drives the gate decision.

questions.question: A team argues that because the project uses an adaptive approach it needs only lightweight governance. The product is subject to contractual and regulatory obligations. How should the project manager respond?
choices: Agree with the team, since an adaptive approach inherently calls for lighter governance than a predictive one would.
Apply the organization's full predictive governance process to the team unchanged so the regulatory obligations are certainly met.
Refer the governance question to the steering committee and let them determine the appropriate level of rigor later.
Apply governance rigor based on the contractual, regulatory, risk, and organizational requirements — the development approach alone does not set it.
questions.explanation: Governance rigor is set by contractual, regulatory, risk, and funding requirements, not by the delivery approach; an adaptive project under regulatory obligations can still demand formal governance, with the approach tailoring the mechanisms rather than the obligation. Conceding that adaptive means lighter, imposing the full predictive process wholesale, or deferring a known obligation all misread this. Closest distractor: (B) — full predictive governance does honor the obligations, but it over-controls the adaptive work instead of tailoring the mechanisms to fit it.

questions.question: A team member states that the sponsor 'owns the business case and personally secures all project funding,' and asks the project manager to escalate a funding shortfall to the sponsor on that basis. How should the project manager characterize the sponsor's role?
choices: The sponsor provides resources and support and is accountable for enabling project success; specific funding and decision authority depend on the organization's governance.
The sponsor alone is solely responsible for personally obtaining every single dollar of funding the project will ever need throughout its entire life.
The sponsor owns the business case and therefore personally holds approval authority over every change and scope decision on the project.
The sponsor's involvement is limited to signing the project charter at initiation and does not extend meaningfully beyond that early point.
questions.explanation: The sponsor supplies resources and support and is accountable for enabling success, while specific funding and decision authority are defined by the organization's governance — not a blanket rule that the sponsor personally raises every dollar or approves every change. Reducing the role to charter-signing understates it just as badly as the over-broad claims. Closest distractor: (C) — sponsors often do weigh in on major changes, but change authority is set by governance, not by owning the business case.

questions.question: To speed up analysis, the team wants to upload customer personal data into a third-party AI service. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Assess whether sending that data to the service complies with applicable data-privacy law, contracts, and organizational policy before any data is shared.
Approve the upload, since the faster analysis clearly benefits the project and the customer is expecting quick results from the team.
Permit the upload provided the data is fully anonymized by the team before any of it leaves the organization's environment.
Prohibit the use of any external AI service on this project because customer personal data is involved throughout the work.
questions.explanation: Sending customer personal data to an external AI service triggers data-privacy, contractual, and regulatory obligations that must be checked before any data leaves the organization. Approving for speed skips that check, a blanket prohibition overstates the constraint rather than assessing it, and anonymizing first still needs the compliance assessment to confirm the technique and the transfer are actually permitted. Closest distractor: (C) — anonymization is a sound safeguard, but validating compliance is the prerequisite first step, not a substitute for it.

questions.question: A project manager has compiled a long list of legal, contractual, and organizational compliance requirements. To manage them effectively, what should the project manager do NEXT?
choices: Classify the requirements by source and by the severity of noncompliance, then plan and prioritize accordingly.
Treat every requirement on the list as equally critical so that none of them is ever overlooked.
Address the legal requirements first and defer the contractual and organizational obligations for a later date.
Assign the whole list to a single compliance owner to track and report on centrally.
questions.explanation: Classifying the requirements by source and by severity of noncompliance turns a raw list into a prioritized, manageable set. Treating all as equally critical spreads effort thin, deferring contractual and organizational obligations is unsafe because they can exceed the legal minimum, and handing the list to one owner without classifying it still leaves the work unprioritized. Closest distractor: (D) — a single accountable owner helps, but it organizes ownership rather than the prioritization the requirements actually need.

questions.question: The project manager must decide how much effort to invest in a particular compliance area. What BEST informs that decision?
choices: The direct cost of performing the compliance activities themselves within the current project budget.
Whether competitors in the same market currently comply with this identical requirement or not.
The consequences of noncompliance — legal, financial, safety, operational, and reputational exposure for this project.
The team's remaining capacity in the current iteration to absorb the additional compliance work.
questions.explanation: Sizing the exposure from noncompliance — legal, financial, safety, operational, and reputational — is what justifies the level of effort. The cost of compliance alone ignores the far larger downside, competitor behavior does not define this project's obligations, and iteration capacity is a delivery constraint rather than the basis for the decision. Closest distractor: (A) — compliance cost is a real input, but effort should be driven by the consequence of getting it wrong, not the price of getting it right.

questions.question: Midway through execution, a newly effective regulation now applies to the project's product. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Continue operating under the requirements that were in effect when the project first started, to protect the approved baseline and avoid rework.
Submit a formal change request to add the new compliance scope before analyzing how the regulation actually affects the project's work, plans, and deliverables.
Ask the organization's legal department to handle the new regulation entirely on its own, without involving the project team or its plans.
Assess how the new regulation affects the project and determine the actions needed to meet it, routing any resulting changes through the applicable process.
questions.explanation: The first move is to assess how the new regulation affects the project and determine the actions to meet it, then route any changes through the applicable change and governance process. Continuing under the old rules risks noncompliance, filing a change request before assessing impact is premature, and offloading it entirely to legal ignores the project's own required actions. Closest distractor: (B) — a change request is likely needed, but only after the impact assessment defines what that change should contain.

questions.question: Governance asks the project manager to demonstrate how well the project is actually meeting its compliance obligations. What is the BEST way to answer?
choices: Provide the team's written assurance that they have followed all of the applicable requirements to date.
Report that no compliance complaints or audit findings have been raised on the project so far.
Report objective measures — audit results, verification pass rates, and percentage of requirements verified against a traceability matrix.
Commit to conducting a full compliance review during project closeout and report the findings to governance then.
questions.explanation: Compliance is demonstrated with objective evidence — audit results, verification pass rates, and traceability of requirements — not with assurances or the absence of complaints. Verbal assurance is unverified, no findings so far is not proof of coverage, and a closeout-only review leaves gaps undetected while the project is still running. Closest distractor: (B) — a clean record so far sounds reassuring, but absence of findings measures nothing about how much has actually been verified.

questions.question: A government software project must obtain an independent security accreditation before it can legally go live, but the launch date is now at risk. A program lead proposes going live on schedule and completing the accreditation afterward. What should the project manager do?
choices: Keep the mandatory accreditation and resolve the launch-date conflict through the applicable compliance, planning, and governance process.
Weigh the schedule gained against the accreditation and decide whether skipping it this once is worthwhile.
Go live on the target date and complete the accreditation retroactively if an auditor later requires it.
Let the sponsoring agency decide whether it would prefer an on-time launch over completed accreditation work.
questions.explanation: A mandatory security accreditation is a compliance boundary, not a schedule trade-off; keep it and address the launch-date conflict through the applicable compliance, planning, and governance process. Treating it as a cost-benefit call, going live and accrediting later, or letting the agency choose speed over accreditation all expose the project to serious legal and security consequences. Closest distractor: (B) — framing it as a trade-off feels like diligent analysis, but a mandatory obligation is not one of the variables available to trade.

questions.question: On a predictive bridge-rehabilitation project, the client's operations director asks the project manager to add a drainage upgrade that would extend the work and raise its cost. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Assess the request's impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, and risk, then route it through change control.
Begin the drainage upgrade promptly so the client's operations director sees the project team as responsive and cooperative.
Decline the request outright to keep the approved scope, schedule, and cost baselines fully intact and protected.
Authorize the upgrade if its estimated cost happens to fit within the project's available contingency reserve.
questions.explanation: A change to a controlled baseline is first assessed for impact across scope, schedule, cost, quality, and risk, then decided through the project's change control process. Starting the work or refusing it without analysis both bypass that process, and contingency reserve funds responses to identified risks — it is not a discretionary budget for approving new scope. Closest distractor: (D) — checking the reserve feels financially responsible, but reserve is not the mechanism for authorizing an unassessed scope addition.

questions.question: After the change control board approves a request to revise a subsystem's interface specification, the project manager turns to carrying it out. What is the correct NEXT step?
choices: Refresh every project baseline and document so that all records remain fully synchronized after the change.
Preserve the original baselines for reference and track the approved change on a separate side log.
Hold the updates until stakeholders notice the change and ask for the revised project documents themselves.
Implement the change and update the plans, documents, and baselines it actually affects, then verify.
questions.explanation: An approved change is implemented and reflected only in the artifacts it actually affects, then verified — approval does not automatically alter every baseline. Refreshing all baselines reflexively, retaining stale originals in parallel, or waiting for stakeholders to prompt the update each breaks the plan's integrity. Closest distractor: (A) — synchronizing records is the right instinct, but updating every baseline regardless of relevance introduces churn instead of controlled, targeted updates.

questions.question: During execution, several small changes were accepted directly by team members and never recorded, and the documentation no longer matches what was built. What should the project manager do?
choices: Leave the accepted changes undocumented, since each one on its own was individually minor and low-impact to the overall work.
Reverse all of the undocumented changes to restore the originally approved baseline exactly as it stood before execution began.
Assess the undocumented changes, take each through the change control process for a disposition, reinforce the process with the team, and update baselines and documents only for approved changes.
Add every one of the accepted changes to the baseline retroactively without first assessing their individual impact or value.
questions.explanation: Small uncontrolled additions are scope creep, and the fix is not merely to document them after the fact: assess each change, take it through change control for a disposition (accept, reject, or defer), reinforce the process with the team, and update the baselines only for changes that are approved. Leaving them undocumented perpetuates the drift; reversing valuable work blindly wastes effort; adding every change to the baseline retroactively without assessment legitimizes the bypass. Closest distractor: (D) — retroactively baselining without assessing impact rubber-stamps the very changes that skipped control.

questions.question: A change request has been under review for a week, and several stakeholders keep asking the project manager when it will be decided. What is the BEST response?
choices: Approve the change ahead of the review to put an end to the repeated questions coming from the stakeholders.
Tell stakeholders the decision will come once it is made and offer no further detail in the meantime.
Update only the person who originally submitted the change request and leave the other stakeholders uninformed for now.
Communicate the current status of the change through the change log and regular reporting until a decision is reached.
questions.explanation: Change status is kept visible through the change log and regular reporting so stakeholders are not left chasing the decision. Rushing approval to silence the questions undermines the process, offering no detail erodes trust, and updating only the original requester leaves other affected stakeholders in the dark. Closest distractor: (B) — it is honest that the decision is pending, but withholding status and detail is the opposite of transparent change communication.

questions.question: On an adaptive project, a stakeholder wants to change the priority of features for the upcoming iteration, and the change affects only work the team has not yet started. How is this BEST handled?
choices: Through a formal change control board, exactly as a predictive project would process such a request.
By reprioritizing the product backlog with the product owner before the next iteration, within that role's authority.
By declining the change because the plan for the upcoming iteration is already agreed with the team.
By interrupting the active iteration to build the newly prioritized feature ahead of the committed work.
questions.explanation: Reprioritizing not-yet-started work is handled through backlog reprioritization with the product owner, within that role's authority — formal change control is reserved for controlled baselines, contracts, or funding. A change board is unnecessary overhead here, declining contradicts the responsiveness adaptive delivery is built for, and disrupting the active iteration violates the protection the iteration is meant to have. Closest distractor: (A) — invoking change control looks disciplined, but applying predictive governance to backlog reprioritization misreads how adaptive work absorbs change.

questions.question: A proposed change would deliver clear customer value but conflicts with a regulatory constraint the product must satisfy. What should the project manager do?
choices: Evaluate the change against the constraint and reject or adjust it so the product remains compliant, involving the appropriate authority as needed.
Approve the change on the strength of its clear customer value, and log the regulatory conflict in the risk register as an accepted risk.
Fast-track the change into the current release and pursue a formal regulatory exemption from the authority in parallel.
Refer the change to the sponsor for a decision, since weighing value against compliance exceeds the project manager's authority.
questions.explanation: Change evaluation weighs value against constraints such as compliance; where they conflict, the change is adjusted or rejected to keep the product compliant, involving the appropriate authority on any exemption. Closest distractor: (C) - pursuing an exemption in parallel looks proactive, but shipping the change before the conflict is resolved risks a noncompliant product.

questions.question: A construction project manager is assembling a change request for a design revision proposed by a subcontractor, so the change control board can decide at its next meeting. What is the MOST important item to include?
choices: The name and role of the subcontractor who first proposed the design revision.
The date the change was logged, along with its current position and status in the project's change log.
A documented analysis of how the revision would affect scope, schedule, cost, quality, and risk.
How much support the proposed revision currently has among the site crew and trade supervisors.
questions.explanation: Decision-makers need the change's assessed impact across scope, schedule, cost, quality, and risk to choose well. The requester's identity, the log position, and crew sentiment are administrative details, not the basis for the decision.

questions.question: A product-launch team cannot proceed because the legal review it depends on sits with the corporate legal group, which the project manager has no authority over, and the delay is stalling the launch. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Move the blocked launch tasks into a later phase and continue with other available work in the meantime.
Engage the legal group's lead to coordinate the review's timing and clear the impediment for the team.
Allow the legal group to complete its review on its own schedule and revisit the launch date afterward.
Have the team proceed without the completed review and adjust the deliverable later if legal raises objections.
questions.explanation: Clearing impediments - here by coordinating with the group that owns the dependency - is core project-manager work. Deferring the tasks, deferring to the group's own schedule, or proceeding without the review leave the team blocked or invite rework.

questions.question: Several impediments surface at once and the project manager has limited time to address them. What is the BEST way to proceed?
choices: Prioritize the impediments by their impact on the team's progress and value delivery, then address the most damaging first.
Work through the impediments in the order they were originally reported so that none of them is overlooked or forgotten.
Clear the quickest impediments first to demonstrate visible early progress to the team and stakeholders.
Escalate all of the impediments to management at once so they can be resolved together in parallel.
questions.explanation: Impediments are sized by impact and urgency so the most damaging blockers are cleared first. Order-of-arrival and ease-first ignore impact, and mass escalation skips the project manager's own triage.

questions.question: On a data-migration project, a risk the team had logged and been monitoring - that a legacy interface might fail during cutover - has just materialized and is now disrupting the cutover. How should the project manager handle it?
choices: Continue managing it as an open, uncertain risk within the risk register, since the team had already identified and been actively tracking it.
Treat it as an issue now, execute the planned response, and update the risk register to reflect the occurrence and residual risk.
Remove the entry from the risk register now that the outcome has become certain rather than uncertain.
Escalate the situation to the sponsor because a tracked risk was permitted to occur despite the monitoring.
questions.explanation: A materialized risk becomes a current issue: manage it through issue management, execute the planned response, and update - not delete - the risk register for status and any residual or secondary risk. Closest distractor: (A) - it was identified, so leaving it 'open' feels right, but once it has occurred it is no longer uncertain and must move to issue management.

questions.question: An issue cuts across several stakeholder groups, and no single person has the authority or knowledge to resolve it alone. What is the BEST approach?
choices: Assign the cross-cutting issue to whichever team member is most available and have them drive it to closure on their own.
Escalate the issue to senior executives for a ruling before analyzing it with the groups involved.
Collaborate with the relevant stakeholders to agree on a resolution approach, then assign a clear owner and due date.
Continue to monitor the issue and allow it to resolve itself as the work progresses.
questions.explanation: Cross-cutting issues are resolved by collaborating with the affected stakeholders on an approach, then assigning ownership and a due date and tracking to closure. Arbitrary assignment, premature escalation, and passivity all skip the collaborative problem-solving the situation needs.

questions.question: The same impediment has blocked the team three times this quarter even though it was 'cleared' each time. What should the project manager do?
choices: Investigate the systemic root cause and fix it once so the recurring blocker stops returning, while continuing to reassess.
Clear the impediment once more using the same approach that was applied before, and consider the recurring matter closed for the quarter.
Accept the recurring block as an unavoidable characteristic of the current work environment and its processes.
Log the pattern for discussion at the project's closeout review later in the year.
questions.explanation: A recurring impediment signals a systemic cause worth fixing once to remove a whole class of future blockers, alongside continual reassessment. Closest distractor: (B) - re-clearing it the proven way is fast, but treating the symptom again guarantees the block returns.

questions.question: An impediment is slowing the team, but its true effect on the schedule and deliverables is not yet clear. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Treat the impediment as a minor nuisance for the moment and keep the whole team focused on delivering the current committed work without any interruption to the flow.
Escalate the impediment to management as a critical blocker right away so that it receives prompt, high-priority attention.
Remove the affected work from the current iteration's scope entirely until the impediment has been investigated and resolved.
Evaluate the impediment's impact - what is affected, whether the critical path or value is at risk, and how urgent it is - to inform how to respond.
questions.explanation: Sizing the impediment's impact first - what is affected, whether the critical path or value is at risk, and how urgent it is - informs the right response. Closest distractor: (B) - escalating as critical gets attention, but labeling it critical before assessing impact may misprioritize it.

questions.question: A risk has a 40% probability of occurring and would add $50,000 in cost if it does. What is the threat's expected cost exposure (the EMV magnitude) used to inform reserve analysis?
questions.explanation: Expected cost exposure = probability x impact = 0.40 x $50,000 = $20,000, the positive magnitude used to size contingency. $50,000 ignores probability, $30,000 wrongly applies the 60% non-occurrence probability, and $70,000 adds the expected value on top of the full impact.

questions.question: A project manager compares two mutually exclusive options. Option A: 60% chance of a $100,000 gain and 40% chance of a $20,000 loss. Option B: 80% chance of a $50,000 gain and 20% chance of a $30,000 loss. Based on expected monetary value, which is the better choice?
choices: Option B, with an EMV of $34,000.
Option A, with an EMV of $60,000.
The two options have equal expected monetary value.
Option A, with an EMV of $52,000.
questions.explanation: Option A EMV = 0.6($100,000) + 0.4(-$20,000) = $52,000; Option B EMV = 0.8($50,000) + 0.2(-$30,000) = $34,000, so Option A is better. Closest distractor: (A) - $34,000 is Option B's correct EMV, but B's higher probability of a smaller gain still loses to A on expected value.

questions.question: A project manager sets aside budget for identified risks that have planned response strategies, and this amount is included in the cost baseline. What is this called, and how does it differ from management reserve?
choices: Management reserve; the contingency reserve is instead held outside the cost baseline to cover currently unknown and unidentified risks that emerge.
Management reserve; it covers identified risks that have planned responses and is released by the project manager as needed.
Contingency reserve; it is essentially the same as management reserve but simply held by the project manager.
Contingency reserve; management reserve covers unforeseen work within the approved scope, sits outside the baseline, and is released by management.
questions.explanation: Contingency reserve funds identified risks with planned responses and is part of the cost baseline; management reserve covers unforeseen work still within the approved scope, sits outside the baseline, and is released by management through governance. Closest distractor: (A) - it correctly separates the two reserves but mislabels the baseline-included fund as management reserve.

questions.question: A high-priority threat cannot be eliminated, but the team can add testing and a prototype to lower both its likelihood and its impact. Which response strategy is this?
choices: Accept
Mitigate
Transfer
Avoid
questions.explanation: Reducing a threat's probability and/or impact is mitigation. Accept takes no proactive action, transfer shifts impact and response ownership to a third party, and avoid eliminates the cause so the threat cannot occur.

questions.question: A threat identified on the project would affect the entire program and lies beyond the project's authority to address. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Accept the threat within the project's scope and set aside a contingency reserve to cover its potential impact.
Escalate the threat to the appropriate authority outside the project, then monitor its impact on project objectives.
Mitigate the threat using the project's own resources even though it is a program-level concern.
Transfer the threat to a vendor through a clause added to an existing contract.
questions.explanation: When a risk is beyond the project's scope or authority, ownership is escalated to the appropriate level while the project keeps watching its impact on its own objectives. Closest distractor: (C) - mitigating with the project's own resources feels responsible, but a program-level threat outside the project's authority is not the project's to own.

questions.question: A project team identifies an opportunity that would significantly benefit the project, and it wants to make sure the opportunity is realized rather than left to chance. Which positive-risk strategy is this?
choices: Enhance
Share
Exploit
Accept
questions.explanation: Exploit makes an opportunity certain to occur so its benefit is captured. Enhance only increases its likelihood or impact, share assigns it to a partner better able to capture it, and accept welcomes it passively without acting to ensure it.

questions.question: The exposure of a key risk has increased significantly, and stakeholders are not yet aware. What should the project manager do?
choices: Manage the increased exposure within the project team to avoid causing unnecessary alarm among the wider stakeholder group at this stage.
Hold off on informing stakeholders until the risk actually materializes into a live project issue.
Communicate the changed risk status and impact to the relevant stakeholders and governance, update the risk register, and reassess the response.
Downgrade the risk's rating in the register so that it draws less stakeholder concern for now.
questions.explanation: Rising exposure is communicated to stakeholders and governance so they can act, with the register updated and the response reassessed. Closest distractor: (A) - containing it within the team seems calm and low-drama, but withholding a materially increased exposure denies stakeholders the chance to respond.

questions.question: At the end of each iteration, an adaptive team examines what went well and what to improve, then commits to one or two changes for the next iteration. This practice primarily supports which objective?
choices: Verifying the product increment satisfies its acceptance criteria so it can be formally accepted.
Continuous improvement through applying lessons learned during the project, not only at closeout.
Surfacing individual performance data to inform functional managers' appraisal decisions.
Fixing the velocity baseline so external release dates can be forecast reliably.
questions.explanation: The retrospective's primary aim is continuous improvement — capturing and applying lessons throughout the project rather than only at closeout. Confirming acceptance criteria is the separate iteration review, individual performance reporting is not its purpose, and velocity forecasting is at most a by-product.

questions.question: An organization has a large store of lessons learned from past projects, but teams rarely reuse them. What is the BEST way to close this gap?
choices: Ensure lessons are reviewed during planning and the organizational process assets are kept updated and accessible so teams actually apply them.
Require every project to produce a detailed lessons-learned report at closeout and file it in the central repository as an official record.
Appoint a knowledge manager to catalog, tag, and index every stored lesson so the repository is easier to search.
Mandate that every team read the entire lessons repository during onboarding before they begin planning or execution work.
questions.explanation: A lesson creates value only when it is applied at the moment of reuse — reviewed during planning and kept in accessible, current OPAs. Closeout reports keep filling the store, cataloging aids discovery not application, and forcing full-repository reads is impractical. Closest distractor: (B) — mandating closeout reports feels like the standard knowledge fix, but it grows an unused store rather than driving reuse.

questions.question: A process problem has recurred on several projects across the organization. To drive lasting improvement, what should the project manager do?
choices: Resolve the problem completely on the current project and record the corrective action so this project's own team benefits from it.
Handle each occurrence as a project-specific issue and solve it locally on whichever project it happens to surface next.
Escalate the issue to management and let them decide whether to standardize a fix across the organization's projects.
Capture the lesson and update the shared organizational process assets so future projects avoid the problem, following any required approval.
questions.explanation: A recurring cross-project problem is resolved by feeding the lesson into shared OPAs, with any required approval, so future projects benefit. Fixing one project or treating each case as unique lets it recur, and leaving it to management abdicates the improvement.

questions.question: Partway through a two-year logistics-automation program, the project manager wants continuous improvement to be part of how the team works rather than a one-time event. Which approach BEST embodies that mindset?
choices: Gather every process pain point now and schedule all the fixes for the program's closeout retrospective.
Inspect and adapt the processes at regular intervals, favoring small changes and larger ones when evidence warrants.
Lock the processes once they are established so the delivery team is never disrupted by ongoing change requests.
Assign all process improvement to a separate quality department so the delivery team can focus on output.
questions.explanation: Continuous improvement means inspecting and adapting throughout, favoring incremental change while allowing larger change when the evidence supports it. Deferring all fixes to closeout, freezing processes, or isolating improvement in a separate function each limit the team's learning.

questions.question: A team's retrospective produces a genuinely better estimating template. To make sure the improvement is not lost, what should the project manager do?
choices: Keep the improved estimating template within the current team, since it was tailored specifically to this project's context.
Apply the improved template for the rest of this project and then archive it together with the other closeout records.
Update the organizational process assets with the improved template, following any required approval, so future projects can reuse it.
