Hold off on sharing the template organization-wide until several more projects have confirmed it consistently produces better estimates.
questions.explanation: An improvement becomes durable only when written back into shared OPAs, with any required approval, so the whole organization can reuse it. Keeping it local, archiving it at closeout, or delaying indefinitely for more proof all waste the gain.

questions.question: Before rolling out a system that will significantly change how three departments work, the project manager wants to plan adoption support. What should be assessed FIRST?
choices: The organizational culture and the departments' readiness to adopt and sustain the change.
The system's technical performance and stability under the peak transaction load expected in production.
The budget still available to fund the rollout, training, and post-launch support activities.
The amount of schedule float remaining before the committed go-live date.
questions.explanation: Assessing culture and readiness first reveals gaps in preparedness, capability, and support so they can be closed before deployment. Technical performance, budget, and schedule float matter but do not address the human side of adoption that determines whether benefits are realized.

questions.question: A project's deliverable will substantially change a department's daily workflow, and adoption depends on people changing established habits. To support adoption, what should the project manager do?
choices: Concentrate on delivering a technically correct solution and leave user adoption entirely to the operations team once the handover is complete.
Postpone all adoption planning until after go-live so the delivery team can stay focused on completing the build.
Require all affected staff to use the new workflow from go-live day, backed by executive authority to enforce compliance.
Evaluate the change's impact on affected stakeholders and plan enabling actions such as communication of the purpose, training, and reinforcement.
questions.explanation: Realizing benefits requires managing the people transition — assessing stakeholder impact and planning communication, training, and reinforcement alongside delivery. Delivering technology alone, deferring adoption planning, or mandating use without readiness all invite resistance. Closest distractor: (C) — an executive mandate can force day-one usage, but without readiness it breeds resistance rather than sustained adoption.

questions.question: After a new system launches, a group of employees actively resists using it. What is the BEST response?
choices: Enforce adoption by applying penalties or performance consequences for the employees who refuse to use the system.
Continue the rollout as planned and allow the resistance to subside on its own over the coming weeks.
Engage the group to understand the reasons for the resistance — which may reveal genuine issues — and respond appropriately.
Roll the system back entirely and revert to the previous process to avoid further conflict with the affected group.
questions.explanation: Resistance often carries information about readiness gaps, incentives, trust, or even a genuine flaw, so understanding it before acting enables adoption. Penalties, a full rollback, or letting it fade all act before understanding the cause. Closest distractor: (B) — giving resistance time looks measured, but it forfeits the chance to learn what the pushback is signaling.

questions.question: Midway through the project, a company restructuring changes the sponsor and shifts organizational priorities. What should the project manager do?
choices: Continue executing the existing plan exactly as before, treating the restructuring as an organizational matter unrelated to the project's delivery work.
Evaluate how the restructuring affects the project's objectives, scope, and business case, and determine the required actions with the new sponsor and governance.
Pause all project work until the restructuring is fully complete and the new reporting lines have clearly settled.
Rebaseline the project plan on your own authority to fit the new organizational priorities, without first engaging the incoming sponsor or the governance body.
questions.explanation: A significant organizational change is assessed for impact on objectives, scope, and business case, with actions determined through the new sponsor and governance. Pressing on with a stale plan, an indefinite pause, or unilaterally rebaselining all skip that assessment. Closest distractor: (D) — rebaselining to the new priorities is directionally right, but doing it without the incoming sponsor and governance bypasses the required change process.

questions.question: A project delivering a major organizational change is struggling with slow adoption, and the sponsor has been largely absent from communications and reinforcement. What should the project manager do?
choices: Engage the sponsor to provide active, visible support — advocacy, resources, and reinforcement — appropriate to their role in enabling the change.
Fill the sponsorship gap yourself by personally directing employees across the departments to adopt the new way of working.
Go over the sponsor's head to senior executives and ask them to compel the departments to adopt the change.
Accept the slow adoption as a normal feature of any major change and simply give it more time to improve on its own.
questions.explanation: Active, visible sponsorship — advocacy, resources, decision support, reinforcement — is what strengthens adoption, so the project manager engages the sponsor to fill that role. Substituting the PM's authority, going over the sponsor, or giving it more time all leave the sponsorship gap unfilled. Closest distractor: (B) — stepping in personally feels proactive, but it cannot replace the sponsor's authority and only masks the real gap.

questions.question: A regulation expected to take effect next year could change requirements for the project's product, which is due to launch in eight months. What should the project manager do?
choices: Hold off on taking any action until the regulation is finalized and legally mandatory, then respond to it at that point.
Assess the potential regulation's impact on scope, backlog, and the business case, and prepare a response through the appropriate process.
Treat the pending regulation as outside the project's control and take no action on it for now.
Leave the pending regulation for the legal department to manage on its own without involving the project team.
questions.explanation: Scanning external changes and assessing their impact on scope, backlog, and business case lets the project respond before disruption. Delaying until the rule is mandatory, dismissing it, or assuming legal handles it alone all risk a costly late scramble. Closest distractor: (A) — waiting for the final rule avoids rework on a maybe, but an eight-month launch may leave no time to comply once it lands.

questions.question: Two-thirds of the way through building a proprietary payments feature meant to differentiate the product, an industry consortium publishes an open standard that delivers the same capability at no cost. What should the project manager do?
choices: Keep building the proprietary feature exactly as scoped, since it was already approved, funded, and baselined.
Cancel the entire project right away to stop spending on a capability that is now effectively commoditized.
Hold back news of the consortium's new standard for now so that stakeholders and the team stay confident in the current plan.
Assess the shift's impact on value and the business case, then raise options — reprioritize, rescope, or pivot — through governance.
questions.explanation: A material external shift calls for reassessing value and the business case and raising options through governance, weighing value against obligations. Delivering the now-commoditized scope on inertia, unilaterally cancelling, or concealing the change are all poor responses. Closest distractor: (B) — cancelling reacts to the lost value, but it pre-empts the governance decision and the option analysis that should come first.

questions.question: The risk heatmap plots five identified risks by probability and impact. R1 (very-high probability, very-high impact) is already under an active response. Based on exposure, which risk should the team address NEXT?
choices: R2, in the low-probability / very-high-impact cell.
R3, in the high-probability / medium-impact cell.
R4, in the very-low-probability / high-impact cell.
R5, in the medium-probability / low-impact cell.
questions.explanation: Exposure = probability x impact. With R1 (5x5 = 25) already being managed, the next-highest exposure is R3 at 4x3 = 12, ahead of R2 at 2x5 = 10. R2 (A) is the closest miss — its very-high impact draws the eye, but its low probability makes its exposure lower than R3's; R4 (4) and R5 (6) are lower still. Closest distractor: (A) — high impact alone is not high exposure; probability x impact ranks R3 first.

questions.question: Geopolitical instability threatens the supply of a component critical to the project. What is the BEST first action?
choices: Proceed on the expectation that the component supply will stay stable, and continue with the current plan unchanged.
Halt the entire project until the geopolitical situation fully resolves and the outlook for the critical component's supply chain becomes clear and stable again.
Assess the disruption's impact on the project's objectives and schedule, and develop response options such as alternative sourcing, engaging the appropriate stakeholders.
Treat the geopolitical instability as entirely outside the project's scope of control and take no action in response.
questions.explanation: Assessing the external impact and developing response options such as alternative sourcing, while engaging the right stakeholders, manages the threat proactively. Proceeding on the assumption of stability, halting the project outright, or ignoring the disruption all leave the project exposed.

questions.question: An economic downturn cuts the funding available to the organization's project portfolio, and the project's budget may be reduced. What is the BEST response?
choices: Continue spending at the originally planned rate until a formal, confirmed budget reduction is actually issued.
Assess the funding change's impact on the project and work with governance to reprioritize scope and value accordingly.
Cut the project team's size right away to bring the burn rate down as quickly as possible.
Proceed on the expectation that another project in the portfolio will end up absorbing the funding cut on your behalf.
questions.explanation: Assessing the external funding impact and reprioritizing scope and value with governance responds responsibly to reduced funding. Spending unchanged, cutting the team without analysis, or assuming the cut lands elsewhere all ignore the changed environment.

passages.title: Scenario: Earned-value status (Questions refer to this data)
passages.text: At month 6 of a 12-month predictive project, the project management information system reports: budget at completion (BAC) = $500,000; planned value (PV) = $250,000; earned value (EV) = $200,000; actual cost (AC) = $250,000.

questions.question: Taking over a stalled healthcare-IT patient-portal program, a newly assigned lead finds the governance board frames success as regulatory compliance, the engineers frame it as platform modernization, and the clinical sponsor frames it as shorter patient wait times. Before facilitating a session to reconcile these competing views, what must the lead do first?
choices: Confirm which stakeholder holds final authority to arbitrate scope so session decisions will actually hold
Survey the delivery team's morale to gauge how the ambiguity is affecting their throughput
Draft a unified vision statement and circulate it for the groups to react to beforehand
Map each group's stated goal to the approved business case and the benefits funded
questions.explanation: Best: D — before reconciling divergent goal statements, ground them in the authoritative source of intended value (the business case and funded benefits) so the session compares each view against a common reference rather than negotiating opinions. Closest miss — A: naming the decision owner matters, but arbitrating authority presumes the goals truly conflict; many apparent conflicts dissolve once mapped to funded benefits, so grounding precedes escalating to authority. Also plausible — C, B: drafting a vision to react to anchors on the lead's guess before the sources are understood; a morale survey addresses a symptom of the ambiguity, not the goal-alignment step.
questions.task: Build shared understanding of program goals

questions.question: Eleven months into an 18-month predictive core-banking replacement, a supervisory ruling removes the regulatory driver behind a major module the team has been building. The team is unsettled and unsure whether their remaining work still matters, and the sponsor has not yet re-baselined scope. As the leader, what is the best way to steady the team?
choices: Reassure the team the module will likely be repurposed and ask them to keep building at pace
Redirect the team to other backlog items immediately so momentum and utilization stay high
Wait for the sponsor's formal re-baseline before addressing the team, to avoid sharing unconfirmed changes
Pause visible work on the module and involve the team in reassessing which outcomes still matter
questions.explanation: Best: D — servant leadership under changed conditions means giving the team transparency and involving them in re-examining which outcomes still hold value, which restores purpose and protects trust. Closest miss — B: redirecting to valuable work is right eventually, but doing it immediately without involving the team skips the sense-making that sustains engagement and treats members as interchangeable capacity. Also plausible — A, C: optimism keeps momentum yet builds on an unconfirmed assumption that risks wasted effort and credibility; waiting for the re-baseline respects governance but leaving the team in an information vacuum erodes morale.
questions.task: Maintain team purpose through disruptive change

questions.question: During release planning for a new 5G network-assurance platform, the development squads are visibly enthusiastic, but the network-operations staff who will run it in production sit quietly, contribute no acceptance criteria, and defer every question to their manager. The vision and goals were shaped months earlier by the development squads and product leadership, with no operations representative in the room. Delivery is on track. What is the most likely underlying cause of the operations group's disengagement?
choices: The platform's operational value has not been made concrete for the outcomes they own
They lack the agile training needed to participate confidently in release-planning ceremonies
Their manager has not yet authorized them to commit any team capacity to this initiative
They had no hand in shaping the vision and now see it as imposed
questions.explanation: Best: D — the operations group met a fully formed vision they had no hand in shaping, so they experience it as imposed, which suppresses ownership and participation; re-engaging them in co-defining operational outcomes is the fix. Closest miss — C: deferring to the manager hints they may lack authority to commit, but authorization alone rarely produces silence on acceptance criteria; people withhold input mainly when they feel no ownership. Also plausible — A, B: unclear operational value can dampen engagement, yet they have not even probed for value, pointing to exclusion; a training gap would show as awkward participation, not total withdrawal.
questions.task: Engage operations stakeholders in the vision

questions.question: A public-agency permit-processing system passed every acceptance test and satisfied each documented requirement, but the agency director says it 'isn't what we needed' because processing times barely improved. The requirements were signed off by mid-level staff early in the predictive project. What most likely explains the gap between conformance and the director's dissatisfaction?
choices: The acceptance tests were too narrow to reveal defects that surface only under production load
The mid-level staff who signed off lacked authority to represent the director's true requirements
Scope changes during delivery were not reflected back into the signed requirements baseline
Requirements were captured without tracing them to the outcome the project existed to achieve
questions.explanation: Best: D — the deliverable conformed to requirements, but the requirements were never linked to the intended outcome (faster processing), so meeting them could not create the value; the root cause is missing requirements-to-benefit traceability, not flawed execution. Closest miss — B: sign-off by staff without the director's view is a real contributor, but even the director's own requirements would fail if none tied to the target outcome, making the traceability gap more fundamental. Also plausible — A, C: load defects would appear as failures, yet everything passed; unmanaged scope change would break the baseline, but nothing indicates change—only that the baseline never encoded the outcome.

questions.question: A retail e-commerce Scrum team split across three continents ships reliably each sprint, yet several members tell the Scrum Master they no longer feel connected to why their work matters to customers. Velocity is stable and quality is fine. Which action best helps the Scrum Master restore the team's sense of purpose?
choices: Add a recurring agenda item where the product owner shares customer outcomes tied to recent work
Rotate members through customer-support shadowing to expose them directly to user problems
Increase the frequency of retrospectives so the team can raise engagement concerns more often
Invite the team to link recent increments to real customer stories and business goals
questions.explanation: Best: D — restoring the 'why' calls for the team to actively connect their own recent increments to customer stories and business goals, which rebuilds felt purpose more than passive updates do. Closest miss — A: a standing product-owner outcome update helps, but it is one-directional and PO-led, so it informs the team without engaging them in making the connection themselves. Also plausible — B, C: support shadowing builds empathy but is heavier and indirect for a team already delivering; more retrospectives surface feelings yet do not by themselves supply the purpose the team is missing.
questions.task: Instill shared purpose through servant leadership

questions.question: On a manufacturing digital-twin initiative, the team received a polished vision authored entirely by the PMO and shows little ownership of it, though the vision is technically sound and aligned to strategy. The new lead weighs two paths: Approach X, facilitate the team to rewrite the vision themselves; or Approach Y, keep the PMO vision but have the team translate it into goals and measures they define. Which fits best, and why?
choices: Approach X, because deep ownership forms most strongly when the team authors its own vision statement
Approach Y, because rewriting an already-approved vision wastes effort better spent on delivery
Approach Y, because ownership grows from shaping how the vision is pursued, not authoring it
Approach X, because a PMO-authored vision rarely earns a delivery team's genuine commitment
questions.explanation: Best: C — the PMO vision is sound and strategy-aligned, so value comes from preserving direction while the team authors the goals, measures, and approach; ownership is built by shaping the 'how,' which Approach Y delivers without destabilizing alignment. Closest miss — B: also picks Y, but justifies it only as saving rework effort; that efficiency case is weaker than C's point that ownership grows from shaping the pursuit, which is the real reason Y fits. Also plausible — A, D: authorship can build ownership, but rewriting a strategy-aligned vision discards good direction and invites drift; PMO-seeded visions can still earn commitment when teams shape their pursuit, so choosing X on that reasoning is weaker here.
questions.task: Co-create vision to build team ownership

questions.question: Three iterations into a clinical-trial data-capture product, four new engineers join the team and openly ask how their assigned stories connect to the overall product goal. The team is delivering well and the product goal is documented in the backlog. What is the best first action for the team lead?
choices: Ask the product owner to present the roadmap at the next sprint review for everyone
Point the newcomers to the backlog where the product goal and full story mapping are documented
Pair each newcomer with an experienced member to absorb context through the work itself
Connect the product goal to their stories and show how the work ladders up
questions.explanation: Best: D — the newcomers asked for the line of sight between their work and the goal, so the lead directly connecting their stories to the product goal gives immediate purpose and shared understanding. Closest miss — C: pairing builds context over time and is valuable, but it defers the explicit goal linkage they requested and leaves purpose to emerge indirectly. Also plausible — B, A: the documentation exists, yet handing them a link answers 'what' not 'why' and misses the leadership moment; a roadmap at the next review helps everyone but is delayed and broad rather than answering their specific question now.
questions.task: Onboard new members to the product goal

questions.question: In an aerospace avionics team's daily stand-ups, friction between the integration lead and a senior developer has begun surfacing as pointed personal remarks, and the underlying trigger — a disagreement over integration sequencing — is already evident to the team. Other members have started staying quiet, and collaboration is visibly cooling. As the servant leader, what is the best course of action?
choices: Raise the behavior with both privately, then help them address the underlying disagreement together
Set an explicit stand-up ground rule against personal remarks and hold the whole team accountable
Speak with each of the two separately to understand each perspective before intervening further
Bring the two together promptly to surface the real issue and agree on norms
questions.explanation: Best: D — the trigger is already known and it is a two-peer interpersonal conflict, so a servant leader brings the pair together promptly to work the real issue and agree how they will collaborate, targeting the root cause. Closest miss — C: separate fact-finding is reasonable in general, but here the cause is already clear, so meeting each first mainly delays resolution and can entrench positions. Also plausible — A, B: a private word before a joint talk can work but risks framing it as discipline, and a stand-up ground rule curbs the symptom without resolving the underlying conflict.

questions.question: On an energy-grid optimization team, an AI design assistant recommends a load-balancing configuration. One engineer wants to implement it as-is to save time; another wants to discard it based on experience. The team lead is about to facilitate a decision. Before the team accepts or rejects the recommendation, what must happen first?
choices: Establish who on the team is accountable for the final design decision and its outcomes
Document both viewpoints in the decision log so the rationale is traceable for auditors
Run a quick controlled experiment comparing the AI configuration against the engineer's preferred alternative approach
Validate the AI recommendation against the design constraints and evidence behind both engineers' positions
questions.explanation: Best: D — the engineers disagree about facts, so before accepting or rejecting the recommendation the team must validate it against the design constraints and the evidence behind each position; grounding the choice in verifiable data must precede any accept/reject or test. Closest miss — C: an experiment is a strong way to generate that evidence, but designing a fair comparison first requires the constraints and criteria the evidence must meet, so validation framing comes first. Also plausible — A, B: naming the decision owner supports empowerment, but authority without evidence still yields an uninformed choice; logging both viewpoints preserves traceability yet does nothing to resolve which position the facts support.

questions.question: A distributed healthcare-IT team must standardize its daily sync time. Two options work equally well for coverage; two members each prefer a different one, and the choice is genuinely low-stakes. The Scrum Master wants a decision that sticks without lingering resentment. What is the best way to resolve it?
choices: Choose the option that best fits the majority's working hours and communicate the decision
Let the two members negotiate directly and adopt whichever time they agree on together
Facilitate a quick team decision using a method everyone agrees is fair
Alternate between the two times each week so neither preference is permanently overridden
questions.explanation: Best: C — for a genuinely low-stakes, reversible choice, durability comes from the team deciding via a method they accept as fair, producing commitment without a winner-and-loser dynamic. Closest miss — B: letting the two negotiate can settle it, but it narrows a team-wide norm to a two-person deal and can leave others uninvested in a standard everyone must follow. Also plausible — A, D: a majority-fit decision is efficient but, imposed by the lead, can seed the resentment the Scrum Master wants to avoid; alternating dodges the choice yet defeats the goal of standardizing and adds recurring coordination cost.

questions.question: On a bridge-construction project, the steel subcontractor and the owner's project team disagree over whether a delivered girder assembly is acceptable; each cites a different clause of the same agreement, and schedule pressure is mounting. The project manager weighs two approaches: Approach X, issue a formal contractual nonconformance determination; or Approach Y, convene a joint technical review with both parties before invoking any remedy. Which fits best, and why?
choices: Approach X, because schedule pressure makes decisive contractual action the responsible choice
Approach X, because the signed agreement is the authority and a formal determination resolves it fastest
Approach Y, because the subcontractor will more readily accept an outcome it helped shape
Approach Y, because a collaborative review can reconcile the interpretations and preserve the working relationship
questions.explanation: Best: D — when both sides read the same agreement differently, the dispute is about interpretation; a joint technical review can align understanding and resolve the substance while preserving the relationship, with formal remedies still available if it fails. Closest miss — C: also selects Y and is partly right about buy-in, but it frames the review as getting the subcontractor to accept an outcome rather than genuinely reconciling the interpretation, which is the real purpose. Also plausible — B, A: the agreement is authoritative, but a formal determination on a contested clause invites a dispute before facts are aligned; schedule pressure is real, yet decisive action on an unresolved interpretation can trigger claims that cost more time.

questions.question: A banking-software team's working agreement calls for one person to speak at a time, but as a release deadline nears, a respected senior developer routinely talks over quieter members in refinement sessions. Their input is valuable, yet others are contributing less and two members have quietly raised the pattern with the Scrum Master. What is the best way for the Scrum Master to respond?
choices: Privately ask the senior developer to make room for quieter members and honor the shared agreement
Revisit whether the working agreement still fits the team under current deadline pressure
Directly enforce the agreement in the moment by redirecting airtime during the sessions
Surface the pattern to the team and let them reaffirm their own working agreement
questions.explanation: Best: D — the team owns its working agreement, so surfacing the pattern to the team and having them reaffirm and enforce it strengthens self-organization and shared accountability instead of casting the Scrum Master as enforcer. Closest miss — A: a private word respects the individual and often works, but it keeps ownership with the Scrum Master and treats a team-norm issue as one person's problem. Also plausible — C, B: in-the-moment redirection protects participation but makes the Scrum Master the referee, weakening team ownership; re-examining the agreement's fit has merit, yet the issue is adherence under pressure, not a flawed norm.
questions.task: Uphold team ground rules and self-organization

questions.question: A newly formed cross-functional team on a smart-city sensor rollout keeps stumbling over how decisions get made and who speaks when, producing repeated low-grade friction. Individually the members are capable and willing. The program manager wants to reduce the friction at its source. What is the most effective first step?
choices: Assign clear roles and a decision-making authority for each type of decision
Add a facilitator to each meeting to manage turn-taking and keep discussions orderly
Hold a retrospective so the team can vent the friction and propose fixes
Facilitate the team to co-create working agreements covering decision rights and communication
questions.explanation: Best: D — the friction comes from missing shared norms in a forming team, so facilitating the members to co-create working agreements on decision-making and communication addresses the source and builds ownership of the fix. Closest miss — A: defining roles and decision authority solves part of it, but top-down structure wins less commitment than team-built norms and omits the 'who speaks when' dimension. Also plausible — B, C: a meeting facilitator smooths symptoms session to session without equipping the team to self-manage; a retrospective surfaces the friction, but without co-created agreements it is likely to recur.

questions.question: Before a multi-partner satellite-ground-station program begins, the program manager runs a readiness pulse across the four partner teams. Results (1-5, higher better): shared goal clarity 4.4, role clarity 2.1, agreed escalation path 1.8, psychological safety 3.9. Trust is high but two scores lag. Which interpretation best guides where to focus to keep future disagreements constructive?
choices: High psychological safety suggests conflicts will largely self-resolve, so concentrate on delivery
Low goal clarity is the main risk, so the manager should re-facilitate the shared program vision
Undefined roles and escalation paths are the likely fault lines; establish both before work starts
High trust offsets the low scores, so lightweight norms can be deferred until issues actually arise
questions.explanation: Best: C — role clarity (2.1) and escalation path (1.8) are the low scores; ambiguous responsibilities and no agreed escalation route are where multi-partner disagreements turn destructive, so defining both before mobilization targets the real fault lines. Closest miss — D: high trust genuinely buffers conflict and some norm-setting can wait, but leaving roles and escalation undefined until problems appear is exactly what lets early friction escalate across organizations. Also plausible — A, B: psychological safety helps surface conflict yet does not resolve structural ambiguity, and steering to delivery ignores the data; goal clarity already scores high (4.4), so re-facilitating the vision solves a problem the data says is not there.

questions.question: Two developers on adjacent squads in a pharma-manufacturing platform agreed weeks ago on how to split responsibility for a shared data interface. The split was clear at the time, but the old friction between them has quietly returned, with each again assuming the other owns the edge cases. Delivery hasn't slipped yet. What is the most likely root cause of the recurring friction?
choices: Changes in the interface since the agreement have quietly outdated who owns which part
One developer is deliberately renegotiating the agreement to offload work onto the other squad
The two never genuinely accepted the split and only agreed to end an uncomfortable conversation quickly
The agreement addressed the visible split but never resolved the ambiguous boundary cases between them
questions.explanation: Best: D — the pair still agree on the clear split but keep colliding on edge cases, which shows the original agreement never defined the ambiguous boundary; the friction recurs exactly where ownership was left implicit. Closest miss — C: a superficial peace-making agreement would also resurface, but the symptom is specifically edge cases each assumes the other owns, pointing to an undefined boundary rather than wholesale non-acceptance. Also plausible — B, A: intentional offloading is possible, yet nothing signals bad faith and both, not one, are stepping back; interface drift could reassign ownership, but the gap sits at edge cases never assigned, not at parts newly changed.
questions.task: Diagnose and resolve recurring team conflict

questions.question: Midway through refining a payments-platform backlog, two engineers voice sharp but respectful disagreement over an integration approach, and their exchange exposes several dependency risks nobody had logged. Other members go quiet, unsure whether the debate is helping. As the Scrum Master facilitating the session, what is the best response?
choices: Invite the product owner to decide the integration approach so the team can re-focus.
Table the technical dispute to a spike and keep refinement moving to protect the timebox.
Ask the two engineers to resolve the approach offline and bring back a recommendation.
Capture the newly surfaced risks, then guide the team to a shared decision.
questions.explanation: Best: D — a servant-leader harnesses respectful disagreement as risk discovery, logging the risks and facilitating the team toward a shared, owned decision rather than shutting the exchange down. Closest miss — C: pushing the two engineers to resolve it offline is time-efficient and reasonable, but it strips the wider team of the shared learning and collective ownership the open debate created. Also plausible — B, A: B protects the timebox yet defers the value the conflict just surfaced; A respects that the product owner owns priorities, but the integration approach is a team technical decision, not the PO's to make.

questions.question: A capable, self-organizing delivery team is performing well. Which TWO actions best reflect how a servant leader supports such a team?
choices: Remove organizational impediments the team cannot clear on its own.
Assign each member's daily tasks to keep utilization high.
Approve every technical decision before the team proceeds.
Ensure the team has the capacity, skills, and context to make its own decisions.
Route the team's external communications through yourself.
questions.explanation: Best: a servant leader clears impediments (A) and enables the team's own decision-making (D). Closest miss — B: assigning daily tasks looks like helpful coordination and suits a junior team, but for a capable self-organizing team it removes the ownership that drives performance. Also plausible — C, E: approving every decision and channeling all communication centralize control the team has earned, slowing flow and eroding autonomy.

questions.question: During an active two-week iteration building a clinical-trial data-capture module, a senior director pushes to add a new regulatory field the team says will endanger the iteration goal and testing quality. The product owner is on leave for two days. Before the project manager agrees to any mid-iteration change, which action must come first?
choices: Ask the team to absorb the field and de-scope lower-priority testing to hold the end date.
Add the field to the next iteration's backlog and tell the director it waits.
Escalate to the sponsor that management is destabilizing the iteration and request a scope freeze.
Assess the impact on the iteration goal with the product owner and team before deciding.
questions.explanation: Best: D — a mid-iteration change may proceed only after its impact on the sprint goal and quality is assessed with the team and the product owner, who owns backlog priority; the change is a negotiation, not a directive to absorb. Closest miss — A: trading away testing to hold the date is a real option, but committing to absorb the field before any impact analysis or PO involvement sacrifices quality prematurely. Also plausible — C, B: C escalates before the facts are gathered; B defers to the next iteration, yet that priority call belongs to the product owner, not the project manager working around their absence.
questions.task: Support team performance and negotiate scope

questions.question: For four consecutive sprints, a software team has missed its definition of done and post-release defects have climbed, even though velocity looks stable and members report being 'done' each sprint. Estimates are met, but rework spikes the following sprint, and retrospective actions are logged yet rarely completed. What is the MOST LIKELY underlying cause?
choices: The team keeps over-committing at sprint planning beyond its actual sustainable capacity.
Requirements are ambiguous, so acceptance criteria are interpreted inconsistently across the team.
The product owner keeps accepting increments without enforcing the agreed acceptance criteria.
A weak or unshared definition of done lets defects pass as done.
questions.explanation: Best: D — work reported 'done' that still ships defects and forces next-sprint rework is the signature of a weak or unshared definition of done that lets quality gaps pass the gate. Closest miss — A: over-commitment is a classic cause of missed criteria, but stable velocity and met estimates argue the team is not overloaded; the failure is in quality definition, not quantity. Also plausible — B, C: B (ambiguous requirements) would surface as scope disputes more than escaping defects; C shifts the gap to acceptance, yet the internal quality gate the team controls is the definition of done.

questions.question: A delivery team building a citizen-services portal is stalled because the identity-management group in another division will not provision a test environment it controls, and the team has no authority to compel it. Two sprints of progress are at risk, and the identity group cites its own backlog. As the project lead, what is the best first action?
choices: Stand up a temporary mock environment so the team can proceed without the real dependency.
Escalate immediately to the sponsor to direct the identity group to provision the environment.
Re-sequence the team's work to lower-priority items until the environment becomes available.
Engage the identity group's manager to understand constraints and negotiate a workable provisioning date.
questions.explanation: Best: D — the impediment sits with another manager, so the servant leader first engages that manager directly to understand the constraint and negotiate a date, using influence rather than positional authority. Closest miss — B: escalating to the sponsor can unblock this, but jumping to it before a peer-level conversation burns goodwill and is premature. Also plausible — C, A: C keeps the team productive but leaves the block unresolved; A's mock environment unblocks work yet risks rework and masks the unmet real dependency.

questions.question: A wind-farm program's engineering team spans four countries, wide seniority gaps, and several disciplines. The program manager wants this diversity to sharpen decisions rather than fragment them. One school of thought favors standardizing communication and decision norms to reduce friction; another favors deliberately structuring for dissent and rotating who leads discussions. Which approach better fits this goal, and why?
choices: Standardize norms, because a single shared process minimizes misunderstanding across cultures and specialties.
Structure for dissent and rotate facilitation, turning diverse views into better decisions.
Standardize norms first, then add dissent structures only if decision quality later proves inadequate.
Rotate facilitation only, since shared norms would suppress the very differences the manager values.
questions.explanation: Best: B — the stated goal is better decisions from diversity, so deliberately structuring for dissent and rotating facilitation harnesses cognitive diversity and gives junior or quieter voices real influence. Closest miss — C: standardizing first and adding dissent later is a sensible staged hybrid, but it treats diversity as friction to manage before it is value to capture, delaying the intended benefit. Also plausible — A, D: A reduces misunderstanding yet optimizes smoothness over decision quality; D rotates facilitation but discards the shared norms that make inclusion safe, over-correcting toward unstructured debate.

questions.question: A skilled, distributed engineering team has grown disengaged midway through a long, repetitive regulatory-remediation release. There is no emergency and quality is holding. Which TWO actions are MOST likely to rebuild the team's intrinsic motivation?
choices: Introduce individual cash bonuses tied to the number of items each person closes weekly.
Give the team autonomy over how they meet the remediation objectives.
Increase the frequency of status check-ins so management can see momentum.
Route the most tedious items to the newest members so senior engineers stay fresh.
Connect the repetitive work to its purpose — the risk it removes for real customers.
questions.explanation: Best: for experienced knowledge workers the durable motivators are intrinsic — autonomy (B) and a clear sense of purpose (E). Closest miss — A: pay-per-item rewards can lift output briefly but tend to crowd out intrinsic motivation and invite gaming of the metric. Also plausible — C, D: more oversight usually lowers engagement, and reshuffling the tedium just moves the problem without addressing why the team disengaged.

questions.question: Three weeks after onboarding five new members, a project's metrics show: 18% of tasks touched by more than one owner, 9% of committed tasks with no owner at closeout, cycle time up 30%, and rising cross-team clarification messages. Morale surveys are stable. Which conclusion do these indicators most support?
choices: The team is in the storming stage and needs conflict-resolution facilitation to reset norms.
Onboarding was too fast, and new members need more technical training to reach capacity.
Cycle time rose because scope grew, so re-baselining the schedule is the priority.
Decision and task ownership are unclear, so roles and responsibilities need explicit clarification.
questions.explanation: Best: D — overlapping owners, unowned tasks at closeout, and a spike in clarification traffic are signatures of role ambiguity, resolved by explicitly clarifying who owns which decisions and tasks. Closest miss — A: newly mixed teams do storm, but stable morale and the specific ownership overlap point to a structural roles gap, not interpersonal conflict. Also plausible — B, C: B reads the churn as a skills shortfall, yet the data show ownership collisions, not capability gaps; C blames scope for cycle time without any evidence scope actually grew.

questions.question: A hybrid modernization program runs two parallel streams. Stream one is a newly formed team tackling an unfamiliar, high-risk data-migration task; stream two is a seasoned team doing well-understood interface work it has delivered before. The program manager is deciding how to lead each. Which leadership pairing best fits the two streams, and on what principle?
choices: Lead both directively until the migration risk is retired, then delegate to both teams.
Lead both delegatively to reinforce empowerment and consistent treatment across the program.
Lead stream one directively and stream two delegatively, per competence and task risk.
Lead stream one delegatively to build ownership and stream two directively to hold standards.
questions.explanation: Best: C — situational leadership matches style to development level and task risk: a new team on a high-risk task needs more direction, while an experienced team on familiar work performs best when delegated to. Closest miss — B: leading both delegatively honors empowerment and fairness, but identical treatment underserves the new team facing unfamiliar, high-risk work. Also plausible — A, D: A controls risk by directing both yet micromanages a proven team toward disengagement; D's 'delegate to build ownership' is appealing but inverts the pairing, leaving the novice team unsupported.

questions.question: Six weeks in, a newly assembled product team that began with easy politeness now argues openly about architecture and process, and two members challenge the tech lead's choices in front of a stakeholder. The stakeholder privately urges the manager to swap out 'the difficult members.' Delivery is still on track. Which interpretation best explains what is happening?
choices: The team has become dysfunctional and needs membership changes to restore collaboration.
The team has entered storming, a normal stage to coach it through.
The tech lead has lost authority and should be replaced to stabilize the team.
Personality conflicts are escalating and require formal HR involvement before delivery slips.
questions.explanation: Best: B — moving from polite cooperation into open disagreement about approach while still delivering is textbook storming; the manager's role is to coach the team through it, not disband it. Closest miss — A: reading the friction as dysfunction and changing membership is the stakeholder's instinct and superficially reasonable, but it would reset team development and destroy forming progress. Also plausible — C, D: C mistakes healthy challenge for lost authority; D escalates to HR as if the conflict were personal, when it is approach-based and delivery is intact.

questions.question: Deep into execution of a medical-device software release, the project manager discovers that a national regulator must formally review two key deliverables before market launch, yet this body was never identified as a stakeholder or built into the plan. Launch is four months out. Before adjusting the schedule or committing to a new date, which action must come first?
choices: Add the regulatory review as milestones and rebaseline the schedule to the new critical path.
Notify the sponsor that launch will slip and request approval to extend the date.
Assess the regulator's requirements and timelines, then update the stakeholder register and plan.
Fast-track development so deliverables reach the regulator earlier and preserve the launch date.
questions.explanation: Best: C — a mandatory but unidentified stakeholder must first be analyzed for requirements, review timelines, and criteria and added to the register; only that information can drive a sound schedule or launch-date decision. Closest miss — A: rebaselining to include the reviews is the eventual step, but committing to a new critical path before knowing the regulator's lead times bakes in guesses. Also plausible — B, D: B tells the sponsor the date will slip before the impact is known; D compresses development to hold the date without understanding what the regulator will require.

questions.question: On the grid, S1 and S2 both sit high on power, but S1 also has high interest while S2 has low interest. A new project manager plans to give both the same intensive, collaborative engagement. Why should the engagement of S1 and S2 differ?
choices: S1 should be kept satisfied and S2 managed closely, matching effort to who has more time to engage.
Both warrant the same close management, because high power is what determines engagement effort.
S1 is a key player to manage closely as an active partner, whereas S2 should be kept satisfied without day-to-day detail.
Both should simply be monitored, since neither sits in a low-power quadrant.
questions.explanation: Best: engagement is set by BOTH power and interest — S1 (high power, high interest) is a key player to manage closely as a partner, while S2 (high power, low interest) is kept satisfied without overwhelming detail. Closest miss — B: high power does drive effort, but engaging both identically ignores the interest axis and over-engages a low-interest stakeholder who will resent the load. Also plausible — A inverts the two, and D under-serves two high-power stakeholders by treating them as mere 'monitor' cases.

questions.question: On a data-platform program, the executive sponsor asks to see only outcome-level signals — value delivered and risk trend — while the lead architect needs granular design and defect data to steer the build. Both complain the current single status report serves neither well. How should the program manager best resolve this?
choices: Ask the sponsor and architect to agree on a single shared level of reporting detail.
Keep one comprehensive report but add an executive summary layer for the sponsor to read.
Draw two tailored views from one data source: an outcome summary and design-detail report.
Produce the detailed report and let each reader extract the parts relevant to them.
questions.explanation: Best: C — communications should be tailored to each audience's needs from one source of truth, so the sponsor sees outcomes and the architect sees design detail without duplicating or diluting data. Closest miss — B: adding an executive summary on top is partial tailoring and better than today, but it still forces both readers through one artifact rather than a fit-for-purpose view. Also plausible — A, D: A asks two roles with legitimately different needs to converge on one detail level, misdiagnosing the issue; D is essentially the failing self-serve report they already have.

questions.question: A department director who championed a supply-chain analytics project from the start has, over the last month, stopped attending steering reviews and no longer answers status emails. Nothing in the project's scope, sponsor, or delivery performance has changed, and the director stays cordial in hallway encounters. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Escalate to the sponsor that a key stakeholder has disengaged and ask them to intervene.
Re-engage the director directly in a brief one-on-one to learn what changed and how they want to stay involved.
Scale back the director's inclusion in reviews to match their apparent drop in interest.
Continue as normal and assume the director will re-engage when a decision needs them.
questions.explanation: Best: B — a previously committed stakeholder going quiet is a cue to re-engage directly and diagnose the cause (workload, waning relevance, or feeling sidelined) before assuming why; a short one-on-one both surfaces the reason and repairs the relationship. Closest miss — A: escalating to the sponsor may help eventually, but jumping to it before a direct conversation is premature and can strain a champion relationship. Also plausible — C, D: cutting the director's involvement (C) reads a temporary dip as permanent and risks losing an advocate, and waiting passively (D) lets disengagement harden.

questions.question: Delivering a shared-services HR platform depends on sustained cooperation from a payroll department head who does not report to the project manager and is juggling year-end priorities competing for the same staff. Early ad hoc requests are increasingly deprioritized. To secure reliable cooperation over the coming months, what should the project manager do first?
choices: Escalate to a shared executive to mandate the payroll head's participation and resource commitment.
Offer to reciprocate by supporting the payroll head's own initiatives in exchange for cooperation.
Meet the payroll head to align on shared goals and a sustainable commitment.
Formalize the dependency in a written agreement specifying deliverables, dates, and responsibilities.
questions.explanation: Best: C — sustained cooperation from a peer you cannot direct rests first on aligning around shared goals and agreeing a commitment the department head can realistically sustain, the foundation the other tactics build on. Closest miss — B: offering reciprocal support is a strong influence-without-authority move and may well follow, but trading favors before establishing shared purpose can feel transactional and fragile. Also plausible — A, D: A's executive mandate forces short-term compliance yet breeds resentment and rarely yields durable cooperation; D formalizes the dependency, but an agreement without genuine buy-in gets deprioritized like the ad hoc requests already are.
questions.task: Collaborate with stakeholders and influence without authority

questions.question: A payments platform's product owner must sequence two competing epics for the coming quarter but has capacity for only one. A fraud-alert dashboard scores 8 for business value, 10 for time criticality, and 6 for risk reduction, with a job size of 3. A loyalty-rewards module scores 20, 12, and 8 on the same factors, with a job size of 8. Using Weighted Shortest Job First, which epic should be sequenced first?
choices: The loyalty-rewards module, because its WSJF of 5.0 justifies the larger investment
The loyalty-rewards module, because its cost of delay of 40 exceeds the dashboard's 24
The fraud-alert dashboard, because its WSJF of 8.0 exceeds the loyalty module's 5.0
Either epic, splitting the quarter's capacity evenly between both to satisfy both sponsors
questions.explanation: Best: WSJF equals cost of delay divided by job size; the dashboard's 24/3 = 8.0 beats the module's 40/8 = 5.0, so it is sequenced first. Closest miss - B: cost of delay alone favors the module, but WSJF deliberately divides by size to maximize value per unit of effort. Also plausible - A, D: A cites the module's real WSJF yet misreads the lower score as better, and D is a genuine capacity compromise that defeats WSJF's purpose of forcing a value-based sequence.

questions.question: A newly appointed operations vice-president at a manufacturing firm has begun skipping iteration reviews and withholding sign-offs after the division shifted from stage-gated delivery to short iterative cycles. Stakeholder analysis flags the VP as influential but increasingly disengaged from the new way of working. Which is the MOST likely underlying cause of this resistance?
choices: The VP lacks the technical background to interpret incremental product demonstrations
The VP was never consulted before the division adopted iterative delivery
The VP fears losing the scope and schedule predictability that stage gates provided
The VP is shielding division headcount that automation in the release threatens
questions.explanation: Best: resistance aimed at the delivery approach itself, not the project's content, most commonly stems from a perceived loss of the predictability and control that gated delivery gave executives. Closest miss - B: exclusion from the decision genuinely breeds resistance, but the symptom here is approach-specific disengagement rather than grievance over process. Also plausible - A, D: technical unfamiliarity (A) and protecting headcount (D) are real drivers a PM should check, yet neither explains resistance targeted precisely at iterative cadence as directly as lost predictability.

questions.question: Kicking off a cross-functional program to integrate three hospital systems onto a shared electronic-health-record platform, a program manager wants engagement to be effective from the very start. Clinical, IT, and administrative groups all have a stake. Which action will most effectively establish sound stakeholder engagement at the outset?
choices: Draft a communications management plan specifying reporting cadences, formats, and distribution channels
Identify stakeholders and analyze their interests, influence, and expectations to shape engagement
Schedule standing steering-committee meetings with executive sponsors and clinical department leads
Publish a program charter defining objectives, high-level scope, and governance authority
questions.explanation: Best: identifying stakeholders and analyzing their interests, influence, and expectations is the foundation that every subsequent engagement and communication decision depends on. Closest miss - A: a communications plan is essential but should be informed by the stakeholder analysis, so it follows rather than precedes it. Also plausible - C, D: standing committees (C) and a charter (D) both support engagement, yet each is more effective once the analysis has revealed who needs what and how much.

questions.question: A light-rail extension involves dozens of stakeholder groups - regulators, neighborhood associations, utility owners, contractors, and elected officials - and the project manager has limited bandwidth for engagement. She wants a deliberate plan that avoids treating every group the same way. Which approach best supports differentiated stakeholder engagement here?
choices: Assign a dedicated relationship owner to each stakeholder group to personalize all outreach
Rate every group's current involvement level in the register and update it monthly
Distribute tiered newsletters segmented by stakeholder category and preferred update frequency
Classify stakeholders on a power/interest grid and tailor engagement by quadrant
questions.explanation: Best: a power/interest grid prioritizes and classifies stakeholders so effort is matched to each group's influence and interest, precisely the differentiation she needs with limited bandwidth. Closest miss - B: tracking current involvement is a real step, but rating alone, without classifying by influence and interest, does not tell her where to concentrate effort. Also plausible - A, C: a relationship owner per group (A) is thorough but unaffordable at this scale, and tiered newsletters (C) are a useful tactic that should follow, not replace, classification.

questions.question: Two weeks before a major planning workshop for an aerospace avionics program, the project manager wants to minimize the risk of disruptive surprises - late objections, blindsided executives, or reopened decisions - during the session. Several influential stakeholders hold strong but unvoiced opinions. Which preparatory step should take priority before the workshop?
choices: Circulate the complete workshop materials to all invitees on the morning of the session
Pre-socialize the draft agenda and key decisions individually with influential stakeholders beforehand
Build extra agenda time to absorb objections that surface during the workshop itself
Arrange to record the session and distribute minutes so absentees stay informed afterward
questions.explanation: Best: pre-socializing the agenda and key decisions one-on-one surfaces objections privately and lets the PM address them before the room convenes, which is what actually prevents surprises. Closest miss - C: reserving time to handle objections is prudent, but it manages surprises after they erupt rather than preventing them. Also plausible - A, D: same-morning materials (A) arrive too late to shape opinions, and recording with minutes (D) informs absentees but does nothing to defuse live disruption.

questions.question: A merchandising lead insists the new checkout flow must include gift-wrap selection, stating 'our customers expect it,' yet usage analytics show negligible interest and recent user research surfaced no such need. The product owner suspects the requirement rests on belief rather than evidence. Which best explains the stated requirement?
choices: A contractual or regulatory obligation compels the feature regardless of measured demand
The analytics instrumentation is failing to capture the segment that actually wants gift-wrapping
The stakeholder is voicing a proposed solution based on personal assumption, not evidenced need
The item was mis-sequenced in the backlog and truly belongs in a later release
questions.explanation: Best: an expectation asserted as fact but unsupported by analytics or research most likely reflects the stakeholder's personal assumption expressed as a solution rather than an evidenced need. Closest miss - B: before dismissing the request, a rigorous PO checks whether the data itself has a blind spot, making faulty instrumentation a genuine alternative worth ruling out. Also plausible - A, D: a hidden compliance driver (A) or a mere sequencing error (D) are real possibilities, but neither fits a requirement justified purely by unverified belief as squarely as an untested assumption.

questions.question: During a series of expectation-alignment meetings on a telecom operations-support-system rollout, a junior business analyst repeatedly freezes when presenting to senior stakeholders, though she is clearly eager to grow into the role. The project manager, practicing servant leadership, wants to develop her. What is the best way to support her growth?
choices: Deliver the senior-stakeholder presentations yourself until she gradually gains more experience over time
Enroll her in a formal presentation-skills course scheduled for the following quarter
Pair her with a mentor and offer graduated, lower-stakes speaking chances to build confidence
Provide her with detailed written scripts to read aloud during every stakeholder meeting
questions.explanation: Best: mentoring combined with progressively higher-stakes speaking opportunities builds real capability while providing support, the essence of developing a team member through servant leadership. Closest miss - B: formal training helps, but a course next quarter is delayed and detached from the live context where she must perform. Also plausible - A, D: presenting for her (A) removes the growth opportunity entirely, and scripts (D) offer a short-term crutch without building the underlying confidence.

questions.question: On a pharmaceutical data-migration effort, clinical operations considers a shared patient-registry deliverable 'complete' when records load without errors, while the IT department considers it complete only after full reconciliation and audit logging. Both must accept the deliverable. Which should the project manager do first to resolve the conflicting expectations?
choices: Escalate the disagreement to the two sponsors and let them rule which definition governs
Adopt the stricter reconciliation-and-audit definition to minimize downstream data-quality and compliance risk
Record both definitions in the register and let each department accept on its own terms
Facilitate a joint session to agree one definition of done and shared acceptance criteria
questions.explanation: Best: the PM should facilitate the two departments to co-create a single, explicit definition of done and acceptance criteria, resolving the ambiguity at its source before any sign-off. Closest miss - A: escalation is a legitimate fallback, but imposing a sponsor's ruling before the parties have tried to align wastes the chance for shared ownership. Also plausible - B, C: defaulting to the stricter definition (B) may over-engineer the deliverable, and documenting both definitions (C) preserves the conflict rather than settling it.
questions.task: Align expectations on definition of done

questions.question: After categorizing stakeholders for a bank's digital-onboarding release, the project manager finds several high-influence, high-interest leaders pulling in different directions: compliance demands tighter identity controls, sales wants the fastest possible signup, and operations wants lower support load - all for the same release. What is the best way to move forward?
choices: Ask the sponsor to decide whose goals take priority for this particular release
Facilitate a working session to surface competing goals and negotiate shared release objectives
Spread each leader's goals across successive releases so every stakeholder is eventually satisfied
Weight the backlog by each leader's influence score and prioritize the highest-scoring goals
questions.explanation: Best: facilitating the influential leaders to surface trade-offs and negotiate shared release objectives aligns them on common outcomes and preserves their collective ownership. Closest miss - A: sponsor arbitration is appropriate if facilitation stalls, but reaching for authority first forfeits the alignment that collaboration can achieve. Also plausible - C, D: sequencing goals across releases (C) still leaves this release contested, and influence-weighting (D) can systematically sideline compliance or operations concerns that carry genuine risk.

questions.question: An enterprise-software team delivers a potentially shippable increment every two weeks, but a key customer expects to see working software every week and values frequent visibility into progress. The team has determined that switching to one-week iterations would materially increase planning and review overhead for this kind of work. Comparing a shift to one-week iterations against keeping the two-week cadence with an added interim mid-iteration demo, which approach best fits and why?
choices: Shorten iterations to one week so delivery frequency matches the customer's stated expectation exactly
Keep the two-week cadence but add an interim mid-iteration demo of in-progress work
Explain that a two-week cadence is standard practice and ask the customer to accept it
Release partial features weekly outside the iteration boundary to meet the customer's request
questions.explanation: Best: adding an interim demo satisfies the customer's real need - frequent visibility - without halving iteration length and absorbing the extra planning, review, and overhead a one-week cadence imposes. Closest miss - A: switching to one-week iterations literally meets the request, but the added ceremony can cut throughput and may not suit the work's natural batch size. Also plausible - C, D: setting the expectation that two weeks is standard (C) risks appearing dismissive of a reasonable ask, and releasing features off-cadence (D) undermines the very rhythm that protects quality.

questions.question: A capability an internal customer had expected was quietly descoped early in the project to protect the schedule, but no one told the customer, who will encounter the gap at next week's release review. The project manager learns of this today. What is the best course of action?
choices: Add the missing capability to the next release's backlog and brief the customer then
Escalate to the sponsor to authorize restoring the capability before the release review occurs
Inform the customer now, explain the schedule trade-off, and jointly decide how to handle the gap
Prepare a written change log documenting the descoping decision for the customer's later reference
questions.explanation: Best: proactively informing the customer today, explaining the trade-off, and deciding together restores transparency and trust before the review turns into an ambush. Closest miss - B: escalating to restore the capability may be warranted, but it skips the essential customer conversation and presumes restoration is the right fix. Also plausible - A, D: deferring to the next backlog (A) still delays honest disclosure, and a change log (D) documents the decision but leaves the customer to discover it unaided.

questions.question: Across three releases with constant feature-delivery volume, internal-customer satisfaction held steady at 4.3, 4.4, and 4.3 out of 5, while the external-customer Net Promoter Score fell from +28 to +15 to -4. The project manager reviews these trends before planning the next release. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
choices: External customers' expectations are diverging from what the releases deliver, warranting focused re-engagement
Overall satisfaction is stable, since the internal average stays high across all three releases
The declining Net Promoter Score is likely statistical noise given constant delivery volume
Internal and external customers value different features, so entirely separate roadmaps are required
questions.explanation: Best: steady internal scores alongside a sharply falling external NPS signal that external customers' expectations are outpacing what the releases deliver, so targeted external re-engagement is the indicated response. Closest miss - D: differing internal and external priorities is a fair reading, but jumping straight to separate roadmaps over-reaches before the divergence is even understood. Also plausible - B, C: averaging in the stable internal figure (B) masks the external collapse, and dismissing a swing from +28 to -4 as noise (C) ignores a clear, consistent downward trend.

questions.question: Over successive releases of a fixed-price utility SCADA upgrade, an external customer's expectations have expanded well beyond the contracted scope, even though the signed scope has not changed. The customer now assumes several unbudgeted capabilities are included. The project manager must respond. What is the best course of action?
choices: Quietly absorb the added expectations to protect the long-term customer relationship and goodwill
Decline the added expectations, citing the contract, and hold firmly to the baseline scope
Log every new expectation and defer all of them to a future contract-renewal negotiation
Realign expectations to the baseline, then route genuinely valued additions through change control
questions.explanation: Best: transparently resetting expectations against the contracted baseline while offering change control for additions the customer truly values protects the agreement and the relationship at once. Closest miss - B: a contractual refusal is legitimate and defensible, but a purely defensive stance forgoes the value and goodwill that a governed change path can capture. Also plausible - A, C: absorbing the scope silently (A) erodes margin and sets a precedent, and deferring everything to renewal (C) leaves today's misunderstanding unaddressed.

questions.question: On a hybrid public-sector case-management project, a key customer keeps requesting small refinements after every sprint demonstration - each minor on its own, but collectively straining the plan. Comparing handling them through the prioritized backlog and change process versus implementing each tweak immediately, which approach best fits and why?
choices: Refuse further post-demo refinements and admit changes only at formal milestone gate reviews.
Capture each refinement in the prioritized backlog; take an item through change control only when it affects the controlled baseline, contract, or funding.
Implement every small refinement right after each demo to keep the customer continuously satisfied.
Route every refinement, however small, through the formal change control board before it may enter the backlog.
questions.explanation: Best: B — on a hybrid project, ongoing refinements flow through the prioritized backlog, and formal change control is invoked only when a refinement affects the controlled baseline, a contract term, or a funding threshold — not for every tweak. Closest miss — C: implementing tweaks immediately reflects a sound agile instinct to satisfy the customer, but without prioritization it is exactly how incremental scope creep accumulates. Also plausible — A, D: gate-only changes (A) are too rigid for a hybrid cadence, and sending every small item to a change board (D) over-controls normal backlog management and stalls flow.

questions.question: Before planning the next increment, a project manager surveys an internal finance customer, scoring four candidate features on importance and current satisfaction (each out of 5): automated reconciliation 4.8 / 2.1; custom dashboards 3.9 / 3.6; bulk export 4.2 / 3.9; audit trail 4.6 / 4.4. Which feature should anchor the next increment?
choices: Custom dashboards, because its importance and current satisfaction are both comfortably above average
Audit trail, because its high importance score signals a critical, compliance-related capability need
Bulk export, because its importance modestly exceeds its current satisfaction level
Automated reconciliation, because its high importance and low satisfaction show the largest value gap
questions.explanation: Best: the widest gap between importance and current satisfaction - automated reconciliation at 4.8 versus 2.1 - marks where the customer values most and is served least, so it delivers the greatest value if improved next. Closest miss - B: audit trail is highly important, but at 4.4 satisfaction it is already well met, so investing there yields little additional value. Also plausible - A, C: dashboards (A) are already satisfactory with a tiny gap, and bulk export (C) shows only a slim shortfall, both far smaller opportunities than reconciliation.

questions.question: Six weeks after a patient-intake module went live, the clinic's operations director reports that a new state regulation changed their booking workflow, so the delivered feature no longer matches how staff actually work. The product now sits in a support-and-enhancement phase with a standing backlog and an assigned product owner. What should the delivery lead do first?
choices: Reconfigure the workflow immediately to restore the operations director's daily productivity.
Add the request to the product backlog for the owner to reprioritize by value.
Raise a formal change request and route it through the enhancement change-control board for approval.
Reopen the closed project and reconvene the original delivery team to rework it.
questions.explanation: Best: B — in a support-and-enhancement phase with a standing backlog, the evolved need is new value the product owner should prioritize against other work, keeping outcomes aligned. Closest miss — A: reconfiguring immediately is responsive and customer-focused, but it bypasses the owner's prioritization and can crowd out higher-value work. Also plausible — C, D: a formal change request adds governance overhead before value is weighed, and reopening the closed project is heavier than the standing backlog requires.

questions.question: An avionics program's only engineer fluent in a legacy test-harness scripting language transfers to another program in two sprints. The program manager wants paired sessions where the engineer coaches two teammates, but coaching time is limited. Before those sessions can genuinely protect the program, what must happen first?
choices: Identify which harness tasks are business-critical and at risk to focus the sessions.
Draft a comprehensive written manual covering every script the engineer has ever authored.
Extend the engineer's program assignment until every piece of knowledge is transferred.
Assign both teammates to shadow the engineer on whatever tasks arise each day.
questions.explanation: Best: A — scoping which harness knowledge is business-critical and at risk lets the limited coaching time target the highest-value tacit skills before the engineer leaves. Closest miss — D: shadowing does transfer knowledge, but without prioritization scarce time may go to low-risk routine tasks. Also plausible — B, C: full documentation is slow for tacit skills, and extending the assignment may be outside the manager's authority to grant.

questions.question: In a clinical-trial analytics project, the richest knowledge — why certain statistical modeling choices were made — lives tacitly with three senior biostatisticians and rarely reaches the wider team. Existing documentation captures the what but not the reasoning behind it. What is the best way to spread this tacit knowledge across the team?
choices: Require the senior biostatisticians to write design-rationale documents for every model.
Record the seniors presenting each finished model in a shared video library.
Bring in a consultant to interview the seniors and build a knowledge base.
Pair juniors with seniors on live modeling work with regular collaborative reviews.
questions.explanation: Best: D — tacit reasoning transfers through socialization: joint work and dialogue where juniors watch decisions made in context. Closest miss — B: recorded walkthroughs share more than plain documents, yet stay one-way and capture conclusions more than in-the-moment reasoning. Also plausible — A, C: rationale documents and an external knowledge base are legitimate explicit-capture efforts, but both struggle to externalize genuine judgment.

questions.question: On a core-banking migration, engineers keep private runbooks, decline to cross-train, and route every question about their module back to themselves. Prior restructurings at the bank retained whoever looked irreplaceable. The engineers are skilled and are not overloaded. What most likely explains the knowledge-hoarding behavior?
choices: Engineers lack the facilitation and coaching skills that teaching peers would demand.
The project's runbook tooling is inadequate for sharing knowledge across the team.
Being the sole knowledge holder is seen as protecting one's job.
Cross-training was never written into the team's working agreements.
questions.explanation: Best: C — when history signals that indispensability protects jobs, capable people rationally hoard knowledge; the incentive, not skill or tooling, drives it. Closest miss — D: missing working agreements remove a prompt to share, but adding them rarely overcomes a felt threat to job security. Also plausible — A, B: weak coaching skills and poor tooling can dampen sharing, yet the stem shows able, unburdened engineers deliberately routing questions to themselves.

questions.question: Halfway through a multi-phase rollout of bridge-inspection software, the project manager notices each phase repeats the same stakeholder sign-off errors made in the prior phase. Retrospectives are scheduled only at project close. The team is willing to improve but has no routine to surface and act on lessons during delivery. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Introduce short recurring retrospectives to capture and apply lessons within each phase.
Escalate the repeated errors to the sponsor and request added review resources.
Update the lessons-learned register now with the sign-off errors seen so far.
Assign a team member to audit each phase's sign-offs before the next begins.
questions.explanation: Best: A — frequent retrospectives create a feedback loop that surfaces and corrects recurring errors while the project runs, not after. Closest miss — C: updating the register captures the lessons, but recording without a cadence to apply them is exactly why the mistakes repeat. Also plausible — B, D: escalating for review resources and adding a sign-off audit catch errors through inspection rather than building the team's own improvement habit.
