questions.question: Two feature squads in a telecom program — one in Dublin, one in Bangalore — are each about to build a near-identical API rate-limiting library, unaware of the other's plan. Both have capacity and their own designs. The program manager learns of the overlap at a scrum-of-scrums. What should the program manager do?
choices: Let each squad proceed and afterward compare the libraries to keep the better one.
Assign the library to one squad and redirect the other to different work.
Escalate the duplication to the sponsor as a resource-efficiency risk.
Bring both squads together to share designs and agree how to converge.
questions.explanation: Best: D — surfacing the overlap to both self-organizing squads lets them share designs and decide jointly to converge or split, removing duplication while preserving ownership. Closest miss — B: reassigning the work ends the overlap, but a top-down split skips the teams' knowledge sharing and may discard the better design. Also plausible — A, C: running both wastes capacity, and escalating adds delay when the squads can resolve it directly.

questions.question: A grid-monitoring platform is transitioning to a 24/7 network operations center that will run and troubleshoot it. The team has delivered runbooks, architecture diagrams, and recorded demos. Before the operations manager will accept the handover as complete, what should the project manager ensure happens first?
choices: Deliver a signed operations manual and archive all of the project's technical documentation.
Have operations staff resolve simulated incidents with the team available to coach.
Schedule a formal handover ceremony with sponsors to mark the transition.
Provide a 90-day warranty during which the team fixes any defects found.
questions.explanation: Best: B — readiness is proven when operations staff handle realistic incidents themselves with the team coaching, turning documentation into working capability before ownership passes. Closest miss — D: a warranty period is a prudent safety net, but it lets the team keep solving problems instead of confirming operations can. Also plausible — A, C: a signed manual and a handover ceremony are normal closeout steps, yet neither shows operations can actually run the platform.

questions.question: Kicking off a hybrid retail-analytics program, the manager must communicate with C-suite sponsors, store managers, and floor end users at once. One option is a single weekly all-hands update sent to everyone; another is segmented communications tailored to each group's decisions and detail needs. Which approach fits this stakeholder mix better, and why?
choices: The single all-hands update, because one consistent message prevents contradictory information.
The single all-hands update, because it is the most efficient use of time.
Segmented communications, because each group needs different content and detail to act.
Segmented communications, because executives should receive information the others never see.
questions.explanation: Best: C — tailoring content and depth to each audience's decisions is what makes communication effective across a diverse hybrid stakeholder set. Closest miss — D: segmentation is the right approach, but the reasoning is wrong — it matches information to needs, not withholds information from groups. Also plausible — A, B: a single update aids consistency and saves time, yet one message buries executives in detail and leaves end users missing what they need.

questions.question: A newly formed, cross-functional team is quiet in reviews; members rarely raise concerns or admit mistakes. Which TWO actions best build the psychological safety needed for candid input?
choices: Respond to surfaced problems and mistakes with curiosity and support rather than blame.
Ask the most senior member to summarize the team's view so meetings stay efficient.
Model fallibility by openly acknowledging your own uncertainties and errors.
Reward the person who reports the most issues each week.
Keep concerns in private one-on-ones so no one is put on the spot in the group.
questions.explanation: Best: safety grows when problems meet curiosity, not blame (A), and when the leader models fallibility (C). Closest miss — E: routing concerns to private one-on-ones feels protective and is sometimes useful, but it prevents the team-level candor that psychological safety is meant to create. Also plausible — B silences other voices by deferring to the senior member, and D invites gaming by rewarding issue-count rather than genuine openness.

questions.question: A sponsor receives this weekly extract: 47 tasks in progress, 12 blocked, 210 story points completed, 38 open defects, 6 pull requests merged. She says she still cannot tell whether the project will hit its committed release date. What does her feedback most directly indicate the report is missing?
choices: More granular task-level detail showing exactly what each engineer is doing.
A risk register summarizing the probability and impact of each blocked task.
A financial view showing budget consumed against the work completed so far.
Outcome indicators relating progress to the release date and scope remaining.
questions.explanation: Best: D — the sponsor needs progress framed against the goal — a forecast of date and remaining scope — not raw activity counts; the report lists outputs with no line of sight to the outcome. Closest miss — C: a budget-versus-work view adds health context, but her stated concern is the release date, which cost figures do not answer. Also plausible — A, B: more task detail moves the wrong way, and a blocker risk register helps yet still does not convert activity into a schedule forecast.

questions.question: An automotive-software squad is half on-site and half remote. The team's kanban board, burndown chart, and impediment list live on the office wall, and remote members repeatedly say they feel out of the loop and miss decisions. The team values its physical radiators. What should the scrum master do?
choices: Photograph the wall artifacts each day and email them to the remote members.
Move the radiators to a shared digital tool used live by everyone.
Add a daily call where on-site members read the board out to remote staff.
Rotate remote members on-site periodically so they see the boards in person.
questions.explanation: Best: B — a shared digital radiator gives every member the same live information regardless of location, removing the office-centric asymmetry. Closest miss — C: a read-out call does share the board, but it keeps the office as the source of truth and adds synchronous time for remote members. Also plausible — A, D: daily photos and periodic on-site rotations help at the margin, but both leave remote members working from stale or occasional views.

questions.question: A public-sector IT program must submit prescribed governance artifacts — requirements traceability, milestone plans, gate approvals — at each phase gate, while its software is built in two-week iterations. The PMO insists the gates stay; the teams resist heavyweight reporting that stalls their flow. What should the project manager do?
choices: Ask the PMO to waive the phase-gate reports for the adaptive work.
Have the teams pause iterations near each gate to assemble the artifacts.
Generate the governance artifacts from the teams' existing iteration data and tooling.
Appoint an analyst to produce the gate reports separately from the teams.
questions.explanation: Best: C — tailoring lets required governance artifacts be derived from data the teams already produce, meeting compliance without a parallel reporting burden. Closest miss — D: a dedicated analyst shields the teams, but reports built apart from their real data risk drifting from ground truth and duplicating effort. Also plausible — A, B: seeking a waiver may breach mandatory governance, and pausing iterations sacrifices the flow the adaptive approach exists to protect.
questions.task: Tailor governance in a hybrid life cycle

questions.question: During a site walk, a project's construction manager and the lead architect informally agreed to switch the building's cladding material. The structural engineer, client representative, and safety officer learned of it later, were caught off guard, and trust dipped. What should the construction manager do now?
choices: Convene the affected stakeholders to openly review the decision and its impacts.
Send a written notice documenting the decision so a clear record exists.
Reverse the cladding decision until it passes through formal change control.
Apologize individually to each stakeholder for not informing them sooner.
questions.explanation: Best: A — convening the affected stakeholders to examine the decision and its impacts restores transparency, subjects the choice to proper scrutiny, and rebuilds trust at once. Closest miss — C: routing it through change control is the right governance instinct, but reversing first can discard a sound decision a transparent review might confirm. Also plausible — B, D: a written record and individual apologies each address part of the problem, but neither reopens the decision to the group that should have been involved.

questions.question: A global program's steering group has 8 members who currently communicate with one another ad hoc, and stakeholders complain of message overload. Three regional leads are about to join the group, each communicating directly with everyone. Using the communication-channels formula, how many additional channels will adding the three members create?
choices: 24 new channels — each new member linked only to the eight prior members.
30 new channels — the three new members each linking to the other ten.
55 new channels — the total channels once all eleven members are counted.
27 new channels — the eleven-member total minus the original eight-member total.
questions.explanation: Best: D — channels equal n(n-1)/2; eleven members give 55 and the original eight give 28, so 27 channels are added. Closest miss — B: counting each new member against ten others yields 30 but double-counts the three new-to-new links. Also plausible — A: 24 counts only new-to-existing links and omits the three among the new members; C: 55 is the full total, not the increase over the original 28.

questions.question: A telecom program bundles two workstreams under one plan: a lawful-intercept compliance component whose specifications are fixed by a national regulator and will not change, and a subscriber-experience component whose features are still being discovered through beta feedback. Leadership wants a single delivery approach imposed across both to simplify governance. How should the program manager respond?
choices: Standardize on predictive delivery so the regulator-facing governance and audit trail stay uniform across both components
Standardize on agile delivery so the whole program can absorb the subscriber component's evolving requirements
Tailor the approach per component, running the compliance work predictively and the subscriber work adaptively under one plan
Defer the decision to each component lead and consolidate whatever cadences they independently select
questions.explanation: Best: tailoring the life cycle to each component's requirement stability is the ECO/PMBOK 8 stance; fixed regulatory specs suit predictive, discovered features suit adaptive, and both can coexist under one integrated program plan. Closest miss — A: uniform predictive governance is defensible for auditability but forces the discovery-driven component into rigid up-front scope, raising rework. Also plausible — B, D: agile-everywhere is reasonable for the subscriber work but mishandles frozen regulatory specs, and delegating to leads is a real move yet abandons the program manager's integration duty and risks incoherent cadences.
questions.task: Select delivery approach / life cycle tailoring

questions.question: Before recommending how a multi-country pharmacovigilance platform should be delivered, a program manager wants a defensible basis for the choice rather than a personal preference. Several sponsors each favor a different method based on past projects. What should the program manager do FIRST to ground the recommendation?
choices: Poll the sponsors and adopt whichever development approach the majority of them prefer
Assess suitability factors such as requirement stability, risk, regulatory constraints, and team distribution
Select the approach used on the organization's most recent successful platform of similar size
Draft the schedule and cost baselines and let the resulting constraints reveal the approach
questions.explanation: Best: an evidence-based approach selection starts by assessing suitability factors (requirement volatility, risk, compliance load, team setup) — that is the defensible basis the ECO expects before recommending a method. Closest miss — C: reusing the last comparable success is a real heuristic and better than guessing, but it substitutes precedent for analysis of this platform's actual drivers. Also plausible — A, D: canvassing sponsors respects stakeholders and building baselines is real planning work, yet a majority vote and back-derived constraints both skip the deliberate suitability analysis that should precede them.

questions.question: A public infrastructure authority mandates that environmental and social sustainability be weighed in every project decision, not just reported afterward. A project manager beginning a light-rail extension wants this mandate to actually shape trade-off choices about routing, materials, and phasing throughout delivery. Where should the sustainability considerations be embedded so they influence ongoing decisions rather than sit as a static statement?
choices: In the project charter's purpose statement so the sustainability intent is authorized from the outset
In the decision criteria used to evaluate options, alternatives, and change requests throughout delivery
In a standalone sustainability report issued to the authority at each phase gate
In the risk register as environmental threats with assigned owners and responses
questions.explanation: Best: to shape ongoing trade-offs, sustainability must live inside the decision/evaluation criteria applied to alternatives and change requests, so every routing, material, and phasing choice is scored against it. Closest miss — A: charter authorization matters and signals intent, but a purpose statement alone does not enter day-to-day option evaluation. Also plausible — C, D: periodic reporting satisfies the authority and a risk register captures environmental threats, yet both treat sustainability as something tracked or disclosed rather than a criterion actively weighed in each decision.

questions.question: On an aerospace avionics upgrade, different leads produced the scope, schedule, cost, and resource plans in parallel. Integrating them, the project manager notices the cost plan funds two systems engineers for the integration phase while the schedule shows three engineers working that phase in parallel to hit the milestone. What does this signal most directly?
choices: The cost estimate is understated and should be raised to fund the third engineer
The schedule is too aggressive and the integration milestone should be moved out
The component plans were built on inconsistent assumptions and must be reconciled
The resource-leveling was skipped and the schedule should be leveled to two engineers
questions.explanation: Best: a staffing figure that differs between the cost and schedule plans is a classic symptom of components built in isolation on conflicting assumptions; the integrative act is to reconcile them before deciding which figure is right. Closest miss — D: leveling to two engineers is a plausible reconciliation, but choosing that fix presumes the cost plan is correct without validating which assumption holds. Also plausible — A, B: raising cost or slipping the milestone are each real resolutions, yet both prematurely pick one plan as truth instead of first surfacing and resolving the assumption mismatch.

questions.question: Midway through a hospital electronic-records migration, several planning assumptions collapse: a vendor API is deprecated, and a partner hospital's data-readiness date slips by a quarter. Parts of the integrated management plan no longer reflect reality, and the team is unsure which baseline still governs. What is the most appropriate action for the project manager?
choices: Continue executing to the approved baseline to preserve stability until the phase gate
Assess the impact of the invalid assumptions and process baseline updates through integrated change control
Revise the affected plan sections directly and brief the team on the new working baselines
Escalate to the sponsor for a decision on whether to replan the entire migration
questions.explanation: Best: when assumptions underlying the baseline prove invalid, the integrative response is to assess impact and route the needed baseline changes through integrated change control, keeping the plan authoritative. Closest miss — D: sponsor escalation is warranted if impacts breach thresholds, but escalating before assessing impact skips the analysis that tells the sponsor what decision is even needed. Also plausible — A, C: holding to the approved baseline preserves discipline and updating plan sections is the eventual work, yet executing a known-invalid baseline courts rework and editing baselines outside change control breaks configuration control.

questions.question: On a banking core-modernization project, an AI assistant ingests the charter, contracts, and design documents and returns 140 candidate risks, many overlapping or generic. The project manager must turn this raw output into something the team can act on. Which approach should the project manager take with the AI-generated list?
choices: Add all 140 items to the risk register so no identified risk is lost before analysis
Have the team perform qualitative analysis to de-duplicate, assess, and prioritize the candidates
Accept the AI's implied ranking and address the risks in the order the tool listed them
Discard the list as unreliable and run a fresh human risk-identification workshop instead
questions.explanation: Best: AI output is an input to risk identification, not a finished register; the team should apply qualitative analysis to consolidate, assess probability/impact, and prioritize before acting. Closest miss — D: a human workshop produces quality risks and is defensible, but discarding usable AI candidates wastes signal and duplicates effort rather than curating what exists. Also plausible — A, C: registering all 140 preserves completeness and following the tool's order is convenient, yet both push unvetted, unprioritized items forward and let the tool substitute for the team's analytical judgment.
questions.task: Use AI-assisted tools / govern risk process

questions.question: After two increments of a retail loyalty-app rebuild, the sponsor asks the project manager to justify continued funding before releasing the next tranche. Early usage data is available, the business case projected specific engagement gains, and market conditions have shifted since kickoff. On what should the continuation recommendation MOST rely?
choices: The percentage of planned scope delivered across the two completed increments so far
Whether measured and projected benefits still justify the remaining investment and case
The team's current velocity trend and its confidence in meeting the release date
The sponsor's stated appetite to keep funding the initiative through completion
questions.explanation: Best: a continue/stop recommendation is a benefits-realization decision — it rests on whether the value the initiative will deliver still justifies the remaining spend against an updated business case, especially as the market shifted. Closest miss — A: scope delivered shows progress and is a real input, but output completed is not the same as value earned or a still-valid case. Also plausible — C, D: velocity informs deliverability and sponsor appetite reflects governance reality, yet neither answers whether continuing remains worth the investment, which is the crux of the justification.

questions.question: A program manager reviews the consolidated plans of six interdependent energy-grid projects. Each project's own manager has validated its plan in isolation. The program manager wants to surface problems that only appear when the plans are viewed together. Which review focus is MOST likely to reveal those cross-project problems?
choices: Verifying each project's internal schedule logic and critical path independently
Examining inter-project dependencies, shared-resource contention, and interface timing across the plans
Confirming every project has a complete risk register with assigned owners
Checking that each project's cost baseline matches its approved budget allocation
questions.explanation: Best: problems invisible to single-project review live at the seams — cross-project dependencies, contended shared resources, and interface timing — so that is where the program-level integration review adds value. Closest miss — A: sound internal schedule logic matters, but validating each critical path independently is exactly the single-project lens that already passed. Also plausible — C, D: complete risk registers and reconciled cost baselines are legitimate quality checks, yet both are per-project attributes that would not expose the emergent conflicts arising from how the projects interact.

questions.question: Leadership will not fund a nationwide smart-metering rollout until they understand how the whole initiative will be sequenced, sourced, and deployed across regions. A PMO analyst is asked to prepare the artifact that gives this end-to-end view for the funding decision. Which artifact best provides that sequenced, high-level picture without committing to detailed task scheduling?
choices: A detailed work breakdown structure decomposing the rollout into work packages
A roadmap laying out phases, major milestones, sourcing, and regional deployment sequence
A resource management plan defining acquisition, roles, and release across the regions
A milestone list enumerating the fixed dates leadership must approve for funding
questions.explanation: Best: a roadmap gives leadership the sequenced, high-level view of phases, sourcing, and deployment order needed for a funding decision, without descending into task-level scheduling. Closest miss — D: a milestone list conveys sequence and key dates and is a real funding aid, but it lacks the sourcing and phase-level narrative that shows how the initiative unfolds. Also plausible — A, C: a WBS and a resource plan are legitimate planning artifacts, yet a WBS decomposes work rather than sequencing the rollout, and a resource plan covers staffing, not the end-to-end deployment story leadership asked for.

questions.question: On an agile insurance-claims platform, several powerful stakeholders keep inserting 'must-have' items directly into the current sprint after it has started, disrupting the team's commitment and eroding predictability. The Scrum Master needs a durable fix rather than a one-time pushback. What is the best way to handle this pattern?
choices: Have the team absorb the urgent items this sprint and renegotiate scope at the review
Route all incoming requests through the product owner and the prioritized product backlog
Ask the stakeholders to formally justify each insertion before the team accepts it
Extend the sprint length so the team can accommodate both committed and injected work
questions.explanation: Best: the durable fix is to protect the sprint by channeling every request through the product owner and the backlog, restoring single-point prioritization and the team's commitment. Closest miss — C: requiring justification adds a filter and is reasonable, but it still admits mid-sprint insertion and does not re-establish the product owner's ordering authority. Also plausible — A, D: absorbing items then renegotiating is a pragmatic short-term move and lengthening the sprint buys capacity, yet both accommodate the disruption rather than correcting the broken intake path that causes it.
questions.task: Protect the team / manage backlog intake

questions.question: A predictive defense-systems contract carries genuinely ambiguous requirements in its sensor-fusion subsystem, and the project manager is worried that misunderstandings will surface only during integration testing as costly rework. Up-front scope must still be baselined. What is the best way to reduce that downstream rework risk while remaining predictive?
choices: Add schedule and cost contingency to absorb the rework when the ambiguities surface later
Build a prototype of the ambiguous subsystem to clarify requirements before baselining scope
Freeze the ambiguous requirements as written and manage changes through change control
Decompose the subsystem into finer work packages to expose the ambiguity in the WBS
questions.explanation: Best: prototyping the ambiguous subsystem elaborates and validates requirements before the baseline, attacking the root cause of downstream rework while keeping the overall approach predictive. Closest miss — A: contingency is prudent and expected, but reserves fund rework after it happens rather than preventing the misunderstanding. Also plausible — C, D: freezing scope with change control imposes discipline and finer decomposition improves clarity of known work, yet neither resolves the underlying ambiguity — locking in unclear requirements or subdividing them still leaves the misunderstanding to emerge at integration.

questions.question: Having secured an approved scope statement for a water-treatment plant upgrade, the project manager needs to convert that scope into discrete deliverables and assignable, estimable work packages before building schedule and cost estimates. Which tool most directly produces those work packages from the approved scope?
choices: Decomposition applied to the scope to create a work breakdown structure
Rolling-wave planning to elaborate near-term work as details emerge
Expert judgment from the engineering leads to estimate each deliverable
Alternatives analysis to compare construction methods for each component
questions.explanation: Best: decomposition is the tool that breaks approved scope into deliverables and work packages via the WBS — precisely the assignable, estimable units needed before estimating. Closest miss — B: rolling-wave planning does elaborate work over time and is a real scheduling technique, but it defers detail rather than producing the full work-package structure from the scope now. Also plausible — C, D: expert judgment supports estimating and alternatives analysis informs method selection, yet neither creates the work-package breakdown; they operate on components decomposition must first define.

questions.question: On a healthcare-IT scheduling product, the product owner and the development team repeatedly clash at reviews over whether a large story is 'finished enough' to demonstrate — one says the happy path works, the other expects error handling and accessibility. These disputes recur across stories and waste review time. What would most reliably prevent them going forward?
choices: Have the product owner specify detailed acceptance criteria on each story before the sprint
Establish and apply a shared definition of done that all stories must satisfy
Split large stories into smaller ones so completeness is easier to judge at review
Add a pre-review checkpoint where the product owner inspects stories before the demo
questions.explanation: Best: recurring disputes about what 'finished' means are resolved by a team-wide definition of done — a shared, standing completeness standard applied to every story, which acceptance criteria and story size do not provide. Closest miss — A: per-story acceptance criteria clarify that story's expectations, but they vary item to item and still leave the systemic 'done' bar (error handling, accessibility) undefined. Also plausible — C, D: smaller stories ease judgment and a pre-review check catches gaps earlier, yet both work around the missing shared standard rather than establishing the common definition that ends the recurring clash.

questions.question: On a manufacturing MES deployment, after stakeholders signed off on the baselined scope, the project manager notices the team has quietly begun building a predictive-maintenance dashboard that no approved requirement or work package covers. The team believes it adds obvious value. What should the project manager do about the unapproved capability?
choices: Halt the unapproved work and submit a change request for the capability through change control
Let the work continue since it adds value and record it as a discovered requirement
Direct the team to stop and drop the capability because it is outside the baseline
Ask the sponsor to expand the budget so the capability can be formally absorbed
questions.explanation: Best: unbaselined work is scope creep; the disciplined response is to stop it and route the capability through integrated change control so its value and impact are evaluated and, if approved, properly baselined. Closest miss — C: stopping the work is right, but flatly dropping a potentially valuable capability forecloses the evaluation that change control exists to perform. Also plausible — B, D: allowing valuable work to continue respects the team's insight and asking the sponsor for budget anticipates approval, yet both bypass change control — legitimizing creep or committing funds before the change is assessed and authorized.

questions.question: A product owner on a fintech app wants to test whether users will actually adopt a new peer-payment feature before the team commits to the full, integrated build. Engineering estimates the complete feature at three months. The product owner asks which lightweight step best validates the core adoption assumption with real users first. Which option best fits?
choices: Release a minimum viable feature with just the core payment flow to real users
Run a full internal QA cycle against the complete feature specification first
Conduct a stakeholder survey asking whether users would use peer payments
Build the complete feature behind a flag and enable it for a small cohort
questions.explanation: Best: a minimum viable feature exposing only the core flow to real users tests the adoption assumption with genuine behavior at the lowest cost before the full build — exactly the validated-learning intent. Closest miss — D: a flagged cohort release does test real users, but it requires building the complete feature first, defeating the goal of validating before the three-month commitment. Also plausible — B, C: internal QA and surveys are legitimate techniques, yet QA verifies conformance rather than adoption, and a survey captures stated intent, not the actual usage behavior the assumption hinges on.

questions.question: A firmware module for a telecom base-station upgrade has passed internal quality control and traces cleanly to every requirement, yet the operator's acceptance test has not been run. The delivery team wants to invoice the milestone and reassign staff. Before this milestone can be recognized as complete, which condition must be satisfied first?
choices: The operator formally accepts the deliverable through the agreed validation activity.
Quality re-runs verification to reconfirm the module meets its requirements.
The team documents lessons learned from the module before reassignment.
The contract's milestone payment clause is reviewed to confirm billing eligibility.
questions.explanation: Best: A — the deliverable is verified (built right) but not validated; formal customer acceptance through the agreed validation activity is the condition that gates completion. Closest miss — D: reviewing billing eligibility is legitimate governance, but acceptance must precede billing, so it is not the first gate. Also plausible — B, C: re-running verification and capturing lessons learned are real closeout actions, yet verification is already done and lessons learned follow acceptance.

questions.question: A clinical-trial data platform must satisfy fixed regulatory validation requirements while its analytics features evolve as investigators learn what they need. The program team debates whether to place all scope under one formal change-control baseline or to run the regulated scope under change control and the analytics scope as an adaptive backlog. Which approach best fits this context, and why?
choices: One baseline under formal change control, keeping full regulatory traceability intact.
Split tracks: regulated scope under change control, analytics on an adaptive backlog.
One adaptive backlog for all scope, accelerating both regulatory and analytics work.
Split tracks, but freeze the analytics backlog at each regulatory submission.
questions.explanation: Best: B — tailoring matches control to variability: the fixed regulatory scope belongs under formal change control for traceability, while the evolving analytics scope suits an adaptive backlog. Closest miss — A: a single controlled baseline preserves traceability but over-controls features that must evolve. Also plausible — C, D: one adaptive backlog under-controls compliance, and freezing the backlog at each submission adds needless rigidity to the flexible track.
questions.task: Tailor delivery approach for the project

questions.question: The backlog for a retail checkout redesign holds far more work than the next two sprints can absorb. The product owner must decide the ordering principle, with options ranging from stakeholder seniority to technical convenience. Which basis for sequencing the backlog BEST supports delivering value early?
choices: Order by the requesting stakeholder's organizational seniority to keep sponsors engaged.
Order by technical dependency so foundational components precede dependent ones.
Order by cost of delay relative to effort, surfacing highest value first.
Order by team preference to sustain morale and delivery velocity.
questions.explanation: Best: C — sequencing by cost of delay relative to effort surfaces the highest value-per-cost items, delivering value earliest. Closest miss — B: technical dependencies genuinely constrain order and must be respected, but they shape feasibility rather than set the value basis. Also plausible — A, D: honoring stakeholder seniority sustains sponsorship and honoring team preference sustains morale, yet neither maximizes early value.

questions.question: Twelve months into a multi-year smart-grid modernization, the utility's executive committee questions whether continued funding is justified. The program manager prepares to make the case at the next portfolio review, with several kinds of evidence available. What would BEST demonstrate the program's value to the executives?
choices: Percentage of planned scope completed and budget consumed against plan.
A revised schedule showing remaining milestones and delivery dates.
Stakeholder satisfaction survey results from the affected operating units.
Benefits realized to date measured against the business case targets.
questions.explanation: Best: D — benefits realized to date measured against the business case targets is the truest evidence that the program is producing value. Closest miss — A: scope and budget performance show the program is well-run, but on-plan spending is not the same as value delivered. Also plausible — B, C: a refreshed schedule builds delivery confidence and satisfaction data signals value, yet both are partial next to realized benefits.

questions.question: As a satellite ground-station upgrade kicks off, the operations lead frames value as system uptime, the finance director frames it as lifecycle cost reduction, and the compliance officer frames it as audit readiness. Each anchors decisions to a different definition. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Facilitate agreement on a shared, weighted value framework spanning uptime, lifecycle cost, and audit readiness, so the dimensions are balanced rather than reduced to one.
Draft a benefits management plan reflecting all three value definitions.
Prioritize the sponsor's definition of value to resolve ambiguity quickly.
Map each stakeholder's value definition to specific project metrics.
questions.explanation: Best: A — with stakeholders anchoring to different but legitimate value dimensions, the first step is to facilitate a shared, weighted value framework that holds all three (uptime, lifecycle cost, audit readiness) rather than forcing a single definition. Closest miss — D: mapping each definition to metrics is useful analysis, but without an agreed, weighted framework it leaves the competing priorities unreconciled. Also plausible — B, C: a benefits plan (B) needs the shared framework first, and deferring to the sponsor (C) sidelines legitimate stakeholder value.
questions.task: Align stakeholders on value and success

questions.question: A retail bank can deliver a new mobile lending experience as a single release in twelve months or as monthly increments to a pilot customer segment. Customer needs are uncertain and competitor moves are frequent, though each release triggers a compliance review. Weighing incremental delivery against a single release, which fits this context better and why?
choices: Single release, since batching avoids repeating the compliance review monthly.
Incremental delivery, since frequent feedback reduces building the wrong product.
Single release, since a complete product creates stronger launch impact.
Incremental delivery, but only after all regulatory requirements are finalized.
questions.explanation: Best: B — high uncertainty in customer needs plus frequent competitor moves make short feedback loops the priority; incremental delivery reduces the risk of building the wrong product. Closest miss — A: batching to avoid repeated compliance reviews is a genuine cost saving, but it delays the learning this context most needs. Also plausible — C, D: a single big launch can create market impact, and waiting for regulatory finalization is cautious, yet both forfeit early validation.

questions.question: A hospital network deployed several electronic-health-record enhancements over the past year, but leadership cannot determine whether any of them actually reduced clinician documentation time as intended. Delivery reports show all features shipped on schedule. What is the MOST LIKELY reason the benefit cannot be assessed?
choices: The features were delivered faster than clinicians could adopt them.
The project closed before the benefits realization period had elapsed.
No baseline or benefit metrics were defined before building the features.
The enhancements addressed requirements that stakeholders later deprioritized.
questions.explanation: Best: C — if no baseline or benefit metrics were defined before building, the benefit is unmeasurable no matter how features perform; that is the root cause. Closest miss — B: closing before the realization period can hide benefits, but even then defined metrics would let leadership assess them later. Also plausible — A, D: slow adoption and later-deprioritized requirements can each dampen benefits, yet neither prevents measurement the way a missing baseline does.

questions.question: The sponsor of an industrial-IoT initiative wants evidence of market value within a quarter. The team could build a polished internal monitoring tool for one plant or run a lightweight pilot with three external customers on a minimal feature set. Budget covers only one path this quarter. What should the project manager recommend to the sponsor?
choices: Build the polished internal tool to demonstrate capability before external exposure.
Run both efforts at reduced scope to compare internal and external signals.
Delay the decision until market research quantifies the opportunity first.
Run the external pilot to test real market demand with minimal investment.
questions.explanation: Best: D — the sponsor wants market value fast; a lightweight external pilot tests real demand with minimal spend, producing validated learning within the quarter. Closest miss — A: polishing an internal tool de-risks quality but proves capability, not market demand. Also plausible — B, C: splitting the budget across both dilutes each signal, and market research is legitimate but consumes the quarter without testing real customers.
questions.task: Validate value with a minimum viable increment

questions.question: During a sprint review for an enterprise CRM module, a senior developer proposes adding several capabilities beyond what stakeholders requested, convinced they will delight users. The additions are technically easy and the developer is eager, but the product owner has not requested them. How should the project manager respond?
choices: Route the ideas to the product owner to evaluate against backlog priorities.
Approve the additions, since they are low-effort and may raise satisfaction.
Decline the ideas to protect the committed sprint scope from disruption.
Add the capabilities to the product backlog for a future release automatically.
questions.explanation: Best: A — the product owner owns value and priority decisions, so unrequested ideas should be routed there to weigh against the backlog. Closest miss — D: parking them in the backlog is close, but doing so automatically bypasses the product owner's prioritization. Also plausible — B, C: approving low-effort extras is tempting gold plating, and declining outright protects sprint scope, yet both preempt the owner's call.

questions.question: Halfway through a wind-farm control-system upgrade, updated figures show the remaining cost to complete is 2.4 million and the present value of remaining benefits is 3.1 million, while sunk cost to date is 5 million; the original business case assumed 6 million in total benefits. Considering only forward-looking economics, what do these figures indicate?
choices: Cancel the project, since total lifetime benefits now fall short of cost.
Continue, because the remaining benefits exceed the remaining cost to complete.
Reduce remaining scope to improve the benefit-to-remaining-cost ratio.
Commission a reserve analysis before judging whether to proceed.
questions.explanation: Best: B — forward-looking economics ignore the 5 million sunk cost; remaining benefits of 3.1 million exceed the 2.4 million remaining cost, so completion is justified. Closest miss — A: comparing total benefits to total cost suggests cancelling, but that reasoning improperly counts sunk cost. Also plausible — C, D: trimming scope could improve the ratio and a reserve analysis adds rigor, yet the read already shows continuing is warranted.

questions.question: An upcoming feature on a payments-platform team requires deep expertise in tokenization that no current team member holds. The feature is two sprints away, and the scrum master and team surface the gap during backlog refinement. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Hire a contractor with tokenization expertise before the feature begins.
Reorder the backlog to defer the feature until the skill is acquired.
Work with the team to assess options for closing the skill gap.
Arrange training so an existing member builds the needed expertise.
questions.explanation: Best: C — assessing options with the team before committing respects self-organization and avoids locking in a solution prematurely. Closest miss — A: hiring a contractor can close the gap, but choosing it before assessment skips the analysis. Also plausible — B, D: deferring the feature or training an existing member are both valid remedies, yet each presumes a decision the team should help shape first.
questions.task: Manage skill gaps / build team capability

questions.question: A senior geotechnical engineer is scheduled full-time on two concurrent public-works projects during the same six-week window, and both project managers insist their need is critical. The engineer reports through a functional manager in a matrix organization. As the program manager overseeing both projects, what should you do?
choices: Assign the engineer to the project with the earlier contractual deadline.
Split the engineer's time equally between the two projects for six weeks.
Escalate to the functional manager to reassign resourcing as they choose.
Prioritize by each project's value and risk, then negotiate allocation.
questions.explanation: Best: D — as program manager you own cross-project trade-offs; allocate by each project's value and risk, then negotiate the arrangement. Closest miss — A: prioritizing by the earlier deadline is a reasonable single-factor heuristic, but value and risk give a fuller basis. Also plausible — B, C: an equal split is a common compromise that may satisfy neither, and escalating to the functional manager abdicates the program authority to decide.

questions.question: A specialized environmental test chamber needed for a satellite qualification activity will arrive 8 working days later than planned. The activity that uses it has a total float of 5 working days, and it feeds directly into the launch-readiness milestone on the critical path. Absent any corrective action, how much will the project finish date slip?
choices: The finish date slips by 3 working days.
The finish date slips by 5 working days.
The finish date slips by 8 working days.
The finish date does not slip at all.
questions.explanation: Best: A — the activity has 5 days of total float, so an 8-day delay consumes the float and pushes the critical-path milestone by the remaining 3 working days. Closest miss — C: 8 days is the raw delay but ignores the float that absorbs part of it. Also plausible — B, D: 5 days is the float value itself, and 0 days assumes the float fully covers the delay, but the delay exceeds the float.
questions.task: Analyze schedule impact of a procurement delay

questions.question: A construction schedule shows three critical-path crews at 130 percent allocation for the next month while two non-critical crews sit at 40 percent. The current plan still forecasts an on-time finish, but only if the overallocated crews sustain overtime. What does this resource picture most strongly imply the project manager should do?
choices: Accept the overtime plan, since the schedule still forecasts on-time finish.
Rebalance by reassigning suitable work from the overallocated critical crews to the idle crews (resource optimization).
Crash the critical path by adding new crews to overallocated activities.
Fast-track by overlapping downstream activities to relieve the schedule.
questions.explanation: Best: B — idle non-critical crews alongside overallocated critical crews call for resource optimization: reassign suitable work to available capacity, using leveling if the finish date may move or smoothing if it must hold. Closest miss — C: crashing by adding new crews could shorten the path but spends money while internal capacity sits idle. Also plausible — A, D: relying on sustained overtime is fragile even if the plan still shows on-time finish, and fast-tracking adds rework risk without fixing the imbalance.

questions.question: A mature, self-organizing data-science team on a fraud-detection product wants to choose their own task assignments each iteration rather than have them assigned. Delivery has been reliable and quality high. The servant-leader project manager considers how to handle work assignment going forward. How should the assignment be handled?
choices: Assign tasks by each member's documented skills to optimize throughput.
Let the team self-assign, but require PM approval of each plan.
Enable self-assignment while ensuring priorities and constraints stay clear.
Rotate assignments so every member gains exposure across task types.
questions.explanation: Best: C — a servant-leader empowers a proven self-organizing team to self-assign while ensuring priorities and constraints are clear, pairing autonomy with direction. Closest miss — B: allowing self-assignment but gating each plan on PM approval reinserts the control that undermines empowerment. Also plausible — A, D: skills-based assignment can optimize throughput and rotation builds broader skills, yet both impose structure on a team that has earned self-direction.

questions.question: A biotech firm is standing up a new fill-finish line that blends facility construction with a bespoke batch-control software layer. The delivery lead needs a defensible estimate of labor hours, cleanroom materials, and validation equipment before the budget is locked. Some construction tasks resemble past builds, while the software integration has no precedent. Which estimating approach will produce the most reliable resource estimate for this mixed work?
choices: Apply analogous estimating drawn from the firm's prior line builds across the entire scope of work
Use bottom-up estimating for the novel software integration and parametric or analogous methods where historical data exists
Ask the vendor and construction crews for a single rolled-up figure and reconcile the reported totals
Build a three-point PERT estimate for every task to absorb the uncertainty in both delivery streams
questions.explanation: Best: matching technique to the nature of each work package — bottom-up where the work is novel, parametric/analogous where reliable data exists — is the tailoring the ECO rewards and yields the most defensible resource estimate. Closest miss — D: three-point estimating genuinely addresses uncertainty and is reasonable, but applying it to well-understood construction tasks is wasteful and still fails to decompose the unprecedented software; the discriminator is fit-to-work versus blanket application. Also plausible — A, C: analogous estimating across all scope leans on irrelevant history for the software, and a single vendor roll-up is real expert input yet skips the decomposition that makes the novel estimate credible.

questions.question: A telecom operator is outsourcing a small network-analytics module whose requirements keep shifting as spectrum rules evolve. Procurement leadership prefers a firm-fixed-price deal for budget certainty, while the technical team argues for time-and-materials because the work cannot be fully specified yet. Weighing these two positions against the reality of undefined scope, which contracting choice best balances cost control with the shifting requirements?
choices: Award firm-fixed-price now, since fixed price transfers cost risk to the seller and protects the budget ceiling
Award open-ended time-and-materials so the seller can flex to changing requirements without renegotiation each cycle
Use time-and-materials with a not-to-exceed ceiling and defined rates now, converting to firm-fixed-price once scope stabilizes
Delay the award until requirements are fully baselined, then run a competitive firm-fixed-price bidding process
questions.explanation: Best: time-and-materials with a not-to-exceed ceiling suits work that cannot be specified yet while capping the buyer's exposure, and the planned conversion to fixed price restores certainty once scope firms up. Closest miss — D: waiting to baseline then bidding fixed-price gives the cleanest cost control, but the evolving spectrum rules keep the baseline moving and stall value; the discriminator is progressing under uncertainty versus freezing. Also plausible — A, B: fixed-price now shields the budget but forces the seller to pad or dispute undefined scope, and open-ended time-and-materials flexes to change yet abandons the ceiling that keeps cost defensible.

questions.question: On a municipal water-treatment upgrade, a specialty coatings subcontractor has missed two consecutive milestones, and its finished surfaces pass inspection only intermittently. The subcontractor was selected on lowest price and onboarded quickly to hold the schedule. Reviewing the procurement file alongside progress data, the prime's project manager weighs several explanations. What is the most likely underlying cause of the combined schedule slip and inconsistent quality?
choices: The award emphasized price over capability, so the subcontractor lacks the capacity and process maturity the work demands
The inspection acceptance criteria were never agreed, so quality results vary from one surface to the next
The subcontractor is deliberately slowing the work to justify submitting a later, larger change order
The progress-reporting cadence is too infrequent to catch emerging problems while they are still small
questions.explanation: Best: a lowest-price award with rushed onboarding most economically explains both symptoms at once — thin capacity drives the missed milestones and immature process drives the inconsistent quality — which is exactly what a single root cause should do. Closest miss — B: undefined acceptance criteria is a credible driver of variable quality and worth checking, but it does not account for the schedule slips; the discriminator is explaining both symptoms versus only one. Also plausible — C, D: deliberate slow-rolling for a change order is a genuine procurement risk yet unsupported by the file, and a too-slow reporting cadence would delay detection rather than create the underlying performance problem.

questions.question: An aerospace program manager is about to negotiate a multi-year agreement with a sole-source avionics supplier that holds significant leverage. The relationship is strategic and must survive well beyond this deal. Preparation, not improvisation, will decide the outcome. Before the first session opens, what should the program manager establish to negotiate effectively?
choices: A firm walk-away price that will not move regardless of how the discussion unfolds in the room
A public deadline that pressures the supplier to concede on price quickly and close the deal
A detailed counter-schedule listing every concession the supplier is expected to make during talks
The program's prioritized objectives, its best alternative, and the supplier's likely interests and constraints
questions.explanation: Best: effective preparation means knowing your own prioritized objectives, your best alternative (BATNA), and the other party's interests and constraints — this frames trade-offs and protects a strategic sole-source relationship meant to endure. Closest miss — A: a walk-away point is a real and necessary element, but fixing one rigid number without understanding priorities or the supplier's constraints is brittle against a sole source; the discriminator is a full interest-based frame versus a single isolated figure. Also plausible — B, C: an artificial deadline can pressure concessions but corrodes a long-term relationship, and a one-sided concession list is genuine prep yet ignores the mutual interests that make a durable deal.

questions.question: A retail chain wants an external vendor to build its loyalty platform as a stream of prioritized increments, with the backlog reordered every few weeks as market data arrives. Leadership needs the contract to reward delivered, working functionality rather than a fixed up-front specification. Which procurement approach fits this adaptive, frequently reprioritized relationship best?
choices: A firm-fixed-price contract tied to a complete requirements specification signed and frozen at project kickoff
A master services agreement with fixed rates funding prioritized increments and periodic renewal points as work proceeds
A cost-plus-award-fee contract with fees tied to formal annual milestone reviews of overall progress
A single lump-sum contract paired with a formal change-request process for every new feature added
questions.explanation: Best: a master services agreement with agreed rates that funds prioritized increments and renews periodically matches adaptive delivery — it pays for working functionality without freezing scope and lets the backlog reorder freely. Closest miss — C: cost-plus-award-fee is genuinely flexible on scope, but tying fee to annual milestone reviews clashes with a cadence that reprioritizes every few weeks; the discriminator is short-cycle alignment versus long-cycle gates. Also plausible — A, D: fixed-price against a signed spec and lump-sum-plus-change-control both give strong cost certainty, but each assumes stable scope and turns frequent reprioritization into constant, costly renegotiation.

questions.question: A hospital network's EHR vendor has delivered the final release of a scheduling module and submitted its closing invoice. Under the agreement, final payment and contract closure follow acceptance. The project manager wants to release funds correctly and avoid a disputed closeout. Which step must be completed before authorizing the vendor's final payment?
choices: Archive the procurement records and capture lessons learned for the organization's next sourcing cycle
Release the retainage and issue a favorable past-performance reference for the departing vendor
Verify the deliverables against the contract's acceptance criteria and confirm no open claims remain
Obtain the sponsor's sign-off on the overall project's benefits realization and outcome targets
questions.explanation: Best: contractual acceptance — verifying that deliverables meet the agreed acceptance criteria and confirming no claims are outstanding — is the gate that must precede final payment and formal closure. Closest miss — A: archiving records and capturing lessons is a real and required closeout activity, but it follows acceptance and payment rather than preceding them; the discriminator is sequence within closeout. Also plausible — B, D: releasing retainage with a performance reference is a legitimate closeout act yet presupposes acceptance already granted, and sponsor sign-off on benefits realization is sound governance but addresses outcomes, not whether the contract's terms were met.

questions.question: A buyer and seller sign a fixed-price-incentive-fee contract with a target cost of $500,000, a target fee of $50,000, a 70/30 buyer/seller share ratio, and a $650,000 price ceiling. The work finishes at an actual cost of $450,000, below target. Applying the incentive formula, what final price does the buyer pay the seller?
choices: $515,000 — actual cost plus target fee and the seller's thirty-percent share of the underrun
$500,000 — actual cost plus the target fee only, ignoring the underrun share entirely
$535,000 — actual cost plus target fee plus the buyer's seventy-percent share of the underrun
$550,000 — actual cost plus target fee plus the full amount of the cost underrun
questions.explanation: Best: the underrun is $500,000 − $450,000 = $50,000; the seller earns its 30% share ($15,000) on top of the $50,000 target fee, giving a final fee of $65,000 and a final price of $450,000 + $65,000 = $515,000, within the ceiling. Closest miss — C: $535,000 applies the buyer's 70% share to the seller, inverting the share ratio — a natural slip since both percentages are in the stem; the discriminator is which party's share rewards the seller. Also plausible — B, D: B forgets the share incentive altogether, and D credits the seller the entire underrun as if the share ratio were 0/100.

questions.question: A firm-fixed-price (FFP) contract has been signed for a well-defined component. Which TWO statements are true of this arrangement?
choices: The buyer reimburses the seller's actual costs plus a fee.
It is the best fit when requirements are still evolving.
The seller bears the cost risk of performance overruns.
The buyer bears most of the cost risk if effort exceeds estimates.
It suits work whose scope is clear and stable at signing.
questions.explanation: Best: under FFP the seller carries overrun risk (C) and the type fits well-defined, stable scope (E). Closest miss — A: cost-reimbursement is a real, easily-confused contract family, but it describes cost-plus, not FFP. Also plausible — B points to T&M/cost-reimbursable (evolving scope), and D inverts who holds the cost risk under FFP.

questions.question: Midway through an automotive tooling contract, the supplier proposes switching to a higher-grade alloy that raises unit cost but would cut lead time by three weeks and improve durability. The project manager sees the appeal, but the change touches the agreed baseline and the contract price. What must happen before the project manager agrees to the supplier's proposed change?
choices: Immediately update the schedule baseline to capture the three-week lead-time gain the change offers
Evaluate the change through integrated change control and secure the designated change authority's approval
Negotiate the new unit price with the supplier and issue the corresponding contract amendment
Poll the engineering team on whether the proposed alloy meets the durability specification requirements
questions.explanation: Best: a change touching cost and the baseline must run through integrated change control — impact analysis across scope, cost, schedule, and quality — and be approved by the designated change authority before any commitment is made. Closest miss — C: renegotiating price and amending the contract is genuinely required, but doing it before the change is analyzed and authorized commits the buyer ahead of the decision; the discriminator is govern-then-commit sequence. Also plausible — A, D: updating the schedule baseline presumes an approval not yet granted, and consulting engineering on the alloy is valuable evidence but only one input to the broader change evaluation.
questions.task: Manage contract changes through change control

questions.question: At the status date of a data-center build, the project has earned value of $360,000 against an actual cost of $400,000. The sponsor wants both the cost variance and the cost performance index to judge how efficiently the budget is being spent. What are the cost variance and the cost performance index?
choices: CV = -$40,000 and CPI = 0.90 — the project is spending more than the work has earned
CV = +$40,000 and CPI = 1.11 — the project is earning more than spent, running ahead
CV = -$40,000 and CPI = 1.11 — the project is over budget yet apparently cost-efficient
CV = +$40,000 and CPI = 0.90 — the project is under budget but running inefficiently
questions.explanation: Best: CV = EV − AC = $360,000 − $400,000 = −$40,000, and CPI = EV/AC = 360,000/400,000 = 0.90; both signal an over-budget project earning $0.90 of value per dollar spent. Closest miss — C: it computes CV correctly at −$40,000 but inverts the CPI by dividing AC/EV to get 1.11 — a transposition a hurried candidate accepts because the negative CV already looks right; the discriminator is the CPI numerator/denominator order. Also plausible — B, D: each flips a sign — B reverses the CV subtraction and pairs it with the inverted CPI, while D mislabels a positive CV — both internally inconsistent once value-earned logic is applied.

questions.question: Continuing on that data-center build, the budget at completion is $1,200,000 and the cost performance index has settled at 0.75. Management asks what the total project will cost if the current cost efficiency holds for all of the remaining work. Using that assumption, what is the estimate at completion?
choices: $900,000 — the budget scaled down by applying the performance index directly to it
$1,500,000 — the budget increased by adding the current cost-overrun rate to it
$1,600,000 — the budget adjusted for the sustained cost efficiency across remaining work
$1,200,000 — the budget stands, because efficiency below one affects only the schedule
questions.explanation: Best: when current cost efficiency is assumed to continue, EAC = BAC/CPI = $1,200,000/0.75 = $1,600,000. Closest miss — B: $1,500,000 comes from adding the 25% overrun rate to BAC, which treats the shortfall as additive rather than as division by CPI; it lands close enough to look right, and the discriminator is BAC/CPI versus BAC × (1 + (1−CPI)). Also plausible — A, D: multiplying BAC by CPI shrinks the estimate in the wrong direction, and leaving BAC unchanged ignores that a CPI below 1 must raise the forecast cost.

questions.question: The earned-value chart shows PV, EV, and AC at the data date. Which interpretation is MOST accurate?
choices: The project is behind schedule and over budget; both EV−PV and EV−AC are negative.
The project is over budget but ahead of schedule.
The project is behind schedule but under budget.
The project is essentially on budget and on schedule; the lines are close enough to ignore.
questions.explanation: Best: EV ($100k) sits below both PV ($120k) and AC ($130k), so SV = EV−PV = −$20k (behind) and CV = EV−AC = −$30k (over budget). Closest miss — C: candidates who read only the schedule gap can miss that AC is above EV, which is the cost overrun; both variances are negative. Also plausible — B inverts the schedule sign, and D dismisses a real, sizable gap between the curves.

questions.question: A project faces a significant threat: a specialized subcontractor might not be available when needed. Which TWO are valid threat-response strategies?
choices: Exploit the risk to increase the likelihood of its outcome.
Transfer the impact by contracting a standby supplier under a penalty-backed agreement.
Share the risk with a partner to help capture its upside.
Mitigate by pre-qualifying a second subcontractor to reduce the probability of a gap.
Enhance the risk so its benefits are more likely to occur.
questions.explanation: Best: transfer (B) and mitigate (D) are threat responses — one shifts the impact to a third party, the other lowers probability. Closest miss — A: 'exploit' sounds proactive and decisive, but exploit, enhance, and share apply to OPPORTUNITIES, not threats. Also plausible — C and E are likewise positive-risk strategies, misapplied here to a threat.

questions.question: A regional highway resurfacing program reports a budget at completion of $2,400,000 and a current estimate at completion of $3,000,000. The steering committee wants to know the projected budget outcome for the program at its finish. What is the variance at completion, and what does it mean?
choices: VAC = -$600,000; the program is forecast to finish six hundred thousand dollars over budget
VAC = +$600,000; the program is forecast to finish six hundred thousand dollars under budget
VAC = -$600,000; the program has currently overspent six hundred thousand dollars to date
VAC = -$0.80; the program will deliver eighty cents of value for each dollar it spends
questions.explanation: Best: VAC = BAC − EAC = $2,400,000 − $3,000,000 = −$600,000, a forecast of finishing $600,000 above the original budget at completion. Closest miss — C: it reports the correct −$600,000 but frames it as spending to date rather than a completion forecast; VAC projects the final outcome, not a status-date actual, so the discriminator is end-of-program forecast versus current position. Also plausible — B, D: reversing the subtraction turns an overrun into an underrun, and answer D substitutes an efficiency ratio for a currency variance, mixing VAC with CPI or TCPI concepts.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. What is the expected monetary value (EMV) of the delay risk if the team does nothing?
questions.explanation: Best: EMV = probability × impact = 0.40 × $150,000 = $60,000 of expected cost (negative because it is a threat). Closest miss — B: $150,000 is the full impact if the delay occurs, but EMV weights it by the 40% probability. Also plausible — C and D come from applying the wrong probability to the impact.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. Considering mitigation cost plus the residual expected delay cost, which choice is the most cost-effective?
choices: Option A, with a total expected cost of $45,000.
Option B, with a total expected cost of $57,500.
Do nothing, since both mitigations require spending money up front.
Option B, because its lower upfront cost minimizes total spend.
questions.explanation: Best: compare mitigation cost + residual expected loss. Option A = $30,000 + 0.10×$150,000 = $45,000; Option B = $20,000 + 0.25×$150,000 = $57,500; doing nothing = $60,000. Option A is lowest. Closest miss — D: Option B's lower upfront cost ($20k) is tempting, but its higher residual probability makes its TOTAL expected cost higher than Option A's. Also plausible — B states Option B's total correctly yet it is still not the cheapest, and C (do nothing) carries the highest expected cost.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. After choosing Option A, how should the team handle the remaining 10% delay exposure?
choices: Set a contingency reserve for the residual risk and keep monitoring it on the risk register.
Treat the risk as closed, since the chosen mitigation has lowered its probability.
Add a management reserve to the cost baseline to cover this known residual risk.
Escalate the residual risk to the sponsor for a decision.
questions.explanation: Best: residual risk is funded with a contingency reserve and continued monitoring. Closest miss — B: the mitigation lowers but does not eliminate the 10% exposure, so closing the risk would leave it unfunded. Also plausible — C misplaces the tool (management reserve covers unknown-unknowns and is not typically inside the cost baseline), and D escalates a risk the PM can reserve for within their own authority.

questions.question: An enterprise-software team using two-week iterations keeps finding defects in features days after they were marked done, forcing unplanned fixes that disrupt the next iteration. The team debates two remedies: embedding automated tests and peer review into the Definition of Done, or adding a hardening iteration before each release. Which approach better addresses the recurring pattern, and why?
choices: Strengthen the Definition of Done — embedding automated tests per story prevents defects at the source.
Add a hardening iteration — it provides a predictable window to run full regression before release.
Strengthen the Definition of Done — it removes the need for any release-level testing afterward.
Add a hardening iteration — batching fixes late reduces developer context-switching.
questions.explanation: Best: escapes after 'done' signal a weak Definition of Done; building quality in each iteration (automated tests + review) prevents defects at the source rather than inspecting them out later, so A. Closest miss — B: a hardening iteration is a real hybrid practice and does catch escapes, but it defers quality to an appraisal step instead of preventing it, letting the pattern persist. Also plausible — C, D: C picks the right approach with an overstated reason (release testing is still prudent), and D correctly notes late batching reduces context-switching yet still relies on end-of-cycle inspection.

questions.question: A manufacturing project manager is preparing to authorize first-article production of a machined aircraft bracket. The production and inspection teams want to set up their control charts and check sheets, but the project manager recognizes that something must be established before those tools can be meaningful. Which item must be defined first?
choices: The control charts and check sheets operators will use during production runs.
The cost-of-quality budget the sponsor approves for prevention and appraisal.
The applicable regulatory and customer standards, expressed as measurable quality metrics.
The nonconformance records collected during the previous production program.
questions.explanation: Best: quality control tools measure conformance against a standard, so the applicable standards must first be translated into measurable quality metrics (Plan Quality Management) before charts or check sheets have anything to check, so C. Closest miss — A: the control charts and check sheets are genuinely needed, but they are downstream tools that presuppose the metrics — an ordering error, not a wrong tool. Also plausible — B, D: the cost-of-quality budget (B) and prior nonconformance history (D) are useful planning inputs, but neither is the prerequisite that gives the tools their acceptance thresholds.

questions.question: A safety-critical rail-signaling software project must satisfy a stringent safety-integrity standard, with independent certification required before revenue service. Early in initiation, the project manager is deciding how to weave quality and regulatory compliance into the delivery approach. Which course best positions the project to meet the standard without costly late surprises?
choices: Schedule an independent safety assessment near go-live so certification gaps surface before release.
Delegate compliance to the safety engineer as a workstream separate from project quality.
Audit the deliverables against the standard's checklist during final acceptance testing.
Integrate the safety-integrity requirements into the quality plan and design reviews from initiation.
questions.explanation: Best: compliance is cheapest and most reliable when built in — integrating safety-integrity requirements into the quality plan and design reviews from the start prevents nonconformances rather than discovering them at certification, so D. Closest miss — A: an independent assessment is required and valuable, but scheduling it only near go-live makes it an appraisal that surfaces problems when they are most expensive to fix. Also plausible — B, C: assigning a competent safety engineer (B) and auditing against the standard's checklist (C) are both real practices, but siloing compliance or confining it to final acceptance leaves gaps that early integration would have caught.

questions.question: A retail e-commerce program spent $80,000 last release on code review and automated testing, yet leadership wants that spending cut. The same release incurred $310,000 in production-incident remediation, expedited fixes, and customer-service credits. Preparing to defend the review and testing investment, which interpretation of this cost-of-quality data best supports the project manager's position?
choices: Because appraisal spending did not eliminate failures, it is not delivering value and can be reduced.
The failure costs are already sunk, so future conformance spending should be judged on its own budget line.
Conformance spending is small relative to the failure costs, so cutting it without analysis risks increasing total cost of quality.
Prevention and appraisal costs should be moved entirely into a warranty reserve for external failures.
questions.explanation: Best: C — cost of quality weighs conformance (prevention/appraisal) against nonconformance (failure); $80,000 of conformance sits against $310,000 of failure cost, so reducing it without analysis risks raising total cost of quality. The data show the relationship in scale, not proof of exact causation, so the defensible claim is risk, not a guarantee. Closest miss — A: it correctly notes appraisal did not catch everything, but concludes the spend is valueless without weighing the failures it did help avoid. Also plausible — B, D: treating failure cost as sunk (B) ignores that the exposure recurs each release, and shifting spend to a warranty reserve (D) funds external failure without reducing it.

questions.question: A network-operations project keeps seeing the same class of provisioning error reappear across successive software releases, despite quick fixes each time. The team wants to move past symptom patching and understand what is actually producing the error before the next release. Which quality tool best helps them structure the search for the underlying cause?
choices: A Pareto chart, to rank which defect categories occur most frequently.
A cause-and-effect diagram, to structure exploration of the factors producing the error.
A control chart, to judge whether the process stays within statistical limits.
A scatter diagram, to test whether two variables move together.
questions.explanation: Best: a cause-and-effect (Ishikawa) diagram organizes the team's search across categories like people, process, and tooling, structuring the hunt for the root cause of a recurring error — B. Closest miss — A: a Pareto chart is a natural companion and tells the team which defect is worth pursuing, but it prioritizes symptoms rather than exposing why the error occurs. Also plausible — C, D: a control chart (C) reveals whether the process is stable and a scatter diagram (D) tests a suspected correlation, each a genuine analysis input, but neither structures the causal exploration itself.

questions.question: A project manager wants to strengthen quality ASSURANCE (as distinct from quality control). Which TWO activities belong to quality assurance?
choices: Auditing whether the team is following the agreed quality processes.
Inspecting finished units against specification before release.
Running automated tests on a completed build to find defects.
Measuring the defect rate of delivered components.
Improving the process after a retrospective reveals a recurring defect source.
questions.explanation: Best: QA is process-focused — auditing adherence to the processes (A) and improving the process to prevent defects (E). Closest miss — B: inspection feels like 'assuring quality,' but examining finished units against spec is quality CONTROL (product inspection). Also plausible — C and D are also control activities that evaluate outputs rather than the processes that produce them.

questions.question: On a municipal water-treatment upgrade, two pump-system designs both pass every performance and inspection criterion equally well. Design X uses markedly less energy and material over its service life; Design Y costs less to install now. The council has asked the project manager to recommend one. Which recommendation and rationale best reflect a value- and sustainability-oriented decision?
choices: Design Y, because both meet acceptance criteria and the up-front installation budget is the binding constraint.
Design X, because lower energy use guarantees a smaller total project budget in the current year.
Design Y, because lifecycle and sustainability benefits fall outside the project's defined scope.
Design X, because with conformance equal, lifecycle cost and sustainability become the deciding value factors.
questions.explanation: Best: when two options are equal on conformance, the tie breaks on value — and lifecycle cost plus sustainability/ESG outcomes are legitimate value factors under the 2026 emphasis on outcomes, so Design X, making D correct. Closest miss — A: prioritizing the lower install cost is defensible if budget truly is the hard constraint, but it optimizes first cost over total value the sponsor also cares about. Also plausible — B, C: B reaches the right design through a flawed guarantee (energy savings need not lower this year's budget), and C is a reasonable scope-discipline argument that nonetheless ignores value the council explicitly raised.

questions.question: The sprint burndown shows actual work remaining against the ideal line, seven days into a ten-day sprint. What does the trend MOST likely indicate, and what is the appropriate response?
choices: The team is trending behind; the Scrum Master should facilitate the team and product owner in re-planning scope or approach for the sprint.
The team is behind; the Scrum Master should require overtime so the original scope still lands by day 10.
The team is ahead of plan, so no action is needed.
