questions.explanation: Best: C — with a new carbon price imminent and public net-zero commitments, the recommendation should weigh whole-life cost and strategic/ESG impact, which favor the energy-efficient option despite its higher purchase price. Closest miss — A: protecting the approved budget with the lower bid is a real pressure, but lowest initial cost ignores lifetime energy and the coming carbon cost — the classic short-horizon trap. Also plausible — B, D: deferring to the sponsor (B) sidesteps the PM's duty to surface the value case, and waiting for the exact carbon price (D) delays a decision the trends already justify.

questions.question: A public-sector project must choose between two compliant designs, and leadership asks the project manager to reflect the organization's sustainability commitments. Which TWO considerations best reflect a genuine whole-life, sustainable approach?
choices: Whichever design has the lowest initial capital cost, to protect the current budget.
Total cost of ownership over the asset's life, including energy and maintenance — not just the lowest bid price.
The design's long-term environmental and community impact against the organization's ESG targets.
The option that finishes soonest, regardless of its operating footprint.
The choice that minimizes near-term reporting effort for the project team.
questions.explanation: Best: sustainability weighs whole-life cost (B) and long-term environmental/community impact against ESG goals (C). Closest miss — A: protecting the current budget with the lowest initial cost is a legitimate pressure, but lowest capital cost often ignores higher lifetime energy and maintenance cost — the opposite of a whole-life view. Also plausible — D and E optimize short-term convenience (speed, less reporting) over sustainable outcomes.

questions.question: A product will transition to an operations team at project closure, but most of its business benefits will accrue over the following year. Which TWO actions best protect benefits realization beyond the project?
choices: Declare the benefits realized at closure because the deliverable met its acceptance criteria.
Close the project's risk register, since any post-closure issues belong to operations alone.
Define benefit metrics and assign ownership for measuring them after handover.
Transfer the knowledge and support operations needs to sustain the outcome.
Defer any benefit measurement until a problem is reported by operations.
questions.explanation: Best: benefits that mature after closure need defined metrics with an owner (C) and a genuine knowledge/support transfer (D). Closest miss — A: meeting acceptance criteria proves the output was delivered, which feels like success, but delivering the output is not the same as realizing the outcome. Also plausible — B and E leave benefits untracked and unmanaged by closing oversight early and waiting for problems to surface.

passages.title: Scenario: Risk mitigation decision (Questions refer to this data)
passages.text: A team is deciding how to handle a possible late delivery of a critical component. If nothing is done, there is a 40% chance of a delay costing $150,000. Two mitigations are available. Option A: expedited logistics, costing $30,000 now, which cuts the delay probability to 10%. Option B: a local backup supplier, costing $20,000 now, which cuts the delay probability to 25%.

passages.title: Scenario: Schedule network (Questions refer to this data)
passages.text: A predictive project has six activities with finish-to-start dependencies. A (4 days) has no predecessor. B (6 days) and C (3 days) both follow A. D (5 days) follows B. E (2 days) follows C. F (3 days) follows both D and E. Only these activities can be crashed, each by whole days at a fixed cost per day: A $1,000/day (max 2 days), B $500/day (max 2 days), D $800/day (max 2 days), F $400/day (max 1 day).

passages.title: Scenario: Program governance and compliance (Questions refer to this data)
passages.text: A regulated infrastructure program runs three delivery teams. The organization's governance framework sets a change-authority threshold: changes above $50,000 in cost impact require steering-committee approval; the project manager may approve smaller changes. Midway through, a national safety regulation is amended, adding mandatory requirements to work already in progress.

questions.question: A software delivery manager on a hybrid program finds two component leads locked in a design dispute that is stalling the sprint. The manager wants to apply the collaborating (problem-solving) conflict mode. Which TWO behaviors exemplify collaborating rather than compromising or smoothing?
choices: Broker a middle-ground design in which each lead gives up part of their proposal so the sprint can move forward quickly.
Facilitate a joint working session in which both leads surface the underlying interests behind their positions and co-create a single design that satisfies both.
Emphasize how much the two designs already have in common and ask the leads to set the remaining differences aside to preserve harmony.
Treat the disagreement as a shared problem to solve, digging into root causes and data so the resulting solution earns genuine buy-in from both leads.
Direct the leads to adopt the architecture the manager judges technically superior so the team stops losing time.
questions.explanation: Best: collaborating seeks a win-win by integrating both parties' concerns through open, interest-based problem-solving that produces durable commitment (B) surfacing underlying interests to co-create one solution (D) attacking root causes together so both fully own the outcome. Closest miss — A: splitting the difference so each side concedes is compromising (lose-lose partial satisfaction), not the integrative win-win of collaborating. Also plausible — C: downplaying differences to keep peace is smoothing/accommodating. E: imposing the manager's choice is forcing/directing.

questions.question: On a satellite ground-station program, the uplink squad and the telemetry squad each delivered modules that fail to interoperate, and both insist they built exactly to the shared roadmap. Neither wants to change its design. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Bring both squads together to surface how each interpreted the roadmap differently
Expand the roadmap with detailed interface specifications and reissue it to both squads
Direct both squads to adopt the uplink squad's interface design and rework
Reassign all integration work to a single squad to close the coordination gap
questions.explanation: Best: A — identical delivery yet non-integration signals the shared understanding diverged, so surfacing how each squad read the roadmap targets the source before any rework. Closest miss — B: richer interface specs help, but adding documents before understanding why interpretations diverged treats the symptom. Also plausible — C, D: standardizing on one squad's design (C) or consolidating the work (D) forces a fix without learning what caused the gap.

questions.question: Midway through a cross-border payments platform build, a new data-residency law changes the underlying business need, and the sponsor confirms the original project goal no longer reflects the outcome the organization now seeks. How should the project manager handle the project vision?
choices: Revise the vision with the sponsor and key stakeholders, then realign the team
Keep the original vision for stability and manage the change as a scope-change request
Pause the project until the regulator issues final guidance, then reassess the vision
Let each team locally update its own understanding of the goal
questions.explanation: Best: A — when the business need genuinely shifts, the vision is revised collaboratively with the sponsor and stakeholders and then cascaded so the team realigns. Closest miss — C: waiting for final guidance is prudent when requirements are truly unknowable, but the sponsor has already confirmed the outcome changed, so freezing forfeits time. Also plausible — B, D: treating a changed business need as a mere scope change (B) understates it; local reinterpretation (D) fragments the shared vision.

questions.question: Several data scientists join a fraud-detection machine-learning project after it is already underway, and they privately admit they don't see how their assigned tasks connect to the product's purpose or to one another. What is the BEST action for the project manager?
choices: Show the newcomers how their tasks advance the product vision
Ask experienced members to mentor the newcomers on day-to-day technical practices
Add the newcomers to every recurring meeting so they absorb context over time
Give each newcomer a detailed task list so their responsibilities are unambiguous
questions.explanation: Best: A — connecting people to purpose means explicitly linking each person's work to the vision, which drives engagement and aligned decisions and answers exactly the gap they named. Closest miss — B: mentoring builds capability and conveys some context, but it centers technical practice rather than purpose. Also plausible — D, C: task clarity (D) and meeting exposure (C) help operationally but don't directly close the tasks-to-purpose gap.

questions.question: At release planning for a telehealth scheduling product, the product owner presents a clear, compelling product vision to the delivery team before they size and order the work. What does that shared vision primarily provide the team as it plans the release?
choices: A fixed scope baseline that locks the features to be delivered
A common reference that guides prioritization and day-to-day trade-off decisions
A detailed schedule the team can follow without further planning
An assurance that stakeholder expectations will not change during delivery
questions.explanation: Best: B — a vision gives the team a shared 'why' that guides prioritization and the many small trade-offs made during delivery. Closest miss — A: a vision informs scope but deliberately does not lock it; adaptive delivery keeps scope flexible against the vision. Also plausible — C, D: a vision is not a schedule (C) and cannot guarantee expectations stay static (D).

questions.question: Across a multi-year grid-modernization program, teams on three continents risk losing sight of the program vision as priorities shift and members rotate on and off over the years. Which approach keeps the vision meaningful for the distributed teams over time?
choices: Revisit and reconnect the vision to current work at regular program checkpoints
Publish the vision on the program portal and link it in every charter
Send a quarterly newsletter restating the vision and recent milestones
Ask each regional lead to interpret the vision for their teams as they see fit
questions.explanation: Best: A — a vision stays meaningful when it is repeatedly reconnected to the actual work at recurring touchpoints, letting people see how today's tasks serve it. Closest miss — C: regular newsletters keep the vision visible, but one-way restatement rarely re-anchors changing work the way interactive checkpoints do. Also plausible — B, D: portal posting (B) is static reference only; delegating interpretation (D) risks the vision fragmenting across regions.

questions.question: The sponsor of an aircraft-maintenance facility systems project has formally shifted the strategic objective from maximizing throughput to prioritizing regulatory compliance, yet the team still frames its status reviews and decisions around throughput. Which action should the project manager take to realign the team?
choices: Explore why the new objective hasn't landed and realign the team's metrics
Remind the team at the next review that throughput is no longer primary
Update the charter and objectives document so the record reflects the new priority
Ask the sponsor to address the team so the mandate carries executive weight
questions.explanation: Best: A — persistent reference to the old goal signals the change wasn't internalized; understanding why and then realigning the very metrics the team steers by is what actually shifts behavior. Closest miss — D: sponsor reinforcement can help, but delegating the message before diagnosing the gap may leave the underlying metrics and habits unchanged. Also plausible — C, B: correcting the documents (C) and a verbal reminder (B) are necessary housekeeping but rarely change entrenched framing alone.

questions.question: On a nuclear-plant instrumentation upgrade, two lead engineers clash sharply in nearly every design review, and the rising tension is visibly slowing the team and causing other members to disengage. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Meet with each engineer to understand the source and nature of the conflict
Set a ground rule requiring design disagreements to be raised offline rather than in reviews
Escalate the friction to their functional managers for a performance conversation
Separate their work streams so the two engineers rarely need to interact
questions.explanation: Best: A — effective conflict handling starts with understanding the real source before choosing a response, since the clash may be technical, personal, or structural. Closest miss — B: a ground rule can reduce disruption, but imposing process before understanding the cause may just push the conflict out of sight. Also plausible — D, C: separating streams (D) avoids rather than resolves; escalating to managers (C) is premature before the PM has diagnosed it.

questions.question: On a renewable-energy forecasting platform, two architects hold firmly opposing views on the core data architecture. Both are behaving professionally, the decision materially affects the product, and the schedule has room to work it through. Which conflict-handling approach fits this situation?
choices: Collaborate to work through both positions toward the strongest combined solution
Compromise so each architect concedes part of their position to move on quickly
Have the more senior architect decide to avoid a prolonged debate
Smooth over the differences to preserve the relationship between the architects
questions.explanation: Best: A — when the issue is important, the parties are constructive, and time permits, collaborating/problem-solving produces the most durable, highest-quality outcome. Closest miss — B: compromise resolves quickly but has each side give something up, yielding a weaker solution than integrating both views when time allows. Also plausible — C, D: forcing via seniority (C) and smoothing (D) trade the best technical answer for speed or harmony the situation doesn't require.

questions.question: On a public benefits modernization project, community stakeholders report that the AI model used to rank applications for review appears to flag one demographic group far more often than others, and the concern is spreading. How should the project manager respond?
choices: Add a disclaimer that rankings are advisory and require the model's logic be published
Reassure stakeholders the model is vendor-certified and keep using it while gathering feedback
Switch off the AI model immediately and revert all ranking to manual review
Investigate the concern with the data and product teams, then act on findings
questions.explanation: Best: D — a credible fairness concern warrants investigation with the people who own the data and model to establish whether bias exists, then a response proportional to the evidence. Closest miss — C: disabling the model guards against harm, but doing so before analysis may over-react and remove a tool later shown sound. Also plausible — B, A: leaning on vendor certification (B) dismisses the concern; a disclaimer (A) addresses transparency but not the possible bias itself.

questions.question: A newly assembled team drawn from engineering, marketing, and legal is meeting to launch a regulated product, and interpersonal friction is already rising as members clash over priorities and working styles. What is the BEST proactive step for the project manager?
choices: Facilitate the team in creating a working agreement covering norms and decisions
Assign clear individual roles so members focus on their own work and interact less
Wait to see whether the friction settles as the team moves through forming tensions
Raise the friction with each member's functional manager before it affects delivery
questions.explanation: Best: A — a new team's friction is best addressed proactively by co-creating a team working agreement that sets shared norms for how members interact and decide. Closest miss — C: some forming-stage tension is normal, but waiting it out is passive when the PM can proactively establish norms that prevent escalation. Also plausible — B, D: narrowing roles to reduce contact (B) suppresses the needed collaboration; involving managers (D) is premature before the team sets its own ground rules.

questions.question: A platform team working under an established working agreement has one member who routinely talks over colleagues in stand-ups and misses the updates they committed to. Other members are visibly frustrated and starting to disengage. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Raise the behavior in the next retrospective so the group can address it together
Reassign that member's commitments to more reliable colleagues to protect the work
Remind the whole team of the working agreement without singling anyone out
Speak privately with the member, referencing the agreement, to understand what's happening
questions.explanation: Best: D — a private, respectful conversation that references the shared agreement lets the PM understand the cause and address the behavior without public embarrassment. Closest miss — A: a retrospective can reinforce norms, but airing one person's conduct to the group first risks defensiveness before the PM understands the cause. Also plausible — B, C: reassigning work (B) treats a symptom and signals avoidance; a generic reminder (C) is weaker than addressing the specific behavior directly.

questions.question: A contracted integrator has delivered a controls module for a water-treatment upgrade. The project team argues it does not meet the specification, while the integrator maintains it fully conforms, and tension is building between the two groups. How should the project manager BEST approach the disagreement?
choices: Evaluate the module against the contract's acceptance criteria with both parties present
Accept the module conditionally to preserve the vendor relationship and log the concerns
Direct the internal team to document every defect and formally reject the delivery
Escalate the dispute to procurement to renegotiate the statement of work
questions.explanation: Best: A — an acceptance dispute is resolved against the objective, pre-agreed acceptance criteria in the agreement, evaluated jointly so the decision rests on evidence rather than positions. Closest miss — C: documenting defects is part of any rejection, but jumping to formal rejection before a joint criteria-based evaluation hardens the conflict. Also plausible — B, D: conditional acceptance (B) may waive rights and defer the real issue; escalating to procurement (D) is premature before the criteria are checked.

questions.question: During an intense but respectful backlog-refinement session on a fintech lending app, the team's disagreement surfaces several delivery and compliance risks no one had previously raised, and the team stays collaborative throughout. How should the team facilitator interpret this conflict?
choices: As a relationship problem to monitor in case the disagreements turn personal
As a warning sign that the team lacks alignment and needs firmer facilitation
As evidence the refinement session ran too long and should be time-boxed tighter
As constructive, task-focused conflict that improved the team's shared understanding of risk
questions.explanation: Best: D — respectful, task-focused conflict is healthy, and here it directly produced better risk awareness, a benefit to protect rather than suppress. Closest miss — B: persistent misalignment would justify firmer facilitation, but this episode was respectful and productive, so reading it as dysfunction misdiagnoses a strength. Also plausible — C, A: blaming session length (C) or treating it as latent relationship conflict (A) both frame a productive exchange as a problem.

questions.question: After the project manager facilitates a discussion, two developers who had been at odds agree on how to divide ownership of a shared component, and both leave the meeting satisfied with the resolution. What should the project manager do NEXT?
choices: Confirm the agreed actions and follow up to verify the resolution holds
Document the agreement in the team's records and formally close the issue
Consider the conflict closed and move attention to the next impediment
Ask both developers to present the resolution to the wider team for transparency
questions.explanation: Best: A — resolving conflict includes confirming the specific commitments and following up to ensure the agreement actually holds in practice, not just at the meeting. Closest miss — B: recording the agreement is good practice, but documentation alone doesn't verify the behavior change the resolution depends on. Also plausible — C, D: treating it as closed (C) skips follow-through; a wider presentation (D) may be unnecessary and could reopen a settled matter.

questions.question: In a retrospective on a distributed climate-reporting analytics project, team members tell the project manager that logging every subtask in the tracker and joining twice-daily status calls leaves them no room to organize their own work. Several say they feel micromanaged. What should the project manager do?
choices: Keep the current tracking, but clearly explain to the team why the detail is necessary.
Cut status calls to weekly while still assigning each task to preserve accountability.
Facilitate the team in setting the metrics and cadence they will self-report, then step back.
Replace the daily calls with an automated dashboard the project manager reviews each morning.
questions.explanation: Best: C — empowering the team to co-create its own reporting norms and self-organize directly addresses the felt micromanagement while preserving visibility. Closest miss — D: reducing surveillance helps, but the PM still monitors, so ownership is never transferred. Also plausible — A, B: A keeps the intrusive tracking merely explained; B still assigns every task.

questions.question: On a mature, high-performing agile team building a mobile-banking app, developers repeatedly message the project manager to decide which open-source library to use for routine features well within their expertise, even though they have delivered reliably for months. What is the BEST response?
choices: Coach the team to own decisions within its mandate, engaging only on cross-team impacts.
Make the calls quickly so the capable team is never left blocked waiting.
Route each library question to the designated technical lead for a ruling.
Stand up an architecture board to approve all library selections going forward.
questions.explanation: Best: A — a self-organizing team should own routine technical decisions; the PM coaches that ownership and reserves involvement for cross-boundary issues. Closest miss — C: delegating to a lead removes the PM bottleneck but concentrates decisions in one person rather than building team ownership. Also plausible — B, D: B breeds dependency; D adds governance overhead for routine choices.

questions.question: Midway through a hybrid CRM-migration, two sub-teams have each independently built the same data-cleansing routine, while several migration-validation tasks were left undone because members are unsure who owns which portion of the work, and rework is mounting. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Add a daily coordination checkpoint to surface overlaps as they arise.
Reassign the duplicated and dropped tasks to named individuals right away.
Facilitate the team in building a responsibility matrix for the contested work areas.
Escalate the coordination gap to the sponsor and request additional resources.
questions.explanation: Best: C — clarifying ownership collaboratively (a RACI-style matrix) fixes the ambiguity that is producing both the duplication and the gaps. Closest miss — B: reassigning resolves the current instances but not the ambiguity that will recreate them. Also plausible — A, D: A surfaces overlaps without assigning ownership; D adds resources when coordination, not capacity, is the problem.

questions.question: A software team building a fraud-detection model has stalled because the data-governance office has not yet approved access to production-grade data, and the team itself holds no authority to compel that access. Weighing the realistic options, what should the project manager do?
choices: Escalate at once to the sponsor to force the access through the governance office.
Direct the team to proceed on synthetic data so that no time is lost.
Raise a formal change request to add the data access as a project requirement.
Engage the governance office to understand its concerns and negotiate a compliant access path.
questions.explanation: Best: D — the PM removes the impediment by engaging the blocking party directly to negotiate a compliant path, reserving escalation for if that stalls. Closest miss — A: escalation is legitimate but premature before any attempt to resolve it collaboratively. Also plausible — B, C: B keeps the team busy but risks building on invalid data; C formalizes the need yet is slow and ignores the governance concern.

questions.question: A newly assembled agile team was cordial during its first two weeks. Now, three sprints in, meetings have grown tense. The Scrum Master assesses which Tuckman stage the team is in. Which TWO observations indicate the team has entered the STORMING stage rather than norming or performing?
choices: The team has settled on working agreements and is rebuilding trust, resolving earlier disputes constructively.
The team works interdependently with little oversight, self-organizing to solve problems and consistently meeting its sprint goals.
Members openly challenge the Scrum Master's approach and each other's ideas, with visible friction over roles and direction.
Members are polite and tentative, unsure of their roles and looking to the leader for direction.
Subgroups have formed and are jockeying for influence, and some members resist the chosen process, producing tension and dipping productivity.
questions.explanation: Best: storming is marked by conflict, resistance, and contests for position as members push back on approach and one another (C) open challenges and friction over roles/direction (E) subgroup rivalry and process resistance with reduced output. Closest miss — A: agreeing on working agreements and rebuilding trust is norming, the stage that follows storming. Also plausible — B: interdependent, low-oversight high performance is performing. D: polite, tentative, leader-dependent behavior is forming.
questions.task: People — Build and support the team

questions.question: During design reviews on a class-III medical-device program, a recently graduated engineer's suggestions are routinely talked over or passed by while veteran members' ideas dominate the discussion; over the last few sessions she has begun staying silent. What is the BEST action?
choices: Privately coach the junior engineer to assert her ideas more forcefully in reviews.
Establish and model review norms that ensure every voice is heard safely.
Ask the senior members privately to stop dismissing the junior engineer's input.
Pair the junior engineer with a senior mentor drawn from the review group.
questions.explanation: Best: B — the PM shapes an inclusive environment with facilitation norms that address the systemic dynamic for everyone, building psychological safety. Closest miss — C: directly curbing the behavior helps but singles people out and is less durable than shared norms. Also plausible — A, D: A puts the burden on the person being marginalized; D aids development but doesn't fix the meeting dynamic.

questions.question: Three sprints into a logistics-optimization initiative, a freshly assembled team keeps missing its sprint commitments and delivered quality is uneven across members; the project manager suspects the underlying issue is that members lack a shared understanding of goals and standards. What should the project manager do?
choices: Set clear performance targets and communicate them firmly to the entire delivery team.
Meet members individually to find skill gaps and arrange targeted training.
Introduce more frequent checkpoints to monitor progress against the sprint plan.
Facilitate the team in co-creating a charter of shared goals and working agreements.
questions.explanation: Best: D — co-creating a team charter builds the shared understanding of goals and standards whose absence is driving the underperformance, and it earns ownership. Closest miss — A: clarifying expectations is right, but a top-down target set is narrower than a charter and wins less buy-in. Also plausible — B, C: B chases a different hypothesis (skills); C monitors without creating clarity.

questions.question: In daily standups on an e-commerce replatforming effort, team members repeatedly wait for the scrum master to hand out that day's tasks instead of pulling the next items from the sprint backlog themselves. What is the BEST response to this pattern?
choices: Have a team lead distribute the tasks and report progress to the scrum master.
Continue assigning the day's tasks each morning to keep the sprint on track.
Ask the product owner to prioritize and hand out the daily tasks instead.
Coach the team to self-select work from the sprint backlog and own the standup.
questions.explanation: Best: D — a self-organizing team pulls its own work; the scrum master coaches that ownership rather than assigning tasks. Closest miss — A: shifting assignment to a lead removes the PM bottleneck but keeps work assignment-based, not self-selected. Also plausible — B, C: B sustains the dependency; C miscasts the product owner, who prioritizes the backlog but does not assign daily tasks.

questions.question: The charter has just been signed for a program to build a regional cold-chain distribution network spanning several jurisdictions, regulators, and third-party logistics partners. Before any engagement planning or communications work begins, what is the project manager's FIRST stakeholder-related step?
choices: Draft a stakeholder engagement plan tailored to each anticipated group.
Identify the stakeholders and document their interests, influence, and expectations.
Convene a kickoff meeting with the stakeholders already known to the team.
Assess each stakeholder's current versus desired level of engagement.
questions.explanation: Best: B — you cannot plan, assess, or engage until stakeholders are systematically identified and analyzed. Closest miss — D: assessing current-versus-desired engagement is valuable but presupposes an identified stakeholder list. Also plausible — A, C: A plans engagement before knowing whom to engage; C engages only the already-known, skipping systematic identification.

questions.question: Having compiled a large stakeholder register for a company-wide ERP rollout, the project manager wants a structured way to decide whom to engage most intensively, since attention and time are limited. Which technique most directly supports this prioritization decision at this stage?
choices: A stakeholder engagement assessment matrix comparing current and desired states.
A RACI chart mapping stakeholders to project deliverables and tasks.
A power/interest grid classifying stakeholders by influence and concern.
A communications requirements analysis sizing each group's information needs.
questions.explanation: Best: C — a power/interest (salience) grid prioritizes engagement by classifying stakeholders on influence and interest. Closest miss — A: the engagement assessment matrix drives action on gaps but is a later step and does not itself rank attention by power/interest. Also plausible — B, D: B assigns responsibility for tasks, not stakeholder attention; D sizes communication volume rather than prioritizing whom to engage.

questions.question: A major client sponsor has grown openly skeptical of a digital-transformation program after an earlier release slipped by weeks without any advance warning to her. What is the BEST way for the project manager to rebuild the sponsor's confidence over the coming months?
choices: Present a detailed recovery plan showing how the lost time will be regained.
Increase the frequency and detail of the status reports sent to the sponsor.
Meet the sponsor to explain in full why the earlier commitment slipped.
Acknowledge the miss, agree on transparent metrics, and consistently keep smaller commitments.
questions.explanation: Best: D — trust is restored through candor about the miss plus a demonstrated track record of kept commitments and transparent measures over time. Closest miss — C: acknowledging and explaining is part of it, but explanation without demonstrated reliability won't rebuild confidence. Also plausible — A, B: A fixes the schedule, not the trust deficit; B adds reporting volume without the reliability that changes perception.

questions.question: On a large airport-terminal expansion, a district official who had been one of the project's most active champions has stopped answering meeting invitations and missed the last two design reviews, offering no explanation. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Escalate the official's disengagement to the project sponsor for intervention.
Send a summary of the missed decisions and ask for asynchronous review and input.
Reach out to the official directly to understand the change and any emerging concerns.
Continue documenting decisions and proceed without the official's participation.
questions.explanation: Best: C — engage the stakeholder directly to learn what changed before assuming a cause or acting. Closest miss — B: keeping them informed and inviting input is reasonable but doesn't uncover why a champion went quiet. Also plausible — A, D: A escalates before any attempt to understand; D risks permanently losing an influential supporter.

questions.question: On a hospital-wide EHR implementation, the stakeholder engagement assessment matrix records the chief of surgery — a highly influential stakeholder — as currently 'resistant,' while the desired engagement state for him is 'supportive.' What does this gap most directly call for?
choices: Logging the stakeholder as a project risk to be monitored on the risk register.
Developing targeted engagement actions to move the stakeholder toward supportive.
Reducing the stakeholder's involvement to limit the impact of the resistance.
Accepting the current state, since one individual cannot derail the rollout.
questions.explanation: Best: B — a current-to-desired gap in the matrix exists precisely to trigger tailored engagement strategies that close it. Closest miss — A: the resistance is worth tracking as a risk, but the matrix's purpose is to drive engagement action, not merely log it. Also plausible — C, D: C sidelines an influential stakeholder the project needs onside; D ignores the identified gap.

questions.question: Delivering a shared-services automation initiative depends on ongoing, hands-on cooperation from an IT operations director who reports through a different management chain and is busy protecting her own competing roadmap. Which approach best secures her sustained, willing support over the life of the initiative?
choices: Ask the project sponsor to direct the operations director to prioritize the work.
Offer to reciprocate later by supporting one of the director's own initiatives.
Identify shared goals and show how the initiative advances the director's own objectives.
Escalate to both managers so they can jointly settle the competing priorities.
questions.explanation: Best: C — influence without authority rests on aligning interests so cooperation is willing and durable. Closest miss — B: reciprocal exchange is a genuine influence tactic but is transactional and less lasting than shared-goal alignment. Also plausible — A, D: both apply hierarchical pressure, which buys compliance rather than the sustained, willing support the work needs.

questions.question: Two-thirds of the way through building an autonomous-drone delivery service, a national civil-aviation authority issues new rules that make it a newly relevant regulator for the project; it has never been part of the project's stakeholder identification or engagement. What should the project manager do?
choices: Submit the current design to the authority immediately for its formal approval.
Continue execution and engage the authority at the next scheduled phase-gate review.
Add the authority to the register, analyze its requirements, then plan engagement.
Escalate to the sponsor to decide whether the authority actually applies here.
questions.explanation: Best: C — a newly relevant regulator is a newly identified stakeholder: register it, analyze its requirements and influence, then plan engagement. Closest miss — A: engaging the regulator is right, but submitting a package before analyzing its requirements is premature and likely wrong. Also plausible — B, D: B defers engagement on a compliance-critical stakeholder, raising risk; D treats applicability as open when the new rules already establish relevance.

questions.question: On a cloud-migration initiative, the steering committee asks for a single outcome-focused summary each month, while the platform engineers rely on granular build-and-incident logs to do their work. Both audiences are frustrated by the current shared status report. How should the project manager tailor communications?
choices: Keep a single report but add an executive summary atop the detailed technical sections.
Survey both audiences to re-elicit their information needs before changing any report format.
Provide an outcomes dashboard for the committee and detailed logs for engineers, matching format to audience.
Move both groups to one filterable live workspace so each self-selects its own view.
questions.explanation: Best: C — tailor communication content and method to each audience's decision needs, which the stem already makes explicit. Closest miss — B: eliciting needs is sound, but the needs are already stated, so re-surveying only delays value. Also plausible — A, D: a layered report still forces each audience through irrelevant content; a filterable workspace adds tooling overhead without guaranteeing format matches decisions.

questions.question: A distributed program currently coordinates 6 core members through informal peer-to-peer communication, so every member may contact every other. Three additional workstream leads are about to join under the same open communication model. Before onboarding them, the project manager estimates how much the communication network will grow to gauge the coordination overhead. How many additional potential communication channels will the three new members create?
choices: 18 additional channels
21 additional channels
36 additional channels
45 additional channels
questions.explanation: Best: B — channels = n(n−1)/2; 6 members give 15, 9 members give 36, so 36 − 15 = 21 additional. Closest miss — A: 18 counts only new-to-existing links and omits the 3 among the newcomers themselves. Also plausible — C, D: 36 is the total network, not the increase; 45 mis-sizes the network at ten nodes.

questions.question: Two weeks before a cross-functional release-planning workshop for a connected-device launch, the project manager wants to minimize surprises and disruptive conflict during the session. Marketing, regulatory affairs, manufacturing, and firmware teams will all attend, and several have clashed before. What is the BEST preparatory step regarding stakeholders?
choices: Pre-align the most powerful attendees privately so the workshop ratifies an agreed direction.
Circulate a detailed agenda and ground rules so everyone arrives with aligned expectations.
Invite a neutral facilitator to run the session and manage conflict in real time.
Meet key stakeholders beforehand to understand their positions, interests, and likely points of contention.
questions.explanation: Best: D — pre-engaging to understand positions and interests surfaces likely conflicts so the PM can prepare, directly reducing surprises. Closest miss — C: a facilitator manages conflict live but gives the PM no foreknowledge of positions. Also plausible — B, A: agenda and ground rules set expectations but don't reveal hidden interests; pre-aligning only the powerful can reduce friction yet risks alienating others and biasing the outcome.

questions.question: A shared quarterly analytics report is co-produced by the data-engineering team, which considers it 'complete' when the pipeline runs error-free, and the business-intelligence team, which considers it complete only when narrative insights are reviewed and signed off. Handoffs keep bouncing back. What should the project manager do to resolve the recurring disagreement?
choices: Adopt the business-intelligence team's stricter definition because it sits closer to the customer.
Escalate to the sponsor to impose a single organizational standard for report completion.
Split the deliverable in two so each team applies its own completion definition.
Facilitate the teams in agreeing one explicit shared definition of done and acceptance criteria.
questions.explanation: Best: D — co-creating an explicit shared definition of done with acceptance criteria fixes the root cause (no common completion standard) collaboratively. Closest miss — C: decoupling can reduce friction and is sometimes right, but it fragments a genuinely shared deliverable and defers alignment. Also plausible — A, B: imposing one side's stricter view breeds resentment; sponsor escalation standardizes but is premature before the teams try to align themselves.
questions.task: Build a shared definition of done

questions.question: The executive sponsor of a regulatory-remediation effort insists it must be 'finished by the third quarter' but has never specified what 'finished' includes — whether controls implemented, independently audited, or formally accepted by the regulator. The team is planning around an ambiguous target. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Plan to the most conservative interpretation so the team is covered if scope proves larger.
Work with the sponsor to define measurable completion and acceptance criteria before committing.
Accept the third-quarter date and refine the definition of completion as work progresses.
Ask the regulator directly what evidence they will require to accept the remediation.
questions.explanation: Best: B — clarifying measurable completion and acceptance criteria with the sponsor removes the ambiguity driving planning risk, and it precedes any date commitment. Closest miss — D: the regulator's acceptance evidence matters, but the sponsor owns the internal completion definition and should be engaged first. Also plausible — A, C: conservative planning hedges but may over-scope while leaving the target undefined; progressive elaboration is valid, yet committing to a date with no completion definition invites disputes.
questions.task: Define success criteria with the sponsor

questions.question: During stakeholder-alignment sessions on a data-platform project, a talented junior analyst repeatedly freezes or over-explains when senior executives challenge her estimates, undermining the team's credibility. She has strong technical judgment but little experience presenting to leadership. As a servant leader, what is the BEST response?
choices: Present the analyst's material yourself so leadership hears it delivered with confidence.
Reassign executive communications to a more senior colleague to protect the team's credibility.
Coach her privately, rehearse, and give supported, graduated exposure to senior audiences.
Give her candid feedback after each session so she can correct her delivery next time.
questions.explanation: Best: C — servant leadership develops the person through coaching, rehearsal, and graduated exposure, building lasting capability with a safety net. Closest miss — D: timely feedback is part of coaching, but feedback alone, without preparation and safe practice, may leave her exposed again. Also plausible — A, B: presenting for her protects the moment but removes her growth and ownership; reassigning shields credibility short-term but stunts development.

questions.question: A newly launched self-service customer portal satisfies every signed-off functional requirement, passes all acceptance tests, and yet the head of customer operations — a highly influential stakeholder — is openly dissatisfied, saying it 'misses the point.' Nothing in the documented requirements is unmet. What explains the gap, and what should the project manager do about it?
choices: The requirements were poorly written; rewrite the document and re-baseline the scope.
The stakeholder resists change; arrange training and communications to drive adoption.
Unstated expectations went uncaptured; meet the stakeholder to elicit the real needs and outcomes.
Verification fell short; expand test coverage to catch the hidden defects causing the dissatisfaction.
questions.explanation: Best: C — meeting the written spec while missing tacit, unstated expectations is the inferable gap; engaging to surface the real needs and outcomes is the right next step. Closest miss — B: change resistance is possible and adoption support may help, but assuming resistance skips diagnosing whether a real need was missed. Also plausible — A, D: requirements may have gaps, but rewriting and re-baselining before understanding the shortfall is premature; the product meets spec and passed tests, so more verification chases defects the stem says don't exist.

questions.question: Having completed a stakeholder analysis for an ERP consolidation, the project manager identifies four business-unit directors who are all high-influence and high-interest but want conflicting configurations, each optimized for their own unit. Their support is essential and mutually dependent. What is the BEST next step?
choices: Build individual engagement plans that give each director what their own unit needs.
Ask the sponsor to decide the configuration and direct the four directors to comply.
Proceed with the configuration that serves the largest business unit to maximize benefit.
Convene the directors to surface trade-offs and facilitate a shared, prioritized requirement set.
questions.explanation: Best: D — bringing the conflicting high-power stakeholders together to negotiate trade-offs and converge on shared priorities addresses their mutual interdependence directly. Closest miss — B: sponsor arbitration may ultimately break a deadlock, but it is premature before the directors attempt facilitated alignment. Also plausible — A, C: separate plans satisfy each individually but cannot reconcile mutually exclusive configurations; favoring the largest unit is a defensible value heuristic yet imposes a choice without the others' essential support.

questions.question: Over several sprints of a mobile-banking app, the client's product sponsor keeps describing an alerts feature with steadily expanding capabilities in hallway conversations and emails, though the backlog item has not changed. The team senses the target moving. What is the BEST action?
choices: Continue building to the current backlog item and treat the extra asks as future work.
Make the drift visible by reviewing the item with the sponsor and refining it through the change process.
Absorb the added capabilities now, while the sponsor's expectations are fresh and momentum is high.
Ask the sponsor to stop discussing scope outside formal channels to protect the baseline.
questions.explanation: Best: B — surfacing the drift and reconciling the backlog item with the sponsor through the agreed refinement and change process realigns expectations transparently. Closest miss — A: holding the baseline is legitimate, but ignoring an evident expectation shift risks a dissatisfied customer at delivery. Also plausible — C, D: accommodating everything feels responsive but bypasses prioritization and trade-offs; enforcing formal channels protects the baseline yet shuts down valuable signal and strains the relationship.

questions.question: A servant-leader project manager notices a team member seems hesitant to raise concerns in stand-ups. In a one-on-one, the PM wants to use active listening to build trust. Which TWO practices are genuine active-listening behaviors?
choices: Paraphrase the member's message back and ask 'Did I understand that correctly?' before responding.
Mentally prepare your rebuttal while the person is still speaking so you can respond decisively the moment they stop.
Capture the conversation accurately in meeting minutes and email a summary to the team afterward.
Ask open, non-judgmental follow-up questions and withhold your own response until the person has fully finished, attending to their tone and body language.
Immediately reassure the member that the concern is not a big deal so they feel supported.
questions.explanation: Best: active listening confirms understanding and gives full, non-judgmental attention to both content and cues (A) reflecting/paraphrasing to verify meaning (D) open questions, withholding one's own response, and reading tone/body language. Closest miss — B: rehearsing a rebuttal while the other speaks is pseudo-listening — attention is on your reply, not their message. Also plausible — C: accurate minutes are documentation, not in-the-moment listening. E: premature reassurance minimizes the concern and shuts down disclosure.
questions.task: People — Build shared understanding and trust

questions.question: A logistics client accepted the written specification for a route-optimization increment, and the increment matches that specification exactly. On seeing it in use, the client's operations director says it does not actually reduce their real problem — driver overtime — because it optimizes distance, not hours. What should the project manager do?
choices: Demonstrate the distance savings to prove the delivered value meets the accepted scope.
Log a new requirement for time-based optimization and schedule it for a later release.
Explain that the increment conforms to the agreed specification and needs a formal change request.
Re-engage the client to reframe the real outcome, then realign the backlog and validation criteria.
questions.explanation: Best: D — the gap is a validation failure (met spec, not the business outcome); re-engaging to capture the true outcome and realigning backlog and acceptance criteria fixes the root cause. Closest miss — B: capturing the new need is part of it, but deferring it as a future requirement without reframing the outcome risks repeating the miss. Also plausible — C, A: invoking the specification and change control is contractually valid but leaves the real problem unsolved; showing distance savings defends scope yet ignores that value doesn't address overtime.

questions.question: An internal HR-transformation program tracks a stakeholder pulse survey each month. Over the last three cycles the average satisfaction score has slipped from 4.3 to 4.1 to 3.8 out of 5, yet no team or sponsor has raised a formal concern and delivery metrics remain on plan. How should the project manager respond?
choices: Continue as planned, since delivery metrics are healthy and no formal complaint exists.
Engage stakeholders to understand what is driving the decline before it hardens into disengagement.
Add more communications and status updates to reassure stakeholders and lift the scores.
Wait one more cycle to confirm the decline is a real trend rather than noise.
questions.explanation: Best: B — a sustained three-period decline is a meaningful signal; proactively diagnosing the cause before it worsens is the right move even without a formal complaint. Closest miss — D: confirming signal-versus-noise is reasonable, but three consecutive drops already indicate a trend, and waiting risks deeper disengagement. Also plausible — A, C: healthy delivery metrics can mask eroding relationships, so doing nothing ignores a leading indicator; more communication presumes the cause is information rather than real dissatisfaction.

questions.question: Midway through implementing a construction-management SaaS for an external client, the client's program director has begun expecting weekly live demonstrations of progress. The communications plan calls only for a monthly written report, and the client's satisfaction is visibly slipping. What is the BEST action?
choices: Hold to the monthly report defined in the communications plan to avoid the added overhead.
Immediately start weekly demonstrations to restore the slipping client's confidence in progress.
Offer an on-demand progress portal so the client checks status without scheduled demonstrations.
Discuss the client's needs, then revise the communications plan to add demos at a sustainable cadence.
questions.explanation: Best: D — engaging on the underlying need and formally revising the communications approach to fit both parties balances responsiveness with sustainable overhead. Closest miss — B: starting weekly demos addresses the ask and may restore confidence, but committing without assessing feasibility or renegotiating can overload the team. Also plausible — A, C: honoring the baseline is defensible but rigidly ignores a paying client's evolving needs; a self-service portal is creative yet substitutes the PM's solution for a conversation about what the client wants.

questions.question: While reviewing the upcoming release plan, the marketing director casually references an out-of-scope lead-scoring feature as though it will ship in next month's deliverable. It is not in the agreed scope or the backlog. The director is influential and seems genuinely to expect it. What is the BEST action?
choices: Promptly clarify with the director that the feature is out of scope and explain what will ship.
Quietly add the feature to the next release to meet the director's expectation and keep goodwill.
Clarify current scope with the director and, if wanted, route the feature through change control.
Raise the misunderstanding at the next steering committee so all stakeholders hear the correction.
questions.explanation: Best: C — correcting the expectation directly while offering a legitimate path (change control) both resets the misunderstanding and honors a possibly valuable need. Closest miss — A: clarifying scope is essential, but stopping at 'it's out of scope' without a path forward misses the chance to capture a wanted feature. Also plausible — B, D: silently adding it preserves goodwill yet bypasses prioritization and scope control; surfacing it at the committee ensures shared understanding but delays the correction and may embarrass the director.

questions.question: A product owner on a consumer-fintech app reviews a backlog built eighteen months ago and realizes many high-ranked features reflect what customers valued then, not what recent usage data and interviews show they value now. A release is planned for next month. What is the BEST action?
choices: Archive the aged backlog and rebuild it from scratch using the latest customer research.
Deliver the current top-ranked backlog items as planned, then revisit priorities afterward.
Re-prioritize the backlog against current customer-value evidence and re-plan the upcoming release.
Keep the release scope but add the newly valued items on top of the existing priorities.
questions.explanation: Best: C — reordering the backlog against current value evidence and adjusting the imminent release focuses delivery on what customers value now, the product owner's core duty. Closest miss — A: refreshing from research is directionally right, but discarding everything is wasteful and jeopardizes the near-term release. Also plausible — B, D: shipping the current top items preserves momentum but knowingly delivers lower-value work; adding new items on top without removing outdated ones inflates scope and defers the trade-off.

questions.question: A hydroelectric plant upgrade depends heavily on a lead controls engineer who is the only person fluent in the plant's legacy SCADA configuration. She has confirmed she will retire in about five months, roughly midway through commissioning. The project manager recognizes the concentration of critical, undocumented know-how in one person. To protect delivery, what should the project manager do?
choices: Reassign her sole responsibilities across two junior engineers to spread the dependency.
Offer a retention bonus to delay her retirement until commissioning is complete.
Retain her as an on-call advisor after retirement to answer questions as they arise.
Launch a structured knowledge-transfer plan now, pairing her with successors and documenting critical configurations.
questions.explanation: Best: D proactively transfers both explicit and tacit knowledge to successors while the expert is still available, directly reducing the dependency. Closest miss — C: an advisory retainer preserves some access but relies on her availability and builds no internal capability. Also plausible — B: delaying retirement only postpones the same risk; A: spreading her duties without a transfer plan leaves the knowledge gaps unfilled.

questions.question: On an insurance-platform migration, a veteran claims adjuster consistently spots edge-case fraud that formal rules miss; she applies judgment she struggles to put into words. Leadership wants her intuition available to the wider team before she rotates to another division. The project manager must choose a method to transfer this hard-to-articulate expertise. Which approach is BEST?
choices: Ask her to write a comprehensive manual of her decision criteria.
Build a decision-tree tool encoding her stated rules for others to apply.
Have teammates work live cases beside her, discussing her reasoning over weeks.
Record structured video interviews explaining her representative past decisions.
questions.explanation: Best: C — tacit knowledge transfers through socialization, working side by side and discussing reasoning over time. Closest miss — D: recorded interviews capture some explicit reasoning one-way but cannot surface judgment she applies unconsciously. Also plausible — A, B: a manual and a decision-tree tool try to codify tacit expertise into explicit rules, losing the hard-to-articulate judgment.

questions.question: Following two mergers, a fintech engineering group carries a culture from prior downsizings that spared whoever seemed irreplaceable. Engineers keep undocumented scripts, private runbooks, and personal notes rather than share them. Delivery now stalls whenever one person is unavailable. The project manager wants durable improvement, not token compliance. How can the project manager BEST improve knowledge sharing?
choices: Mandate documentation standards and audit each engineer's compliance weekly.
Partner with leadership to reward collaboration and shared ownership over indispensability.
Introduce a shared wiki and require all scripts committed to a common repository.
Pair engineers on rotation so no task is performed by only one person.
questions.explanation: Best: B addresses the root cause — an incentive structure that rewards indispensability; changing what is rewarded makes sharing rational. Closest miss — D: rotation spreads some knowledge but people still guard value while incentives to hoard remain. Also plausible — A: mandating and auditing breeds minimal compliance; C: tooling without a motivation change goes unused.

questions.question: A hybrid ERP rollout has just chartered its first phase, and a newly assigned project manager is establishing team practices. A team member asks when the project should collect lessons learned, having previously only seen them gathered in a rushed workshop at project end. Considering both predictive and adaptive elements of the delivery, when should lessons learned BEST be captured?
choices: At the end of each major phase, once enough has happened to conclude.
Continuously throughout the project, at reviews, milestones, and phase gates as insights emerge.
During project closure, consolidating experiences into the final report.
Whenever a significant problem or success occurs, as an ad hoc entry.
questions.explanation: Best: B — capturing continuously at reviews, milestones, and gates lets the team apply insights while the project is still running. Closest miss — D: event-driven capture is valuable but incomplete without a regular cadence. Also plausible — A: phase-end capture is periodic but misses in-flight learning; C: closure-only loses detail and cannot benefit the current project.

questions.question: A small satellite firmware project relies on a single engineer who alone understands a proprietary radiation-hardening toolchain acquired from a defunct vendor. Losing his availability for any reason would halt integration. The project manager, aware of the exposure, wants to reduce this single point of knowledge failure without disrupting the current sprint more than necessary. What should the project manager do FIRST?
choices: Immediately assign a second engineer to shadow him on all integration work.
Assess which knowledge is critical and at risk before choosing a transfer method.
Require him to fully document the entire toolchain before taking new work.
Recruit an external contractor already familiar with similar radiation-hardening toolchains.
questions.explanation: Best: B — assessing which knowledge is critical and at risk first lets the transfer effort target what matters before committing people or documentation. Closest miss — A: shadowing is a sound response but premature before identifying what is critical, and may consume the wrong time. Also plausible — C: full documentation blocks delivery and misses tacit skill; D: an external contractor adds cost and may not match the proprietary toolchain.

questions.question: A distributed product team, delivering in two-week iterations, finds that knowledge about newly built components stays siloed with whoever wrote them, surfacing only when someone is absent. The team wants a working practice that spreads understanding continuously as the work is performed, rather than in periodic events. Which agile practice BEST supports continuous knowledge transfer during delivery?
choices: Sprint review demonstrations to stakeholders at the end of each iteration.
Retrospectives held at the end of every iteration.
Pair programming with partners rotating across the codebase.
A definition of done applied to every backlog item.
questions.explanation: Best: C — pair programming with rotating partners spreads knowledge continuously as work is produced. Closest miss — B: retrospectives share learning but only periodically, not during delivery. Also plausible — A: sprint reviews inform stakeholders rather than deepen team knowledge; D: a definition of done standardizes quality, not knowledge spread.

questions.question: On a museum's digital-archive project, two external metadata specialists reach the end of their contracts in about four weeks. Much of the cataloguing logic and their reasoning for tricky classification calls exists only in their heads, not in any repository. The project manager wants the team to retain this after they leave. What is the BEST way to preserve their project knowledge?
choices: Conduct exit interviews capturing their key insights and open issues.
Ask them to write detailed documentation of their cataloguing processes.
Hold structured handover sessions transferring active work to named internal successors.
Record their working sessions for the team to review later.
questions.explanation: Best: C — structured handover to named internal successors transfers active work plus reasoning and confirms uptake before the specialists leave. Closest miss — B: documentation captures explicit process but not tacit classification judgment, and may go unread. Also plausible — A: exit interviews surface only highlights; D: recordings are passive with low retention.

questions.question: A program is launching a new project with a large, diverse stakeholder community spanning regulators, vendors, and distributed internal teams, each with different reporting expectations. The project manager is beginning to plan how the project will communicate. Before selecting tools, cadence, or formats, the project manager wants to start correctly. What is the FIRST step in planning project communications?
choices: Select the communication technology and channels to be used.
Determine the frequency and format of the status reports.
Draft the communications management plan and route it for approval.
Identify stakeholders and analyze their information needs and expectations.
questions.explanation: Best: D — communications planning begins by identifying stakeholders and analyzing their information needs and expectations; every later choice depends on it. Closest miss — C: drafting the plan is the output, but it must be informed by the needs analysis first. Also plausible — A, B: selecting technology and setting frequency and format are downstream decisions driven by the identified needs.

questions.question: A newly promoted team lead on a hybrid analytics project notices that two capable engineers consistently defer to each other; neither drives decisions, and delivery is slowing. There is no interpersonal conflict — ownership is simply diffused. What should the lead do FIRST?
choices: Assign one engineer as technical lead over the other to end the deferral.
Escalate to the functional manager to designate a decision-maker.
Allow the pattern to resolve itself as the engineers gain confidence over time.
Clarify decision ownership with the team so each significant decision has a clear owner.
questions.explanation: Best: diffused ownership is resolved by making decision rights explicit with the team, so each significant decision has a named owner while keeping the team self-organizing. Closest miss — A: naming one engineer as lead does end the deferral, but imposing a hierarchy on two peers can dampen collaboration when the real gap is undefined ownership, not capability. Also plausible — B escalates a decision the team can make, and C lets avoidable slippage continue.

questions.question: Leading a cross-functional initiative across several time zones, a project manager notices that decisions announced in writing are often misinterpreted or missed, even though every message was clearly sent. The manager wants each important message not merely delivered but genuinely understood by its intended recipients. Which approach BEST helps ensure that outcome?
choices: Actively listen and paraphrase the recipient's response to verify meaning.
Choose an information-rich channel suited to each message.
Tailor each message's content and detail to the audience.
Invite feedback and clarifying questions to confirm recipients understood the message.
questions.explanation: Best: D — inviting feedback and clarifying questions confirms the receiver actually understood the sender's message, closing the loop. Closest miss — A: paraphrasing the recipient's response verifies the sender understood the other party, not that the receiver grasped the sender's message. Also plausible — B: a rich channel aids transmission; C: tailoring improves clarity but neither confirms understanding.

questions.question: A contentious change in scope has surfaced disagreement among a sponsor, a lead vendor, and the engineering lead, each holding a different understanding of what was agreed. The issue is nuanced and politically sensitive, and lasting resolution depends on the parties genuinely understanding one another. Members sit in three different locations. Which communication method is BEST?
choices: Circulate a detailed formal written report to all parties.
Open an email thread where each party states its position.
Hold a real-time interactive discussion by facilitated video meeting.
Use a shared document where parties add asynchronous comments.
questions.explanation: Best: C — interactive, real-time communication is best for complex, sensitive matters that require dialogue and mutual understanding, even across locations via video. Closest miss — D: a shared document allows exchange but asynchronously, slowing the shared understanding sensitive issues need. Also plausible — A: a formal report is one-way; B: email lacks immediacy and conveys tone poorly.

questions.question: Several senior stakeholders on an infrastructure program complain that the weekly status reports are dense, technical, and largely irrelevant to the decisions they actually make. The project manager currently sends the same detailed report to every audience. Wanting reports that genuinely serve their readers, what is the BEST action for the project manager to take?
choices: Shorten the reports by cutting their least-used sections.
Add an executive summary to the top of each report.
Ask stakeholders to filter the reports for what matters to them.
Revisit stakeholders' information needs and tailor report content and format.
questions.explanation: Best: D — the reports are misaligned with what stakeholders need; re-analyzing their information requirements and tailoring content and format fixes the cause. Closest miss — B: an executive summary helps navigation but leaves the irrelevant detail and unmet needs in place. Also plausible — A: cutting by usage guesses at needs; C: asking stakeholders to filter offloads the project manager's responsibility.

questions.question: An agile delivery team keeps a physical task board, a burndown chart, and a cumulative flow diagram posted where anyone walking by can see them, and mirrors them in a shared digital dashboard for remote members. A new sponsor asks why the team invests effort in maintaining these displays. What is their PRIMARY purpose?
choices: To replace the need for status meetings and written reports.
To make progress and status transparent and visible to all.
To let managers monitor each team member's individual productivity.
To provide a governance audit trail of task completion.
questions.explanation: Best: B — information radiators exist to make progress and status transparent and visible to everyone, supporting shared awareness and self-correction. Closest miss — A: they can reduce some reporting overhead, but that is a side benefit, not the primary purpose. Also plausible — C: they are team-level displays, not individual surveillance; D: an audit trail is not their intent.

questions.question: A construction fit-out project has slipped two weeks behind the approved schedule baseline after a permit delay, and the steering committee, which can authorize corrective action and additional funds, meets tomorrow morning. The project manager has drafted the update she will present. To serve the committee's decision well, what should her communication BEST do?
choices: State that recovery actions are underway and the team expects to recover.
Present the two-week variance and ask the committee how to proceed.
Present the variance and defer options until deeper analysis is done.
Present the variance, its baseline impact, and recovery options with a recommendation.
questions.explanation: Best: D — transparent disclosure of the variance with its baseline impact plus recovery options and a recommendation gives the committee what it needs to decide and fund action. Closest miss — B: transparent, but handing over options-free variance abdicates the project manager's analysis and leaves the committee unable to choose. Also plausible — A: an optimistic 'already recovering' framing risks understating the slip; C: deferring options leaves the committee without a decision basis at tomorrow's meeting.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. What is the expected duration of the path?
choices: 24 days
19 days
21 days
18 days
questions.explanation: Best: beta-PERT expected = (O+4M+P)/6 per activity: X=(4+24+14)/6=7, Y=(5+32+11)/6=8, Z=(3+20+13)/6=6, summing to 21 days. Closest miss — B: 19 comes from using the simple average of O, M, P rather than the 4-weighted most-likely. Also plausible — A, D: 24 and 18 drop or mis-weight an activity.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. What is the standard deviation of the path duration?
choices: About 2.56 days
About 1.67 days
About 4.99 days
About 6.56 days
questions.explanation: Best: activity SD=(P-O)/6 gives 1.67, 1.0, 1.67; the path variance is the SUM of variances (2.78+1.00+2.78=6.56), so path SD=√6.56≈2.56 days. Closest miss — D: 6.56 is the path VARIANCE, not its square-root. Also plausible — B is a single activity's SD, and C wrongly adds the SDs (1.67+1.0+1.67≈4.99) instead of the variances.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. What completion range should the manager use as the approximate 95% (±2 standard deviations) planning forecast?
choices: About 11 to 31 days
About 18 to 24 days
Exactly 21 days
About 16 to 26 days
questions.explanation: Best: ±2σ around the 21-day mean is 21 ± 5.12, i.e. roughly 16 to 26 days, the ~95% range. Closest miss — B: 18 to 24 is the ±1σ band (~68% confidence), too narrow for 95%. Also plausible — C ignores variability entirely, and A (±4σ) is far wider than 95%.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. If the seller's actual cost is $90,000, what are the final fee and final price?
questions.explanation: Best: a $10,000 underrun earns the seller its 20% share = $2,000, so final fee = $10,000+$2,000 = $12,000 and final price = actual cost + fee = $90,000+$12,000 = $102,000. Closest miss — D: $112,000 adds the fee to the target cost instead of the actual cost. Also plausible — A ignores the incentive, and C reduces the fee as if the underrun were an overrun.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. If the actual cost is $120,000, what is the final price?
questions.explanation: Best: a $20,000 overrun cuts the seller's fee by its 20% share = $4,000, so final fee = $10,000−$4,000 = $6,000 and final price = $120,000+$6,000 = $126,000, still under the $130,000 ceiling. Closest miss — B: $130,000 assumes the ceiling is hit, but $126,000 is below it. Also plausible — C forgets the fee reduction, and A omits the fee entirely.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. Above what actual cost does the seller bear 100% of any further overrun (the point of total assumption)?
questions.explanation: Best: PTA = target cost + (ceiling − target price)/buyer share = $100,000 + ($130,000 − $110,000)/0.80 = $100,000 + $25,000 = $125,000; beyond it the seller absorbs all added cost. Closest miss — B: $130,000 is the ceiling PRICE, not the PTA cost. Also plausible — C and D confuse target price/cost figures with the PTA.

questions.question: On a predictive infrastructure project with baselined scope, schedule, and cost, a sponsor submits a formal change request expanding the network scope. The PM performs integrated change control. Which TWO activities are genuinely part of integrated change control rather than agile backlog grooming?
choices: Reprioritize and re-estimate items in the product backlog with the team ahead of the next iteration.
Assess the requested change's impact across scope, schedule, cost, quality, and risk before any approval decision is made.
Split a large requirement into smaller, independently deliverable pieces to clarify near-term work.
Log the change request in the register and implement it immediately to avoid delaying the sponsor.
Record the approve/reject/defer disposition (e.g., by the change control board) and update the affected baselines and configuration, then communicate the change.
questions.explanation: Best: integrated change control evaluates a request against all baselines and formally dispositions and configures it (B) cross-baseline impact analysis before deciding (E) documented CCB disposition plus baseline/configuration update and communication. Closest miss — A: reprioritizing and re-estimating the backlog is grooming/refinement — ongoing adaptive work, not formal baseline change control. Also plausible — C: story/requirement splitting is refinement, not ICC. D: implementing without impact analysis or approval skips the control process entirely.
questions.task: Process — Manage project changes / integrated change control

questions.question: Two technical leads on a predictive infrastructure program hold firmly opposed positions on which database platform to standardize on; each has credible reasoning and neither will concede. The architecture decision sits on the critical path and a choice is due this week. What should the program manager do first?
choices: Choose the platform favored by the more senior lead to break the deadlock quickly.
Facilitate a decision using weighted criteria tied to the program's requirements and constraints.
Escalate the disagreement to the sponsor to make the platform selection.
Run both platforms in parallel through the next phase and decide later.
questions.explanation: Best: B converts an opinion deadlock into an objective, criteria-based evaluation anchored to program requirements, producing a defensible decision within the deadline. Closest miss — D: a parallel trial gathers evidence but doubles effort and misses the due date on the critical path. Also plausible — A: deciding by seniority ignores the merits; C: escalating abdicates a choice the team can make.

questions.question: Decomposing the scope of a hospital-construction project, the project manager is deciding how far to break down each branch of the WBS. Some branches are already highly detailed while others remain at a high level. Which criterion best indicates that a branch has been decomposed to an appropriate level?
choices: Each resulting work package can be reliably estimated, assigned, and controlled.
Every branch reaches the same uniform number of levels for consistency.
Each work package represents no more than one week of effort.
Each branch is broken down until no further activities can be identified.
questions.explanation: Best: A states the governing rule — decomposition is sufficient when work packages can be estimated, assigned, and controlled with confidence, regardless of depth. Closest miss — C: a duration rule of thumb can guide decomposition but is arbitrary, not the governing test. Also plausible — B: uniform depth ignores that branches genuinely differ; D: decomposing to individual activities pushes past the work-package level into scheduling.
questions.task: Create the WBS and decompose scope

questions.question: The scope of a predictive data-migration project so far exists only as a hallway discussion and a summary email the sponsor sent afterward. Delivery is about to begin, and the project manager wants a reliable basis for controlling scope and verifying deliverables later. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Treat the sponsor's email as the scope baseline and begin delivery immediately.
Ask the sponsor to expand the email into a more detailed written message.
