Develop a documented scope statement and obtain stakeholder validation and sign-off.
Start work now and document the scope retrospectively as deliverables emerge.
questions.explanation: Best: C establishes a controllable, verifiable basis — an agreed, documented scope statement validated by stakeholders rather than an informal email. Closest miss — B: a fuller email improves the record but remains a one-party, unvalidated artifact. Also plausible — A: baselining an unvalidated email leaves control weak; D: deferring documentation leaves later verification without a firm reference.
questions.task: Define scope and establish the scope baseline

questions.question: On an adaptive product effort where customer needs are still emerging, a governance board asks the delivery lead to explain how scope will be managed given that a fixed, detailed scope baseline cannot be set up front. Which explanation best reflects sound adaptive practice?
choices: Scope is fully specified up front and frozen, then changed only through formal change control.
Scope evolves through a prioritized backlog, refined and re-ordered each iteration as learning occurs.
Scope is left open-ended, and whatever the team completes each iteration defines it.
Scope is set by the vendor contract and cannot change until contract renewal.
questions.explanation: Best: B describes adaptive scope management — a prioritized, continuously refined backlog that absorbs emerging needs iteration by iteration. Closest miss — C: iterative delivery is right, but scope without prioritization drifts and forfeits value focus. Also plausible — A: a frozen baseline contradicts the emergent-needs premise; D: a contract lock removes the responsiveness the board is asking about.
questions.task: Manage scope in an adaptive life cycle

questions.question: Midway through a predictive analytics platform build, the project manager discovers that developers have been adding small unrequested 'polish' features they consider improvements. None were requested by the customer or approved, and the additions are consuming budget that was never estimated. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Allow the refinements to continue since they improve the product at low individual cost.
Submit the refinements retroactively as an approved change to legitimize them.
Ask the customer whether they want to pay for the added features now built.
Stop the unapproved additions and reinforce that scope changes go through change control.
questions.explanation: Best: D halts gold plating that consumes unbudgeted effort and re-anchors changes to the change-control process. Closest miss — B: routing genuinely valuable additions through change control is right, but only after stopping the practice, not to retroactively bless it. Also plausible — A: tolerating additions accepts uncontrolled drift; C: monetizing them still presumes value the customer never requested.
questions.task: Control scope and prevent gold plating

questions.question: A predictive project's key deliverable has passed internal quality checks and been verified as conforming to its documented requirements. The project manager now needs the customer's formal acceptance so the deliverable can be considered complete. What should the project manager do to obtain it?
choices: Present the deliverable to the customer for review against acceptance criteria and sign-off.
Mark the deliverable complete in the register based solely on the passed internal quality checks.
Deploy the deliverable to production and treat customer use as implicit acceptance.
Invoice the customer for the deliverable to trigger the acceptance milestone.
questions.explanation: Best: A obtains formal acceptance by having the customer review the deliverable against agreed acceptance criteria and sign off — validating scope, which is distinct from internal quality verification. Closest miss — C: production use may follow acceptance but does not itself constitute formal sign-off. Also plausible — B: internal completion marking is quality control, not acceptance; D: invoicing records commercial status but skips validation.
questions.task: Validate scope and obtain formal acceptance

questions.question: A PMO analyst must produce a rough order-of-magnitude estimate early, then refine it as the design solidifies. She is deciding between analogous and parametric techniques. Which TWO statements correctly distinguish analogous from parametric estimating?
choices: Analogous estimating uses the actual values of a similar previous project as the basis for the current estimate; parametric multiplies a per-unit rate by the number of units.
Analogous estimating aggregates detailed bottom-up estimates from each work package into a project total.
Parametric relies on a statistical relationship between historical data and project variables, which typically makes it more accurate than analogous when the underlying data is scalable and reliable.
Parametric estimating averages an optimistic, most-likely, and pessimistic value for each activity to account for uncertainty.
Analogous is always more accurate than parametric because it draws on a real, completed project.
questions.explanation: Best: analogous is top-down, using a similar past project's actuals and expert judgment; parametric applies a statistical unit-rate relationship and is often more accurate when data scales (A) contrasts the two mechanisms (C) explains parametric's statistical basis and accuracy advantage. Closest miss — B: aggregating work-package detail is bottom-up estimating, not analogous. Also plausible — D: averaging three points is three-point/PERT, not parametric. E: 'always more accurate' is false — parametric frequently beats analogous.
questions.task: Process — Plan and manage schedule and budget (estimating)

questions.question: A software deliverable meets every product specification and the customer is pleased with it. As the project manager prepares to close the engagement, the contract's included user-training package has not yet been delivered, and the customer has not raised the matter. What should the project manager do before closing?
choices: Close the project, since the software — the primary deliverable — is complete and accepted.
Complete or formally resolve the contracted training package before initiating closure.
Note the training gap in lessons learned and close on the software acceptance.
Transfer the training obligation to the support team as a post-project item.
questions.explanation: Best: B recognizes that all contractual obligations, including the training package, must be delivered or formally settled before closure — an open deliverable is an unmet commitment regardless of the customer's silence. Closest miss — D: reassigning the obligation can work only if the customer and contract formally agree, which is not established. Also plausible — A: closing on software alone leaves a contracted deliverable outstanding; C: documenting the gap does not discharge the obligation.
questions.task: Settle obligations as a precondition to closure

questions.question: On a regulatory-reporting SaaS product, the heads of compliance, sales, and customer support each lobby the product owner to sequence their feature first for the next release. Budget and team capacity are fixed. How should the product owner determine backlog order?
choices: Rank items with a transparent, weighted model combining business value, risk reduction, and effort.
Sequence by each requester's organizational seniority so the highest authority is served first.
Alternate features evenly among the three groups to keep all stakeholders equally satisfied.
Prioritize the smallest items first to maximize the number of features shipped this release.
questions.explanation: Best: A — an objective, weighted model (value, risk reduction, cost of delay versus effort) resolves competing demands transparently and defensibly. Closest miss — D: shortest-job-first raises throughput count but size alone ignores value and risk. Also plausible — B, C: seniority and even-handed fairness are real organizational pressures but neither is value-driven.

questions.question: A transit agency is considering an on-demand ride-pooling app. Executives will not fund the full build until they see evidence that real riders will adopt it. Only a small discretionary budget is available now. What should the team do first to generate that evidence?
choices: Commission a market-research survey asking residents whether they would use such a service.
Develop a high-fidelity clickable prototype and present it to executives for sign-off.
Release a limited pilot MVP in one district and measure actual ridership and retention.
Produce a detailed business case projecting demand from comparable cities' adoption data.
questions.explanation: Best: C — a real pilot MVP produces validated learning from actual rider behavior, the strongest adoption evidence before committing full funding. Closest miss — A: surveys are cheap signal but stated intent routinely overstates real adoption. Also plausible — B, D: a prototype demonstrates the concept and analog data informs projections, but neither measures genuine uptake.

questions.question: After a hospital deploys an AI-assisted triage tool, the sponsor asks how the organization will confirm the promised reduction in emergency wait times is actually achieved. Which approach best answers the sponsor?
choices: Collect user-satisfaction feedback from clinical staff during the first weeks of operation.
Define benefit metrics and baselines now and track them against targets after go-live.
Confirm at go-live that every specified feature passed acceptance testing and works.
Schedule a post-implementation review at closure to document lessons learned.
questions.explanation: Best: B — a benefits-realization plan with baselines, metrics, owners, and measurement dates is what proves the outcome materialized over time. Closest miss — D: a benefits/PIR review belongs in the plan, but a single closure event without defined baselines cannot confirm sustained benefit. Also plausible — A, C: satisfaction is a proxy and acceptance proves output delivered, not the wait-time benefit realized.

questions.question: Midway through an e-commerce program, a competitor launches an augmented-reality try-on feature far ahead of the one still sitting in your backlog, sharply reducing its expected benefit. What should the project manager do next?
choices: Remove the feature from the backlog immediately since the competitor now owns that space.
Accelerate the feature to market quickly to avoid falling further behind the competitor.
Proceed as planned because the feature was already approved in the baseline scope.
Re-evaluate the feature's value with stakeholders and reprioritize the backlog accordingly.
questions.explanation: Best: D — the benefit changed, so reassess value and differentiation with the product owner and stakeholders and reprioritize, rather than presuming the answer. Closest miss — A: dropping it may well be right, but deciding before re-evaluating value is premature. Also plausible — B, C: speeding to market could recover some value and honoring the baseline is orderly, but both skip the value reassessment.

questions.question: Kicking off an internal HR self-service platform, the project lead wants to ensure the team builds what employees will actually value rather than what sponsors assume. What is the best early step?
choices: Engage representative users to define outcomes and acceptance criteria that express value.
Document detailed requirements from the sponsoring executives and freeze them as scope.
Benchmark competitor HR platforms and adopt their most common features as the scope.
Build a broad feature list from all stakeholders and implement it in priority order.
questions.explanation: Best: A — eliciting outcomes directly from representative end users and framing acceptance criteria around value grounds the build in what stakeholders truly value. Closest miss — D: collecting from all stakeholders and prioritizing is reasonable but risks feature count over value without user-validated outcomes. Also plausible — B, C: sponsor requirements and competitor benchmarks inform scope but both assume rather than confirm user value.

questions.question: A sponsor doubts a data-warehouse modernization is producing anything worthwhile and wants tangible proof soon. The program has run two months, so far generating heavy design documentation. What best demonstrates value to the sponsor?
choices: Present the completed architecture and design documents produced so far as progress.
Deliver a working end-to-end slice that reports on real data the sponsor cares about.
Share a burndown chart and velocity trend showing the team is on schedule.
Walk the sponsor through the updated project plan and remaining milestone dates.
questions.explanation: Best: B — a working, demonstrable increment running on data the sponsor values is the most tangible evidence of value produced. Closest miss — C: velocity and burndown show progress and activity but not realized value. Also plausible — A, D: design documents show work done and the plan shows intent, yet neither is a working outcome the sponsor can see.

questions.question: Early in planning a hybrid product launch, the PM wants to build as complete a risk register as possible before any prioritization begins. Which TWO techniques are valid RISK-IDENTIFICATION methods, as opposed to risk analysis or response techniques?
choices: Build a probability-and-impact matrix to rank the risks already recorded in the register.
Perform a Monte Carlo simulation to model the range of possible schedule and cost outcomes.
Facilitate a SWOT analysis and a structured brainstorming session with the team and subject-matter experts to surface threats and opportunities.
Run a Delphi technique gathering anonymous expert input, and review project documents and assumptions to elicit additional risks.
Assign owners and select mitigate or transfer strategies for the highest-priority risks.
questions.explanation: Best: identification techniques generate new risks — brainstorming, SWOT, checklists, document/assumption review, interviews, and Delphi (C) SWOT + brainstorming with SMEs (D) Delphi plus document/assumption analysis. Closest miss — A: a probability-and-impact matrix prioritizes already-identified risks — that is qualitative analysis, not identification. Also plausible — B: Monte Carlo is quantitative analysis, not identification. E: assigning owners and choosing mitigate/transfer is risk response planning.

questions.question: Before executing an offshore wind-farm installation, the project manager must determine which specialist crews, vessels, and materials are needed and when each is required. What is the best basis for this determination?
choices: Decompose the scope into activities and estimate resource types, quantities, and timing per activity.
Copy the resource plan from the organization's most recent comparable installation project.
Ask each functional manager how many of their people they can commit to the project.
Set resource levels to match the fixed budget the sponsor has already approved.
questions.explanation: Best: A — deriving requirements from the decomposed activities and schedule (bottom-up estimating) establishes what is needed and precisely when. Closest miss — B: an analogous plan is a fast starting point but must be tailored to this project's scope. Also plausible — C, D: manager availability and the approved budget are real constraints, but they shape rather than define the resource need.

questions.question: Two concurrent projects both require the organization's only certified cybersecurity assessor during the same two-week window. The two project managers are peers, and neither controls the other's schedule or priorities. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Reschedule your own project's assessment to a later window to avoid the conflict entirely.
Hire an external assessor immediately so your project keeps its original assessment dates.
Ask the assessor to work extended hours to cover both projects within the two weeks.
Jointly raise the conflict to the resource owner or PMO to arbitrate by priority.
questions.explanation: Best: D — a cross-project contention neither peer controls is resolved by the shared resource owner, PMO, or sponsor who can arbitrate on organizational priority. Closest miss — A: self-rescheduling may be the outcome, but conceding before priorities are known can needlessly harm your project. Also plausible — B, C: an external hire raises cost and qualification concerns and overtime risks quality and burnout.

questions.question: A resource histogram shows the lead systems engineer loaded at 60 hours per week for a 3-week task, though her capacity is 40 hours per week. The task lies on the critical path with zero float, and no other qualified engineer is available. If the work is leveled to her 40-hour capacity, how does the project finish move?
choices: The finish slips about one and a half weeks after leveling to capacity.
The finish is unaffected because smoothing keeps the work within available float.
The finish slips about half a week after the excess hours are redistributed.
The finish slips a full three weeks, effectively doubling the task's duration.
questions.explanation: Best: A — 180 total hours (60 × 3) at 40 hours per week needs 4.5 weeks versus 3 planned, and with zero float the finish slips about 1.5 weeks. Closest miss — B: smoothing prevents slippage only when float exists, and here float is zero. Also plausible — C, D: half a week miscounts the excess and three weeks ignores the 40-hour base rate.

questions.question: Custom MRI-shielding panels for a hospital build are held in customs, threatening the equipment-installation milestone three weeks away. The delivery sits on the critical path. What is the best first action for the project manager?
choices: Immediately reorder the panels from a domestic supplier to bypass the customs delay.
Rebaseline the schedule to move the installation milestone out by three weeks.
Assess the hold's cause and expected clearance date, then evaluate response options.
Resequence downstream trades so their work proceeds while the panels remain delayed.
questions.explanation: Best: C — quantify the cause, likely clearance date, and impact before choosing a response, because the right action depends on how long the hold truly lasts. Closest miss — D: resequencing to protect the critical path is a strong response but should follow assessment of the actual delay. Also plausible — A, B: a duplicate domestic order may prove unnecessary and rebaselining concedes the slip prematurely.

questions.question: Planning a new product team spread across three continents and five time zones with no shared office, the project manager wants to set up the team for effective collaboration from day one. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Mandate that all team members shift working hours to overlap with headquarters' time zone.
Establish communication norms, tools, and overlap windows collaboratively with the team.
Schedule a fixed daily all-hands video call at one set time for everyone.
Route all cross-team coordination through regional leads to reduce the meeting load.
questions.explanation: Best: B — co-creating communication ground rules, channels, cadence, and reasonable overlap windows tailors collaboration to a distributed team and builds buy-in. Closest miss — D: a hub-and-spoke through regional leads can help but should emerge from agreed norms, not replace them. Also plausible — A, C: forcing headquarters hours burdens distant members and one fixed meeting time is inequitable across five zones.
questions.task: Plan communications for a distributed team

questions.question: Before sequencing integration work, a project manager needs to confirm exactly when a specialized commissioning crew and a shared environmental test rig are each available. Which input most directly provides this?
choices: The activity list showing the tasks that require the crew and the rig.
The RACI chart identifying who is responsible for the commissioning activities.
The risk register entries covering possible unavailability of the crew and rig.
The resource calendars showing each resource's available working periods.
questions.explanation: Best: D — resource calendars specify the exact periods each resource is available, which is precisely what sequencing against shared constraints requires. Closest miss — A: the activity list shows demand for the resources but not their availability windows. Also plausible — B, C: the RACI shows accountability and the risk register flags possible unavailability, but neither gives the confirmed availability dates.

questions.question: Using the activity-on-node network, what is the critical path and the minimum project duration?
choices: Start–B–D–End, 5 days
Start–A–D–End, 7 days
Start–C–D–End, 10 days
Start–C–D–End, 14 days
questions.explanation: Best: the critical path is the LONGEST path — Start–C–D–End = 7+3 = 10 days — which sets the minimum duration. Closest miss — B: Start–A–D–End (4+3=7) is a real path but shorter, so it has float, not criticality. Also plausible — A is the shortest path, and D adds the durations incorrectly.

questions.question: For a well-defined, stable scope of work, a buyer wants to place the maximum possible cost-overrun risk on the seller. Which contract type best accomplishes this?
choices: Cost plus fixed fee, where the buyer reimburses actual costs plus a set fee.
Time and materials, billed at agreed rates for hours and materials used.
Firm fixed price, where the seller delivers the scope for one set price.
Cost plus incentive fee, sharing savings and overruns by a preset formula.
questions.explanation: Best: C — a firm-fixed-price contract fixes the price so the seller absorbs all cost overruns, and it fits a well-defined scope. Closest miss — D: cost plus incentive fee shifts some risk through a share ratio, but the buyer still bears part of any overrun. Also plausible — A, B: cost plus fixed fee leaves cost risk with the buyer and time and materials exposes the buyer to hours and quantities.
questions.task: Select contract type by risk allocation

questions.question: A pharmaceutical firm is launching a five-year drug-discovery program whose experimental pathways cannot be specified until early results emerge. The sponsor accepts that costs are unpredictable and has agreed to reimburse allowable costs, while still wanting the research partner strongly motivated to control spending. Which contract type best fits these conditions?
choices: Cost-plus-fixed-fee, paying documented costs plus a set fee
Cost-plus-incentive-fee, sharing cost savings and overruns against a target
Time-and-materials, billing agreed rates for hours and materials
Fixed-price-incentive-fee, adjusting fee within a firm price ceiling
questions.explanation: Best: B — costs are reimbursable, which fits the undefined, evolving scope, and the incentive fee ties the partner's fee to controlling cost against a target, matching the sponsor's motivation goal. Closest miss — A: also cost-reimbursable and workable, but a fixed fee gives no incentive to control the spend the sponsor is bearing. Also plausible — C: reimbursable and flexible but lacks any cost-control incentive and suits shorter staff augmentation; D: FPIF needs scope defined enough to set a fair ceiling, which is impossible here.

questions.question: A municipal agency has finalized a fully detailed, stable specification for replacing streetlights across a district, with no anticipated changes. Council members insist above all on knowing the exact total the project will cost before authorizing it. A supplier will deliver and install strictly to the fixed specification. Which contract type best satisfies the council's overriding priority?
choices: Cost-plus-award-fee, reimbursing costs plus a performance-based award
Time-and-materials, billing agreed rates until the work is complete
Fixed-price-incentive-fee, sharing savings beneath a firm price ceiling
Firm-fixed-price, setting one unchangeable total price
questions.explanation: Best: D — with stable, complete scope and cost certainty as the overriding priority, a firm-fixed-price sets one guaranteed total and places cost risk on the seller. Closest miss — C: still fixed-price and capped by a ceiling, but the incentive sharing introduces final-price variability the council explicitly wants to avoid. Also plausible — A: an award-fee arrangement still reimburses uncertain costs, contradicting cost certainty; B: a T&M total is open-ended, defeating the priority.

questions.question: Early in planning, a manufacturer must decide whether to produce a specialized control module internally or purchase it from an external supplier. Internal production is feasible but would consume capacity currently used for other product lines. Which consideration should most appropriately drive the make-or-buy decision?
choices: Total cost of ownership plus strategic factors like capacity, control, and capability
Whether the supplier's quoted unit price is below the internal per-unit cost
Whether internal teams have idle capacity available in the current quarter
Which option adds the least lead time to the project schedule
questions.explanation: Best: A — a sound make-or-buy weighs full total cost of ownership together with strategic factors (capacity impact, control, capability, confidentiality), integrating the other options rather than relying on any one. Closest miss — B: unit-price comparison is central but ignores overhead, risk, and the capacity trade-off the stem highlights. Also plausible — C: capacity is one relevant input; D: lead-time matters but is incomplete on its own.

questions.question: Over the past two months, inspection reports show a contracted supplier's machined parts increasingly failing dimensional acceptance criteria, though none has yet been formally rejected. The working relationship has been productive until now, and the contract includes quality specifications and remedies. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Issue a formal cure notice citing the quality clause and set a remediation deadline
Withhold payment on the affected deliverables until quality measurably improves
Review the quality requirements and inspection data, then discuss the trend with the supplier
Begin qualifying an alternate supplier to reduce dependence on this vendor
questions.explanation: Best: C — before invoking remedies the PM should confirm the data against contract requirements and engage the supplier to understand the cause, preserving a productive relationship and grounding any later action. Closest miss — A: a cure notice is a legitimate remedy but premature before diagnosis and may damage a salvageable relationship. Also plausible — B: withholding payment is a real lever but escalates before facts are established; D: dual-sourcing mitigates risk yet is heavy-handed ahead of understanding the problem.

questions.question: A program will rely on the same specialty-materials supplier across many phases over the next several years, and continuity of supply is critical to on-time delivery. As the project manager prepares to negotiate the master agreement, which negotiation stance is most appropriate given this long-term dependence?
choices: Pursue an integrative approach seeking mutual gains and a durable working relationship
Anchor hard on the lowest price to capture the largest immediate saving
Require the buyer's standard terms unchanged to keep the process efficient
Withhold long-term commitment and re-tender each phase to sustain competitive pressure
questions.explanation: Best: A — a repeated, delivery-critical dependency rewards an integrative, relationship-oriented stance that builds reliability and mutual value across the program's life. Closest miss — D: re-tendering preserves price tension and is a valid sourcing tactic, but it undermines the continuity and partnership the stem makes critical. Also plausible — B: aggressive price anchoring risks the relationship a long dependency needs; C: rigid terms speed the deal but sacrifice flexibility a multi-year partnership requires.

questions.question: A buyer needs a well-understood, tightly specified commodity component delivered to a fixed schedule and wants the cost risk of any overrun to sit with the seller. Which contract type best fits?
choices: Time-and-materials (T&M).
Firm-fixed-price (FFP).
Cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF).
Fixed-price-incentive-fee (FPIF).
questions.explanation: Best: for stable, well-defined scope where the buyer wants the seller to carry overrun risk, firm-fixed-price is the simplest correct fit. Closest miss — D: FPIF also places most cost risk on the seller, but its incentive/share mechanics add complexity that a fully specified, stable requirement does not need. Also plausible — A (T&M) and C (CPFF) shift cost risk toward the buyer, the opposite of what is wanted.

questions.question: Based on the Pareto chart of defects, which action does the data MOST support?
choices: Spread improvement effort evenly across all five categories to be fair to each area.
Focus improvement on the UI and Data categories first, since together they account for about three-quarters of defects.
Begin with the Other and Performance categories because they are easiest to fix quickly.
Take no action until a full root-cause analysis of every category is complete.
questions.explanation: Best: a Pareto chart directs effort to the vital few — UI (45%) and Data (30%) together are ~75% of defects, so tackling them yields the largest reduction. Closest miss — A: spreading effort evenly feels equitable but dilutes impact and ignores the whole point of the Pareto view. Also plausible — C chases the trivial many, and D delays all improvement for analysis the chart already informs.

questions.question: On a fixed-scope predictive project, the budget at completion is $400,000, earned value is $100,000, and actual cost is $125,000. Assuming the cost efficiency experienced so far continues through the remaining work, what is the estimate at completion?
questions.explanation: Best: B — when current cost performance is expected to continue, EAC = BAC ÷ CPI, with CPI = 100,000 ÷ 125,000 = 0.80, giving 400,000 ÷ 0.80 = $500,000. Closest miss — A: $425,000 = AC + (BAC − EV), the EAC formula for a one-time atypical variance, which the stem's 'continues' wording rules out. Also plausible — D: $400,000 assumes no overrun (EAC = BAC); C: $525,000 mistakenly adds actual cost to the full budget.

questions.question: A predictive project reports a budget at completion of $600,000, earned value of $200,000, and actual cost of $250,000. If the cost efficiency experienced to date is expected to persist through the remaining work, what variance at completion is projected?
choices: $50,000 over budget
$100,000 over budget
$150,000 over budget
$250,000 over budget
questions.explanation: Best: C — CPI = 200,000 ÷ 250,000 = 0.80, so EAC = BAC ÷ CPI = 600,000 ÷ 0.80 = $750,000, and VAC = BAC − EAC = 600,000 − 750,000 = −$150,000, a $150,000 overrun. Closest miss — A: $50,000 is the current cost variance (EV − AC), mistaken for the projected variance at completion. Also plausible — B: $100,000 has no consistent derivation; D: $250,000 equals actual cost to date, not a variance.

questions.question: Midway through a highway resurfacing project, the budget at completion is $900,000, earned value is $450,000, and actual cost to date is $500,000. Using the forecasting formula EAC = BAC ÷ CPI, what is the estimate at completion?
questions.explanation: Best: D — CPI = EV ÷ AC = 450,000 ÷ 500,000 = 0.90, so EAC = BAC ÷ CPI = 900,000 ÷ 0.90 = $1,000,000. Closest miss — A: $810,000 comes from multiplying BAC by CPI instead of dividing, a frequent inversion error. Also plausible — B: $900,000 assumes EAC equals BAC (no overrun); C: $950,000 adds the current $50,000 cost variance to BAC rather than applying CPI.

questions.question: A project manager needs to know how efficiently the remaining work must be performed to complete the project within its original approved budget. Current data are budget at completion $500,000, earned value $200,000, and actual cost $250,000. What is the to-complete performance index measured against the budget at completion?
questions.explanation: Best: A — TCPI(BAC) = (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC) = (500,000 − 200,000) ÷ (500,000 − 250,000) = 300,000 ÷ 250,000 = 1.20, so remaining work must run 20% more efficiently than planned. Closest miss — B: 0.80 is the CPI (EV ÷ AC), the past efficiency, not the required future efficiency. Also plausible — D: 1.50 divides by remaining earned value instead of remaining budget; C: 1.00 implies no change is needed, which the overrun contradicts.

questions.question: During cost planning, a project manager quantifies and sets aside a defined amount inside the cost baseline to fund specific identified risks that already have planned response strategies. Within the project manager's delegated authority, it can be drawn on without a separate approval each time. What is this allocation properly called?
choices: Management reserve, held outside the baseline and controlled by the sponsor
A single work package cost estimate rolled up into the baseline
Funding limit reconciliation applied to smooth period expenditures
Contingency reserve, included within the project's cost baseline
questions.explanation: Best: D — contingency reserve covers identified ('known-unknown') risks that have planned responses and sits inside the cost baseline, drawn on within the project manager's delegated authority. Closest miss — A: management reserve is also a reserve, but it sits OUTSIDE the baseline for unknown-unknowns and is released by governance, not the PM. Also plausible — B is a single work-package estimate, and C is funding-limit reconciliation, neither of which is a risk reserve.

questions.question: Well into execution, an in-scope regulatory condition surfaces that no one identified as a risk during planning and that now requires unplanned funding to address. The contingency reserve was budgeted only for previously identified risks. Which funding source is most appropriate for this situation?
choices: Draw from the contingency reserve, since it exists to cover cost risks
Reallocate budget from a lower-priority work package to cover the gap
Apply management reserve, intended for unforeseen but in-scope work
Submit a change request to expand the project's approved scope
questions.explanation: Best: C — management reserve is set aside precisely for unforeseen, in-scope work ('unknown-unknowns') and is accessed through approval, making it the correct source here. Closest miss — A: contingency reserve is tempting but is reserved for previously identified risks, which this condition was not. Also plausible — B: reallocation is a stopgap that underfunds the original work; D: the work is already in scope, so a scope-expansion change is inappropriate.

questions.question: From the earned-value chart (PV $200k, EV $160k, AC $180k at the data date), which statement is MOST accurate?
choices: Cost and schedule are effectively on track; the gaps are within normal noise.
The project is over budget but ahead of schedule.
The project is behind schedule but under budget.
The project is both behind schedule and over budget, and the schedule problem (SPI 0.80) is worse than the cost problem (CPI 0.89).
questions.explanation: Best: EV ($160k) is below both PV and AC, so SV = −$40k and CV = −$20k; SPI = 160/200 = 0.80 versus CPI = 160/180 = 0.89, so the schedule variance is the larger problem. Closest miss — C: it correctly reads 'behind schedule' but calls the project under budget, when AC above EV means it is over budget. Also plausible — B flips the schedule sign, and A dismisses variances of 10–20%.

questions.question: A project manager wants an approved reference that shows planned cumulative spending distributed across the project timeline, typically drawn as an S-curve, so that actual expenditures can be measured against it to detect variances during execution. Which artifact serves this purpose?
choices: The cost baseline, the time-phased approved budget used for comparison
The cost management plan, which defines how costs are managed
The budget at completion, a single total authorized amount
The project budget, comprising the baseline plus management reserve
questions.explanation: Best: A — the cost baseline is the approved, time-phased budget (the S-curve) against which actual costs and earned value are compared to measure performance. Closest miss — D: the project budget includes the baseline but adds management reserve, so it is not the time-phased comparison reference. Also plausible — B: the cost management plan describes processes, not the spend curve; C: BAC is a single value, not a time-phased profile.

questions.question: A sponsor overseeing a hybrid data-platform program challenges the recurring spend on peer design reviews and automated regression suites, describing both as non-value-adding overhead that inflates every release. The program has had no formal quality policy imposed on it. How should the project manager best frame the value of these activities to the sponsor?
choices: Reclassify the reviews as optional and fund only the automated tests, since automation scales more cheaply
Present them as prevention and appraisal costs that reduce far larger internal and external failure costs later
Offer to defer both until a defect trend emerges, then reinstate whichever the data later justifies
Position them as compliance controls required by the organization's quality policy and therefore non-negotiable
questions.explanation: Best: B — the cost-of-quality argument shows that conformance spend (prevention and appraisal) offsets much larger nonconformance (failure) costs, which is exactly the value case the sponsor is asking for. Closest miss — D: a policy framing is legitimate, but the stem says no quality policy is imposed, so it misstates the situation and dodges the value question. Also plausible — A, C: each keeps some quality effort but trades away prevention on an unproven assumption, risking higher total cost.

questions.question: A business analyst complains that a throwaway internal script the team built to migrate data one time — plain command-line interface, no polish — is 'low quality' and should be rebuilt to the company's product standards. The script has run correctly and reliably in rehearsal for its single intended use. How should the project manager respond?
choices: Agree it needs polishing and schedule rework so the tool meets the organization's product-grade UI standards
Document the concern as a quality defect and route it through the formal change control process
Explain that low grade is a deliberate choice and that quality means conformance to the tool's stated requirements
Add a lightweight help menu and friendlier error messages as a compromise before the migration runs
questions.explanation: Best: C — the script conforms to its requirements (high quality) at an intentionally low grade; low grade is a legitimate design decision, not a defect. Closest miss — B: routing it through change control as a 'defect' treats a grade preference as a conformance problem and wastes governance effort. Also plausible — A, D: both invest in raising grade that the single-use scope does not warrant.

questions.question: On a high-volume automotive-component line, the quality lead wants to sharply cut the number of nonconforming parts that reach customers. Several recognized quality principles are on the table, and the team must decide which one should most guide its improvement approach. Which principle should the team let drive its strategy?
choices: Strengthen final inspection and sampling so that more defects are detected before shipment
Optimize the cost of quality by balancing appraisal spend against expected failure cost
Pursue continuous improvement so that defect rates fall gradually across successive production runs
Build quality in through prevention so that defects are avoided rather than caught by inspection
questions.explanation: Best: D — prevention over inspection is the guiding principle; designing defects out addresses root cause and lowers total cost, which most directly reduces escapes. Closest miss — C: continuous improvement is valid and complementary, but it is a slower method rather than the primary principle for reducing escapes now. Also plausible — A, B: inspection detects but does not prevent escapes, and cost-of-quality is an analytical lens, not the driving principle.

questions.question: A consumer-electronics product shows several distinct defect types recurring across builds — solder faults, firmware hangs, and casing cracks. Before committing to fixes, the team wants to map each defect family to the underlying factors that produce it. Which technique best supports this cause analysis?
choices: Construct cause-and-effect diagrams to organize potential causes by category for each defect family
Build a Pareto chart to rank the defect types by frequency and concentrate on the largest
Plot the defects on a control chart to determine whether the process is stable over time
Use check sheets to tally where and when each defect type occurs during assembly
questions.explanation: Best: A — cause-and-effect (Ishikawa) diagrams systematically trace each defect family to underlying causal categories, which is exactly the mapping requested. Closest miss — B: a Pareto chart prioritizes which defects to tackle but does not identify their causes. Also plausible — C, D: control charts assess stability and check sheets collect data, both inputs to analysis rather than cause mapping.

questions.question: A packaging line's fill-weight control chart shows every plotted point inside the upper and lower control limits, yet the last seven consecutive measurements all fall just above the process mean. The process had been well centered for months with no known changes. What is the most appropriate interpretation and response?
choices: Take no action, because all points remain inside the control limits and the process is in control
Stop the line and recall recent output until the upward shift has been fully diagnosed
Treat the run as a non-random signal and investigate the assignable cause even though the limits hold
Immediately widen the control limits so they reflect the process's apparent new operating level
questions.explanation: Best: C — seven consecutive points on one side of the mean is the rule-of-seven non-random pattern, signaling an out-of-control condition despite being within limits, so the assignable cause should be investigated. Closest miss — B: investigation is right, but halting the line and recalling before any diagnosis is disproportionate when output is still within limits. Also plausible — A, D: 'inside limits means do nothing' ignores the run rule, and widening limits masks the signal instead of explaining it.

questions.question: A software team delivering in two-week iterations decides it would rather trim its defect rate by a small, steady amount every iteration than pause development for one large quality overhaul. The team wants the improvement woven into normal work. Which approach best matches this intent?
choices: Schedule a dedicated breakthrough re-engineering effort once enough defects have accumulated to justify it
Adopt incremental continuous improvement (kaizen), embedding small refinements into each iteration
Freeze new features and run a hardening iteration focused solely on removing existing defects
Raise the definition of done and begin enforcing it only from the next major release onward
questions.explanation: Best: B — kaizen is precisely small, continuous, iteration-by-iteration improvement, matching the team's stated intent. Closest miss — C: a hardening iteration does reduce defects but is a one-time concentrated effort, the opposite of steady small gains. Also plausible — A, D: breakthrough re-engineering is a single large change, and deferring a stricter definition of done delays the incremental gains the team wants now.

questions.question: A process control chart shows sample 8 plotting above the upper control limit while all others fall within the limits. What does this indicate, and what is the right response?
choices: A special (assignable) cause at sample 8 — investigate that specific occurrence rather than adjusting the whole process.
Normal common-cause variation — retune the process settings to pull the mean down.
The control limits are too tight — widen them so points stop breaching.
The process is chronically unstable — halt production and re-engineer it end to end.
questions.explanation: Best: a single point beyond a control limit signals special-cause variation, so investigate that specific sample's assignable cause before changing anything. Closest miss — B: adjusting a process for what is actually a special cause is 'tampering' — it treats an outlier as common-cause and usually adds variation. Also plausible — C hides the signal by widening limits, and D overreacts to one out-of-control point as if the whole process were unstable.

questions.question: Using three-point estimating on a design activity, the team provides an optimistic duration of 8 days, a most likely duration of 14 days, and a pessimistic duration of 26 days. Applying the PERT (beta) weighted formula, what expected duration should the schedule use for this activity?
choices: 14 days, taking the most likely estimate on its own
16 days, averaging the three estimates with equal weight
17 days, averaging only the optimistic and pessimistic estimates
15 days, weighting the most likely estimate four times
questions.explanation: Best: D — the beta PERT expected value is (O + 4·ML + P) / 6 = (8 + 56 + 26) / 6 = 90 / 6 = 15 days. Closest miss — B: 16 days uses the triangular average (O + ML + P) / 3, which omits the four-times weight on the most likely value. Also plausible — A, C: 14 days takes the most likely alone, and 17 days averages only the two extremes.

questions.question: In a small predictive network, Activity A (3 days) must finish before both B (4 days) and C (6 days) can start; both B and C must finish before D (5 days) can start. Assuming no leads or lags, what is the project's shortest possible duration, and how much total float does Activity B have?
choices: 14 days duration; Activity B has 2 days of total float
12 days duration; Activity B has 0 days of total float
14 days duration; Activity B has 0 days of total float
18 days duration; Activity B has 2 days of total float
questions.explanation: Best: A — the critical path is A-C-D = 3 + 6 + 5 = 14 days, the shortest possible duration; path A-B-D = 12 days, so B has 14 − 12 = 2 days of total float. Closest miss — C: it correctly finds 14 days but wrongly places B on the critical path with zero float. Also plausible — B, D: 12 days follows the shorter path as if it governed, and 18 days sums every activity as if all ran in series.

questions.question: A construction project's latest earned value report, covering the current reporting period, shows an earned value of $240,000 against a planned value of $200,000 for that same period. Using these figures, what is the schedule performance index, and what does it indicate about schedule progress?
choices: SPI = 0.83, indicating the project is behind schedule
SPI = 1.20, indicating the project is ahead of schedule
SPI = 1.20, indicating the project is over budget
SPI = 0.83, indicating the project is ahead of schedule
questions.explanation: Best: B — SPI = EV / PV = 240,000 / 200,000 = 1.20, and a value above 1.0 means more value was earned than planned, so the project is ahead of schedule. Closest miss — C: it computes the index correctly but misreads it as a cost (budget) indicator rather than a schedule one. Also plausible — A, D: 0.83 inverts the ratio to PV / EV, and pairing 0.83 with 'ahead' compounds the error.

questions.question: A newly assigned project coordinator asks you to explain what the critical path actually represents on a predictive schedule network, noting that several team members describe it in conflicting ways. To give an accurate answer, which of the following statements best describes the critical path?
choices: The longest path through the network, which determines the shortest possible project duration
The sequence of activities that all carry zero total float in every possible schedule
The path containing the project's most costly and highest-risk activities
The shortest continuous path of activities linking the project start to finish
questions.explanation: Best: A — the critical path is the longest-duration path through the network and therefore sets the minimum time in which the project can complete. Closest miss — B: critical activities often have zero total float, but that is a consequence rather than the definition, and float can be non-zero when imposed dates or constraints exist. Also plausible — C, D: criticality is about duration, not cost or risk, and it is the longest path, not the shortest.

questions.question: On a predictive build with a fixed contractual completion date now at risk, the project manager authorizes overtime and brings additional crews onto several critical-path activities, accepting that this will raise costs but expecting it to shorten those activities. Which schedule compression technique is being applied here?
choices: Fast tracking, performing sequential activities in parallel to save calendar time
Resource leveling, adjusting activity start dates to smooth out resource demand
Crashing, adding resources to shorten critical activities at increased cost
Resource smoothing, shifting work within available float to respect a resource limit
questions.explanation: Best: C — adding resources and overtime to shorten critical-path activities while accepting higher cost is the definition of crashing. Closest miss — A: fast tracking also compresses the schedule, but by overlapping activities rather than adding cost or resources. Also plausible — B, D: leveling and smoothing manage resource demand and typically do not shorten the overall schedule.

questions.question: To claw back lost time on a facility build, the project manager begins site construction of the early sections while the design of later sections is still being finalized — two phases that were originally planned to run strictly one after the other. Which technique does this represent, and what is its main trade-off?
choices: Crashing, which compresses the schedule but increases overall project cost
Fast tracking, which compresses the schedule but increases the risk of rework
Rolling-wave planning, which elaborates later work in detail as it approaches
Resource leveling, which extends the schedule in order to respect resource limits
questions.explanation: Best: B — overlapping phases that were meant to be sequential is fast tracking, and its characteristic trade-off is increased rework risk from starting downstream work on incomplete upstream information. Closest miss — A: crashing also compresses the schedule but does so by adding cost or resources, not by overlapping. Also plausible — C, D: rolling-wave is progressive elaboration of planning detail, and leveling adjusts for resources rather than compressing.

questions.question: On the probability–impact heatmap, which risk should receive the HIGHEST response priority by exposure?
choices: R3
R2
R4
R1
questions.explanation: Best: exposure = probability × impact. R4 sits at high/high (4×4 = 16), the largest exposure on the grid. Closest miss — B: R2 has very-high impact (2×5 = 10), which draws the eye, but its lower probability makes its exposure less than R4's. Also plausible — R3 (5×2 = 10) is high-probability/low-impact, and R1 (3×3 = 9) is squarely mid — all below R4.

questions.question: Over the past four sprints, a distributed agile team's completed story points have trended steadily downward, and the product owner is worried about the release forecast. The team has not raised any single blocker, and no members have left. What is the best action for the project manager to take?
choices: Increase the number of stories committed each sprint to push the output back up
Add several developers to the team to restore the previous delivery rate quickly
Use the next retrospective to help the team surface and analyze the causes of the decline
Recalculate the release forecast using the lower recent velocity and inform stakeholders
questions.explanation: Best: C — a sustained velocity decline with no named blocker is a signal to inspect and adapt, and the retrospective is where the team diagnoses the causes before choosing a remedy. Closest miss — D: refeeding the lower velocity into the forecast is prudent and may be needed, but it manages the reporting of the symptom without addressing why velocity is falling. Also plausible — A, B: over-committing ignores capacity reality, and adding people can slow a team further during ramp-up — both act before the cause is understood.

questions.question: A quarterly EVM dashboard for a bridge-refurbishment project shows planned value of $500,000, earned value of $460,000, and actual cost of $520,000 at the data date. The sponsor asks the project manager to report the cost variance so the committee can judge cost performance. What is the CV?
questions.explanation: Best: CV = EV − AC = 460,000 − 520,000 = -$60,000, a cost overrun for the work performed. Closest miss — B: -$40,000 is the schedule variance (EV − PV), not the cost variance. Also plausible — C: +$60,000 reverses the subtraction (AC − EV); D: +$40,000 reverses the schedule variance.

questions.question: Midway through a data-center migration, the performance report lists planned value of $360,000 and earned value of $310,000 for the work completed to date. A stakeholder asks what the schedule variance says about progress, given that SV is expressed in monetary terms. Which statement is correct?
choices: +$50,000; the project is ahead of schedule
-$50,000; the project is behind schedule
-$50,000; the project is over budget
-$0.86; the project is behind schedule
questions.explanation: Best — B: SV = EV − PV = 310,000 − 360,000 = -$50,000; a negative dollar SV means less value earned than planned, i.e., behind schedule. Closest miss — C: the -$50,000 figure is right, but SV reflects schedule position, not cost or budget. Also plausible — A: +$50,000 reverses the subtraction; D: -0.86 computes the SPI ratio rather than the dollar variance.

questions.question: An EVM report for a solar-farm installation shows earned value of $450,000 against actual cost of $375,000 at the reporting date. The project sponsor wants to know the cost performance index and what it signals about cost efficiency. Which statement is correct?
choices: 0.83; the project is over budget
1.20; the project is ahead of schedule
1.20; the project is under budget
0.83; the project is under budget
questions.explanation: Best — C: CPI = EV/AC = 450,000/375,000 = 1.20; above 1.0 means $1.20 of value earned per $1 spent, i.e., under budget for the work done. Closest miss — B: 1.20 is correct, but CPI measures cost efficiency, not schedule. Also plausible — A and D: 0.83 inverts the ratio (AC/EV), which then supports neither interpretation.

questions.question: On an agile mobile-app team, the scrum master wants a single chart that displays, day by day inside the current two-week iteration, how much of the committed work is still left, so the team can see whether they will finish on time. Which artifact best serves this need?
choices: A velocity chart comparing completed story points across recent iterations
A cumulative flow diagram showing work-item counts by workflow state
A burnup chart tracking completed work against the total committed scope
An iteration burndown chart plotting remaining work over the iteration
questions.explanation: Best — D: an iteration burndown plots remaining work against time within the iteration, directly showing whether the team is on track to finish. Closest miss — C: a burnup also trends over time but tracks completed work and total scope, not remaining work. Also plausible — A: velocity compares output across iterations, not within one; B: a CFD shows work-in-progress by state, useful for flow but not a clean remaining-work trend.

questions.question: During a retrospective on a hybrid infrastructure program, the team observes that they spend several hours each week compiling a thick stack of status reports, dashboards, and logs, yet most are rarely opened and few influence any decision. The reporting effort now exceeds the value it returns. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Work with the report consumers to keep only the reports that drive decisions
Continue producing every report to preserve a complete governance and audit trail
Automate generation of the existing reports so they consume less team effort
Reassign report preparation to a junior member to free the delivery team
questions.explanation: Best: engaging the report consumers to right-size reporting to what actually informs decisions removes the waste at its source (tailoring to value). Closest miss — C: automation lowers the effort but keeps maintaining low-value artifacts and may not be worth building; confirm the need first. Also plausible — B: an audit trail may require certain reports, but that justifies keeping specific ones, not all; D: delegating merely shifts the low-value work rather than eliminating it.

questions.question: Sponsors and functional leads spread across four time zones repeatedly email the project manager asking for the latest status, and by the time answers arrive the information is already stale. They complain they cannot see current progress when they need it. Which action best addresses the underlying problem?
choices: Send a detailed written status update to all stakeholders every Friday
Publish a continuously updated shared dashboard stakeholders can view on demand
Add a fuller status section to the existing monthly steering-committee report
Route all status requests through a single coordinator who replies for the PM
questions.explanation: Best — B: a live, self-serve information radiator gives distributed stakeholders current status at any hour, resolving both the staleness and the stream of one-off requests. Closest miss — D: a coordinator reduces the PM's load but still delivers pull-based, potentially stale answers and cannot cover every time zone. Also plausible — A: a weekly push is already stale by mid-week; C: monthly reporting is far too infrequent for on-demand needs.

questions.question: On the cumulative flow diagram, the 'In Test' band steadily widens over time. What does this MOST indicate, and what should the team do?
choices: The team is highly productive, since the total work in the system keeps growing.
Testing is a bottleneck — items arrive faster than they are tested; limit upstream WIP and add test capacity until flow recovers.
Testing is starved of work and the testers are idle; pull more items into test.
The diagram is healthy; a widening band is the normal shape of a CFD.
questions.explanation: Best: a widening band for a stage means arrivals outpace departures there — a bottleneck; the flow response is to cap upstream WIP and reinforce testing until the band stabilizes. Closest miss — A: a growing total can look like productivity, but growth concentrated in one stage is queueing, not throughput. Also plausible — C misreads a widening (not shrinking) band as starvation, and D treats a bottleneck signal as normal.

questions.question: At a status review for a software-integration project, the earned-value figures indicate roughly 40 percent of the work is complete, while the developers verbally insist they are closer to 60 percent done and on track. The two accounts cannot both be right. What should the project manager do?
choices: Rely on the earned-value data as the objective measure and update the team accordingly
Accept the developers' firsthand assessment and revise the performance baseline
Escalate the conflicting numbers to the sponsor to decide which to trust
Investigate how percent-complete is measured and reconcile the two accounts
questions.explanation: Best — D: the discrepancy usually traces to how completion is credited (the EV rules, un-updated actuals, or optimistic self-assessment); reconciling the measurement resolves it before any action. Closest miss — A: earned value is only as good as its inputs, which may be exactly what is wrong. Also plausible — B: changing the baseline on an unverified verbal claim is premature; C: escalating before investigating hands the sponsor an unanalyzed problem.

questions.question: The final deliverables of a predictive records-digitization project have all been produced and internally checked, and the project manager is preparing to move the project into closure. Which of the following is the necessary precondition before the project can be formally closed?
choices: Obtain the customer's formal acceptance and sign-off of the deliverables
Release the project team members back to their functional managers
Archive the project documentation and record the lessons learned
Issue the final performance report and update the estimate at completion
questions.explanation: Best — A: formal customer acceptance (validating scope) is the gate that authorizes closure; without it the project cannot be closed. Closest miss — D: a final performance report is part of closing, but it follows, and does not substitute for, acceptance. Also plausible — B and C: releasing resources and archiving are legitimate closure activities, but they occur after acceptance is secured, not before.

questions.question: A web-platform project repeatedly reaches almost done, only for stakeholders to request just one more small tweak, and the finish line keeps moving. The product owner wants an objective way to determine when an increment is genuinely complete and can be released. What best establishes that readiness?
choices: Impose a firm cut-off date after which no further change requests are accepted
Agree explicit, testable acceptance criteria and a shared definition of done
Route every new tweak through formal change control for approval before work
Freeze the current scope baseline and defer all new requests to a later release
questions.explanation: Best — B: an agreed definition of done with testable acceptance criteria gives an objective, shared bar for complete, ending the subjective drift. Closest miss — C: change control governs whether to accept additions but does not define when the increment itself is done. Also plausible — A: a fixed date is arbitrary and ignores quality and value; D: freezing scope halts creep but still leaves done undefined.

questions.question: A completed monitoring system has passed acceptance and is ready to transition to the operations group that will run it long-term. Before the project manager formally closes the project, which condition is most important to confirm?
choices: The project's financial accounts are fully reconciled and the budget is closed out
The system has run in production incident-free through a defined stabilization window
Operations has accepted the handover and is equipped to sustain the system
The team's lessons learned have been documented in the knowledge repository
questions.explanation: Best — C: a transition is not complete until the receiving operations group can actually sustain the system and has accepted the handover, which is the core precondition to closing. Closest miss — B: a stabilization period is a valuable go-live criterion but may not be in scope and does not by itself equip operations to run the system. Also plausible — A and D: financial reconciliation and lessons learned are closure activities, but neither is the handover-readiness condition.

questions.question: As a program winds down, the project manager wants the closeout to benefit future projects across the organization, not just record what happened on this one. Which closure activity most directly supports organizational learning beyond this project?
choices: Deliver a final report to the sponsor summarizing outcomes, variances, and benefits
Archive all project artifacts in the corporate records repository for future reference
Complete individual performance appraisals and capture development feedback
Register validated lessons learned in the organization's shared knowledge base
questions.explanation: Best — D: eliciting and validating lessons and registering them in the organization's searchable knowledge base makes the learning reusable by other teams. Closest miss — B: archiving preserves raw artifacts but leaves insights buried and hard to reuse, so it supports records more than learning. Also plausible — A: a final report informs this project's stakeholders; C: appraisals develop individuals, not the organization.

questions.question: A specialist contractor supplied and commissioned equipment on an industrial project that is now approaching closure. Before the project manager closes the project, what must be ensured regarding the procurement?
choices: All contractual obligations are met, deliverables accepted, and the contract formally closed
The contractor's final invoice is paid in full without delay to end the engagement
The contractor is added to the organization's preferred-supplier list for future work
Any unspent contract funds are transferred back into the project's reserve
questions.explanation: Best — A: procurement closure requires confirming obligations are fulfilled, deliverables accepted, claims resolved, and the contract formally closed before the project itself can close. Closest miss — B: settling payment is part of closure, but paying immediately before verifying obligations and resolving any claims can be premature. Also plausible — C: a supplier rating is optional and not a closure requirement; D: reserve accounting is housekeeping, not the contractual obligation to close the procurement.

questions.question: Halfway through a product-development project, leadership cancels it because a market shift has made the business case no longer valid. Work stops, but resources, contracts, and partially finished deliverables remain in place. How should the project manager proceed?
choices: Preserve the completed work and lobby leadership to continue the project in a reduced form
Conduct an orderly early closure that settles contracts, captures lessons, and releases resources
Stop all activity at once and immediately reassign the team to other initiatives
Finish the current phase first so the in-progress deliverables are not wasted
questions.explanation: Best — B: a cancelled project still goes through formal closure — documenting the decision and status, settling procurements, capturing lessons, salvaging usable outputs, and releasing resources in an orderly way. Closest miss — D: completing the phase seems to protect value but keeps spending against a business case already judged invalid. Also plausible — A: reversing a leadership decision is not the PM's role once cancellation is set; C: an abrupt stop skips closure obligations such as contract settlement and knowledge capture.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. What is the NET expected monetary value of Option A?
questions.explanation: Best: EMV of the benefit = 0.6×$200,000 + 0.4×$50,000 = $140,000; net of the $80,000 cost = $60,000. Closest miss — A: $140,000 is the gross EMV before subtracting the cost. Also plausible — C uses only the high-benefit branch, and D miscomputes the weighting.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. Turning to Option B, what is its NET expected monetary value?
questions.explanation: Best: EMV = 0.9×$120,000 + 0.1×$60,000 = $114,000; net of the $70,000 cost = $44,000. Closest miss — B: $114,000 is the gross EMV before cost. Also plausible — A is only the high branch (0.9×120k), and C is a rough guess.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. Using expected monetary value as the firm's decision criterion, which option should it choose?
choices: Option B, because its outcomes are more certain even though its net EMV is lower.
Option B, because its lower cost makes it the safer choice regardless of expected value.
Option A, because its net EMV ($60,000) exceeds Option B's ($44,000), accepting its wider spread of outcomes.
Neither, because the benefits are uncertain and cannot support a decision.
questions.explanation: Best: on an expected-value basis Option A's net EMV ($60,000) beats Option B's ($44,000), so it is the value-maximizing choice, with its wider outcome spread noted as the trade-off. Closest miss — A: Option B is genuinely more certain, a legitimate risk-averse preference, but it yields lower expected value, so it wins only if the firm is deliberately trading value for certainty. Also plausible — B fixates on upfront cost, and D ignores that EMV is exactly how such uncertainty is compared.

questions.question: Before launching an enterprise CRM transformation, the change manager assesses whether the organization is truly ready to adopt the change rather than merely technically able to deploy it. Which TWO factors best indicate organizational readiness for change?
choices: A fully detailed project schedule with all milestones and dependencies baselined.
Active, sustained sponsorship from senior leaders who visibly and consistently champion the change.
A clearly articulated, widely shared reason for the change, so stakeholders understand the 'why' and the desired future state.
A technically superior solution that has already been selected, configured, and built.
A firm regulatory deadline that compels the organization to adopt the change on time.
questions.explanation: Best: readiness is about people and leadership adopting the change — visible sponsorship and a shared, compelling case for change (B) active executive championing sustains momentum (C) a clear 'why' and future-state vision drives commitment. Closest miss — D: a superior, already-built solution reflects technical readiness, not organizational readiness to adopt — capability to deploy is not willingness to change. Also plausible — A: a baselined schedule is a delivery artifact, not an adoption indicator. E: a mandated deadline creates pressure but can breed resistance, not readiness.
questions.task: Business Environment — Support organizational change and evaluate readiness

questions.question: Setting up oversight for a new initiative, the project manager wants its governance to fit the way the wider organization already directs and monitors its projects, so reporting and decisions stay consistent across the portfolio. Which approach BEST achieves that?
choices: Tailor the project's governance to fit the organization's existing framework and PMO standards.
Design governance specifically around this initiative's own unique characteristics and its stakeholders.
Copy the governance model wholesale from the organization's most recent successful project.
Let the steering committee define governance independently at its first meeting.
questions.explanation: Best: A — project governance should be tailored from and aligned with the organization's enterprise/PMO governance so oversight stays consistent across the portfolio. Closest miss — C: reusing a proven model borrows some alignment but may not fit this project or current standards. Also plausible — B: project-specific tailoring belongs inside the org framework, not instead of it; D: independent committee design risks diverging from portfolio norms.

questions.question: On a large transformation program, team members are confused about who does what: some take funding requests and go/no-go questions to the steering committee, while others take the same questions to the sponsor, and the two occasionally give different answers. Which statement BEST distinguishes their roles?
choices: The steering committee secures funding; the sponsor manages the program's day-to-day delivery and reporting.
The sponsor and steering committee hold identical authority, so either body may decide any matter.
The sponsor secures funding and owns benefits; the steering committee provides collective oversight and direction.
The steering committee owns the business case; the sponsor represents one department's local interests only.
questions.explanation: Best: C — the sponsor is the accountable individual who secures funding and owns benefits, while the steering committee is the collective body giving oversight and direction. Closest miss — A: plausible-sounding but reversed — the sponsor, not the committee, secures funding, and the sponsor does not run day-to-day delivery. Also plausible — B: their authorities are not identical; D: the sponsor owns the business case and represents the whole initiative, not one department.

questions.question: A medical-device project intends to embed an AI model, trained on historical patient records, into a feature that will influence clinical decisions at the point of care. Development is ready to begin. Before building the feature, what should the team do FIRST?
choices: Confirm the data use, consent, and model meet applicable privacy and device regulations.
Benchmark the model's diagnostic accuracy against clinicians to prove its clinical value.
Document the model's training data and architecture for the eventual regulatory submission.
Pilot the feature with a small clinician group to gather early usability feedback.
questions.explanation: Best: A — using patient data in an AI clinical feature triggers privacy and medical-device regulatory obligations that must be confirmed before development begins. Closest miss — C: documenting for the submission is necessary later, but the lawfulness of the data use and consent must be established first. Also plausible — B, D: accuracy benchmarking and usability piloting add value but presume the data and feature are lawfully permitted.

questions.question: Having logged dozens of mandatory compliance requirements, the project manager can assign only limited assurance resources this iteration and must sequence the work. All requirements must ultimately be met. Four stand out: (W) severe impact, likely to be missed; (X) severe impact, unlikely; (Y) minor impact, likely; (Z) minor impact, unlikely. Where should assurance effort concentrate first?
choices: Requirement X, because a severe-impact requirement always warrants attention ahead of minor ones.
Requirement Y, because a likely miss should be closed before unlikely ones regardless of impact.
Requirement W, where high impact and high likelihood of non-compliance create the greatest exposure.
Split effort evenly so every mandatory requirement receives equal assurance this iteration.
questions.explanation: Best: C — with every requirement mandatory, assurance effort is sequenced by exposure (impact × likelihood), and W scores highest on both. Closest miss — A: severity matters, but X's low likelihood gives it lower exposure than W. Also plausible — B: likelihood alone ignores impact; D: equal splitting abandons risk-based prioritization when resources are constrained.

questions.question: Halfway through building a consumer-finance platform, the project manager learns that a regulation governing a core feature is under formal revision and could change materially before the planned launch. The final wording is not yet published. What should the project manager do?
choices: Build strictly to the current regulation and revise later only if the rules actually change.
Pause the affected feature until the revised regulation is finalized and published.
Design to the team's best guess of the likely new requirements to stay ahead.
Monitor the revision, assess its impact, and plan the feature to adapt as it firms.
questions.explanation: Best: D — an in-flight regulatory change is monitored and impact-assessed so the design can adapt when the wording settles, protecting compliance without stalling. Closest miss — A: building to the current rule is defensible but risks late rework if the change lands unmonitored. Also plausible — B: pausing avoids rework but may forfeit the launch unnecessarily; C: designing to a guess risks building to rules that never take effect.

questions.question: Governance asks the project manager to demonstrate, at the next review, exactly where the project stands against its regulatory and contractual obligations. The project tracks dozens of such obligations across several jurisdictions. Which is the BEST way to provide that evidence?
choices: Present a compliance register mapping each obligation to its current status and supporting evidence.
Provide a written attestation from the project manager that all obligations are being met.
Summarize compliance progress in the standard project status report's risk section.
Commission an external audit to independently verify the project's compliance position.
questions.explanation: Best: A — a maintained compliance register mapping each obligation to its status and evidence demonstrates standing objectively and at the right granularity. Closest miss — D: an external audit is authoritative but heavier and slower than a status demonstration needs. Also plausible — B: an attestation asserts compliance without evidence; C: a status-report section is too coarse to show obligation-level standing.

questions.question: To hit a committed launch date, the team proposes skipping a mandatory environmental-compliance certification that the product legally requires before sale; a key customer has signaled they would accept delivery without seeing it. Missing the date carries contractual penalties. What should the project manager do?
choices: Skip the certification for launch and complete it shortly after, since the customer agreed.
Reduce the product's scope so the uncertified elements are excluded from this release.
Keep the certification as non-negotiable and address the date via replanning or escalation.
Obtain a written waiver from the customer accepting the product without the certification.
questions.explanation: Best: C — a legally mandatory certification cannot be traded for schedule or customer convenience, so the PM keeps it and manages the date through replanning or escalation. Closest miss — B: descoping is legitimate only if the uncertified elements can lawfully be removed, which the stem does not establish. Also plausible — A: launching uncertified breaches the law; D: a customer waiver cannot override a statutory requirement.

questions.question: During verification of a completed customer-portal module, the project manager finds it stores personal data in a way that breaches an applicable data-protection requirement. The module has passed functional testing but has not yet gone live. What is the BEST action to take?
choices: Log the issue in the defect tracker and schedule the fix into a later release.
Release the module as planned and remediate the data-protection breach in a fast follow-up.
Treat the breach as low priority, since the module has not yet processed real user data.
Hold the release, contain the nonconformance, remediate it, and assess notification obligations.
questions.explanation: Best: D — a data-protection breach is a compliance nonconformance, so the PM prevents release, remediates it, and checks whether the incident triggers notification duties.
