Closest miss — A: 900,000 uses the atypical formula (AC + BAC − EV), which the efficiency-persists assumption excludes. Also plausible — C, D: 700,000 merely subtracts the overrun; 640,000 multiplies BAC by CPI.

questions.question: Six days into a ten-day sprint, the burndown shows actual work remaining consistently BELOW the ideal line. What is the best interpretation and response?
choices: The team is ahead of plan; the Scrum Master should have it confirm the goal will be met and, with the product owner, consider pulling in additional value or helping elsewhere.
The team is behind and should add overtime to catch up to the ideal line.
The chart is in error, because actual burndown cannot fall below the ideal line.
The team should slow down to exactly match the ideal line and avoid finishing early.
questions.explanation: Best: actual remaining below the ideal line means the team is ahead of plan, so confirm the goal is safe and collaborate with the PO on additional value or helping others. Closest miss — D: pacing to the ideal line sounds disciplined, but deliberately slowing to avoid early finish wastes capacity that could deliver more value. Also plausible — B misreads 'ahead' as 'behind', and C wrongly claims the actual line cannot beat the ideal.

questions.question: On a medical-device assembly line, escaped defects are reaching hospitals and triggering complaints. The team currently relies on end-of-line testing to find problems. Leadership wants a quality philosophy that reduces the defects customers ever experience, rather than simply catching more of them just before shipment. Which philosophy should guide the team's approach to quality?
choices: Strengthen final inspection so more defects are caught before shipment
Apply acceptance sampling to release only lots that meet an agreed defect threshold
Emphasize prevention over inspection so quality is built in and defects are avoided
Increase the number of quality-control checkpoints late in the workflow
questions.explanation: Best: C — a prevention-over-inspection philosophy builds quality into the process so defects are avoided before they can escape, which is exactly what leadership wants, and prevention is the lowest-cost point in the cost of quality. Closest miss — A: stronger final inspection catches more defects but still detects rather than prevents, and escapes can slip past appraisal. Also plausible — B, D: sampling and more late checkpoints improve detection, not prevention.

questions.question: A firmware module for an autonomous shuttle must satisfy strict functional-safety standards that a national regulator will audit before approval. The engineering lead asks how the quality requirements should be managed across the build. Every listed standard is mandatory, and rework late in the program would be costly. How should the project manager handle these regulatory quality requirements?
choices: Schedule comprehensive compliance testing at the end, before the deliverable is handed over
Capture the standards as acceptance criteria and quality metrics, verifying them throughout the work
Rely on the supplier's certification that the component already meets the standard
Focus verification on the requirements the regulator is most likely to audit
questions.explanation: Best: B — capturing the mandatory standards as explicit acceptance criteria and quality metrics and verifying them continuously builds compliance in and surfaces gaps early. Closest miss — A: a single end-of-line compliance test meets the letter of the requirement but discovers failures late, when rework is most costly. Also plausible — C, D: relying on a supplier certificate or verifying only likely-audited items leaves mandatory requirements unverified.

questions.question: Halfway through a data-platform migration, rework triggered by defects found during late integration testing is consuming nearly a third of the remaining budget. The sponsor asks the project manager to determine where quality money is going and where to invest to bring total quality cost down. What should the project manager analyze?
choices: Compare the cost of quality: prevention and appraisal spend versus internal and external failure costs
Add the recurring rework to the risk register as a new threat with a response
Analyze schedule performance to see how the rework is affecting the critical path
Trace each defect to its originating step and retrain the people responsible
questions.explanation: Best: A — a cost-of-quality analysis compares prevention/appraisal spend against internal and external failure costs, showing that shifting investment upstream can lower total quality cost; late rework is the expensive failure category, so the economics are where the answer lies. Closest miss — D: tracing defects to their origin is useful, but coupling it with retraining assumes people, not the process, are the cause. Also plausible — B, C: logging a risk or checking critical-path impact addresses symptoms, not the quality economics.

questions.question: Throughout execution of a satellite-ground-station build, the project manager wants ongoing assurance that the processes generating the deliverables are sound, not merely that finished items pass at the end. Distributed teams work to documented procedures. Which activity best gives the project manager continuous confidence that the processes themselves will yield quality results?
choices: Inspect completed deliverables against their acceptance criteria to catch defects
Track defect counts on a control chart to watch output variation
Have peers review each deliverable before it advances to the next stage
Audit the processes against the plan and standards to confirm they are followed
questions.explanation: Best: D — auditing the processes against the plan and standards is quality assurance, which provides ongoing confidence that the process itself will produce good results. Closest miss — B: a control chart monitors output variation and hints at process stability, but it watches product data rather than confirming the process conforms to the plan. Also plausible — A, C: inspection and peer review verify finished deliverables, not the processes producing them.

questions.question: During an iteration retrospective, a delivery team notices that the same wiring defect keeps appearing, and every occurrence traces to the same soldering step in the workflow. The defect has recurred across three iterations despite being corrected each time. What should the project manager do?
choices: Perform root cause analysis at that step and improve the process so it stops recurring
Add an inspection immediately after that step to catch the defect each time
Retrain the members who perform that step to lower the error rate
Log the recurring defect as a risk and monitor it in future iterations
questions.explanation: Best: A — a defect recurring at one identified step despite repeated fixes is systemic, so root-cause analysis and a process improvement eliminate it at the source. Closest miss — B: adding an inspection after the step reliably catches the defect but leaves the cause in place and adds permanent appraisal cost. Also plausible — C, D: retraining assumes human error without evidence, and logging it as a risk only monitors a known, repeating problem.

questions.question: A green-building retrofit must hold quality high while respecting a tight budget and aggressive embodied-carbon targets. The client, contractor, and sustainability lead each press different priorities. The project manager must decide how much to invest in quality relative to cost and sustainability. What is the best approach?
choices: Maximize quality regardless of cost, since defects are the most expensive outcome
Meet the agreed requirements and weigh added quality spend against cost and sustainability together
Minimize quality spend to protect both the budget and the sustainability targets
Set quality at the highest grade the budget allows, then review sustainability afterward
questions.explanation: Best: B — meeting the agreed requirements and weighing any additional quality spend jointly against cost and sustainability optimizes value across all three dimensions and avoids gold-plating. Closest miss — D: choosing the highest grade the budget allows and reviewing sustainability afterward treats sustainability as an add-on rather than a joint constraint. Also plausible — A, C: maximizing quality regardless of cost gold-plates, while minimizing spend risks failure costs.
questions.task: Balance quality against cost and value

questions.question: An electrical fit-out network runs two paths from start to finish. Path 1 is Survey (2 days) → Wire (6 days) → Inspect (2 days). Path 2 is Survey (2 days) → Mount (3 days) → Inspect (2 days), sharing the same Survey and Inspect activities. What is the total float of the Mount activity, and which path is critical?
choices: 3 days of float; Path 1 is the critical path
0 days of float; Path 2 is the critical path
3 days of float; Path 2 is the critical path
7 days of float; Path 1 is the critical path
questions.explanation: Best: A — Path 1 totals 10 days versus Path 2's 7 days, so Path 1 is critical and Mount carries 10 − 7 = 3 days of total float. Closest miss — C: the 3-day float is correct, but Path 2, the shorter path, is not the critical one. Also plausible — B, D: 0 days wrongly treats Mount as critical, and 7 days confuses Path 2's length with float.

questions.question: Assigned to a new logistics-automation initiative, a scheduler is eager to begin laying out activities and durations for the timeline. The team, however, has not yet decided whether the work will be delivered predictively, adaptively, or as a hybrid. What should be done before the schedule is modeled?
choices: Decompose the scope into a work breakdown structure to define the activities
Sequence the identified activities to establish their dependencies
Determine the development approach and life cycle, which shapes how the schedule is built
Estimate activity durations using the team's historical data
questions.explanation: Best: C — the development approach and life cycle (predictive, adaptive, or hybrid) determine how the schedule is modeled, so it must be chosen before activities are defined, sequenced, or estimated. Closest miss — A: building the WBS is the right next step, but only after the approach frames how detailed and iterative the plan should be. Also plausible — B, D: sequencing and duration estimating come later in the schedule flow.

questions.question: On a predictive bridge-inspection program, activity duration estimates from the team vary widely and the engineers express genuine uncertainty about how long several tasks will take. The project manager wants estimates the schedule can rely on. Which technique best improves the reliability of these duration estimates?
choices: Use three-point estimating with optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic durations
Apply analogous estimating from a similar past project to set the durations
Use parametric estimating from a rate multiplied by the quantity of work
Ask the most senior engineer for a single expert estimate per task
questions.explanation: Best: A — three-point estimating models optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic durations, directly accounting for the team's uncertainty and yielding a more reliable expected value with a visible range. Closest miss — C: parametric estimating is accurate where a reliable rate exists, but it does not capture the wide uncertainty the team is expressing. Also plausible — B, D: analogous and single expert estimates produce point values that hide the spread.

questions.question: The chart shows actual cumulative spend running below the planned spend curve. On this information ALONE, what should the project manager conclude?
choices: The project is exactly on schedule, since spending is proceeding.
The project is under budget and performing well.
The project is over budget and needs corrective action.
Not enough to judge health — underspend could mean genuine savings OR work not yet done; earned value is needed to separate cost from schedule.
questions.explanation: Best: spend-versus-plan compares planned to actual COST but says nothing about work accomplished; below-plan spend can be real savings or simply work not done, so earned value (EV) is required to interpret it. Closest miss — B: 'under budget, doing well' is the intuitive read, but without EV the underspend may just mean the team is behind schedule. Also plausible — C jumps to over budget with no basis, and A reads schedule status from a cost curve.

questions.question: Two initiatives in the same portfolio depend on a shared testing lab, and their current schedules would both require the lab during the same two-week window. The project manager of one initiative spots the looming collision while reviewing the integrated view. What should the project manager do?
choices: Move your own activities out of the contested window to avoid the collision
Coordinate with the other manager and the program to align around the shared dependency
Escalate the conflict to the sponsor to decide which project has priority
Add a schedule buffer before the shared dependency to absorb any potential overlap
questions.explanation: Best: B — a shared dependency across two projects is a program-level integration issue, so coordinating with the other manager and the program aligns both schedules and manages the constraint jointly. Closest miss — C: escalating to the sponsor may eventually be needed, but it is premature before the managers attempt to coordinate a solution. Also plausible — A, D: unilaterally moving activities or adding a buffer addresses only one side of a shared problem.

questions.question: Trend analysis on an ERP rollout shows the project drifting behind schedule, and an anxious steering-committee member is already urging the project manager to add contractors to catch up. Before committing to any recovery action, the project manager pauses. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Analyze the schedule variance to understand its cause and size before choosing a response
Crash the critical path by adding resources to recover the slippage
Fast-track by overlapping activities to pull the schedule back
Re-baseline the schedule to reflect the current trend
questions.explanation: Best: A — analyzing the schedule variance to understand its cause and magnitude first ensures the recovery action fits the actual problem, despite pressure to act immediately. Closest miss — B: crashing with contractors may prove correct, but committing before diagnosis risks spending on the wrong activities. Also plausible — C, D: fast-tracking adds risk prematurely, and re-baselining hides the slippage instead of addressing it.

questions.question: The critical path on a refinery-turnaround project has slipped, and the go-live date is fixed by a regulatory shutdown window. Budget reserve is available, and several critical activities can each be compressed by adding labor, but at different crash costs per day. The project manager decides to add resources. How should the project manager apply this compression?
choices: Crash every critical activity simultaneously to recover the time as fast as possible
Crash the longest critical activity, since it offers the most room to compress
Crash the lowest crash-cost-per-day critical activities until the lost time is recovered
Fast-track by overlapping critical activities to avoid the added labor cost
questions.explanation: Best: C — with a fixed date and available reserve, crashing critical activities in order of lowest crash cost per day recovers the needed time at the least added cost. Closest miss — B: the longest activity may look like it offers the most room, but duration does not mean it is the cheapest to compress. Also plausible — A, D: crashing everything at once wastes budget, and fast-tracking adds rework risk the chosen compression path avoids.

questions.question: A status report for a bridge-sensor deployment shows earned value (EV) of $120,000, planned value (PV) of $150,000, and actual cost (AC) of $100,000 at the reporting date. What is the schedule performance index (SPI), and what does it indicate about the project?
choices: 1.20; the project is ahead of schedule
0.80; the project is behind schedule
1.25; the project is behind schedule
0.80; the project is over budget
questions.explanation: Best: B — SPI = EV / PV = 120,000 / 150,000 = 0.80; below 1.0 means less work has been completed than planned, so the project is behind schedule. Closest miss — D: 0.80 is the correct value, but SPI measures schedule, not budget, so 'over budget' misreads the index. Also plausible — A, C: 1.20 uses CPI (EV/AC), and 1.25 inverts the ratio to PV/EV.

questions.question: At a checkpoint on a telecom-tower rollout, the project reports earned value (EV) of $300,000, planned value (PV) of $350,000, and actual cost (AC) of $320,000. What is the schedule variance (SV), and what does it indicate?
choices: +$50,000; the project is ahead of schedule
-$20,000; the project is over budget
-$50,000; the project is over budget
-$50,000; the project is behind schedule
questions.explanation: Best: D — SV = EV − PV = 300,000 − 350,000 = −$50,000; a negative SV means the project is behind schedule. Closest miss — C: −$50,000 is the correct value, but SV measures schedule, so 'over budget' describes cost variance, not schedule variance. Also plausible — A, B: +$50,000 flips the sign, and −$20,000 is the cost variance (EV − AC).

questions.question: A newly assigned project manager on a hybrid product-development effort inherits a governance template pack of roughly forty artifacts and dozens of metrics carried over from a prior waterfall program. Many reports go unread, yet the team spends hours each week producing them. The manager must decide which artifacts and metrics the project genuinely needs. What is the best approach?
choices: Retain the full inherited template set for audit safety, adding metrics whenever stakeholders request them.
Map each artifact and metric to a decision or information need, then retire those informing none.
Replace the inherited set with the delivery team's lightweight agile metrics such as velocity and burndown.
Poll the governance committee on which reports they actually read, and keep only those.
questions.explanation: Best: B — tailoring is decision- and information-need driven; keep only artifacts and metrics that inform a real decision or stakeholder need (PMBOK 8 value/tailoring). Closest miss — D: reading habits are a useful signal but capture only the governance audience's needs, missing delivery and team decisions. Also plausible — A: audit-safe but low-value and wasteful; C: team-centric metrics ignore governance and business information needs.

questions.question: On a distributed infrastructure program, engineers and vendors keep working from conflicting copies of the design baseline that were emailed months apart. A recent batch of rework was built against a superseded specification, and several stakeholders report they cannot locate the current version of key documents when they need them. What should the project manager do?
choices: Circulate the latest approved documents by email again and ask everyone to delete older copies.
Establish a single authoritative repository with version control and role-based access to project artifacts.
Assign a document controller to answer version questions from the team as they arise.
Add a mandatory version-check step to the change control board's standing agenda.
questions.explanation: Best: B — the root fix is an information/configuration-management system: one authoritative repository, version control, and role-based access so the current version is always findable. Closest miss — C: a document controller helps but is reactive and person-dependent, and conflicting copies persist. Also plausible — A: re-emailing recreates the same version sprawl; D: a CCB check governs changes but doesn't give stakeholders access to the current artifact.

questions.question: A predictive infrastructure project has an approved budget at completion (BAC) of $1,000,000. At the current status date, earned value (EV) is $600,000 and actual cost (AC) is $700,000. Management requires the remaining work to be completed within the original BAC. What to-complete performance index (TCPI) must the team achieve on the remaining work?
questions.explanation: Best: D — TCPI to finish within BAC = (BAC−EV)/(BAC−AC) = 400,000/300,000 = 1.33. Closest miss — B: 0.75 inverts the ratio, using (BAC−AC)/(BAC−EV). Also plausible — A: 0.86 is CPI (EV/AC); C: 0.40 is remaining work divided by BAC.

questions.question: On an agile software program, the sponsor's dashboard has shown several features at eighty-percent complete for weeks, yet almost nothing has shipped to production. The project manager suspects the team's self-reported percent-complete overstates true progress and wants reporting the sponsor can trust. What should the project manager do?
choices: Ask team leads to re-estimate percent-complete more conservatively each reporting cycle.
Add a quality reviewer to audit the reported percentages before they reach the dashboard.
Track objective done/not-done status: features accepted against acceptance criteria and demonstrated working.
Extend the reporting cadence to monthly so partial work matures before it is reported.
questions.explanation: Best: C — objective binary completion tied to acceptance criteria and a definition of done removes the subjectivity that inflates percent-complete. Closest miss — B: auditing the reported figure still measures a subjective quantity, only more slowly. Also plausible — A: conservative re-estimation is still an opinion; D: monthly reporting hides the signal rather than correcting it.

questions.question: A cycle-time histogram for completed work items is right-skewed with a long tail of slow items. What does this MOST imply for forecasting delivery?
choices: Cycle time is stable, so the simple average is a reliable commitment for every item.
The long right tail means the mean understates risk; the team should investigate the slow outliers and forecast with a percentile (e.g., 85th) rather than the average.
The distribution is normal, so mean ± one standard deviation captures nearly all items.
The tail items are data errors and should be removed before forecasting.
questions.explanation: Best: a right-skewed cycle-time distribution has outliers that inflate delivery risk, so forecasts should use a percentile (like the 85th) and the team should investigate what makes the tail items slow. Closest miss — A: the average is easy to quote, but committing to it ignores the tail and will miss dates for the slow items. Also plausible — C wrongly assumes normality for a skewed shape, and D discards real data rather than learning from the outliers.

questions.question: Executive sponsors on a steering board complain that the weekly thirty-page status pack is far too detailed for them to act on, while the delivery team relies on that same detail to coordinate work. The project manager must keep sponsors informed at a level they can actually use. What is the best approach?
choices: Distribute the full detailed pack to all audiences and let each reader extract what they need.
Replace the written pack with a self-service dashboard that sponsors can query on demand.
Shorten the pack to fifteen pages so one document serves both audiences at once.
Send sponsors a decision-focused one-page summary and keep the detailed pack for the team.
questions.explanation: Best: D — tailor communications to the audience: a concise decision-focused summary for sponsors while retaining full detail for the team. Closest miss — B: a self-service dashboard can work but relies on sponsors pulling and interpreting data rather than a decision-focused push. Also plausible — A: shifts the filtering burden onto readers; C: a middle length fits neither audience well.

questions.question: A predictive project has a budget at completion (BAC) of $600,000 and a cost performance index (CPI) of 0.75. The project manager estimates the final cost using EAC = BAC / CPI, assuming current cost performance continues for the remaining work. What is the resulting variance at completion (VAC)?
questions.explanation: Best: A — EAC = 600,000/0.75 = 800,000; VAC = BAC−EAC = 600,000−800,000 = −$200,000. Closest miss — B: −150,000 comes from BAC×(1−CPI). Also plausible — C: +200,000 drops the sign; D: −800,000 mistakes EAC itself for VAC.

questions.question: The site team on a commercial fit-out project reports that every deliverable has been built and the punch list has been worked down to zero. The project manager is preparing to close the project and has already scheduled the administrative wrap-up activities. What should be done first?
choices: Document lessons learned while the team's memory of the work is still fresh.
Release the contractor and reassign the internal crew to the next project.
Obtain formal client acceptance that deliverables meet the agreed acceptance criteria.
Archive project records and update the organization's asset repository.
questions.explanation: Best: C — formal acceptance that deliverables meet their acceptance criteria is the precondition for closing; "appear complete" is not the same as accepted. Closest miss — A: lessons learned belong in closure but only after the work is accepted. Also plausible — B: releasing resources before acceptance risks unstaffed rework; D: archiving is premature before acceptance.

questions.question: A hybrid data-migration project has delivered its full scope and the sponsor is eager to sign off quickly. Before closing, the project manager wants to confirm the project actually achieved its intended outcomes and value, not merely that it produced the planned outputs. What should be done?
choices: Compare delivered results against the business case objectives and defined success criteria.
Verify that each deliverable passed its full technical acceptance testing.
Confirm the schedule and budget baselines were met within their tolerances.
Survey the delivery team on whether they regard the work as complete.
questions.explanation: Best: A — outcomes are confirmed against the business-case objectives and success criteria, not merely by producing outputs. Closest miss — B: technical acceptance proves outputs conform but not that the intended outcomes and value were achieved. Also plausible — C: baseline conformance is not outcome achievement; D: team opinion is not outcome evidence.

questions.question: A new customer-billing system has passed testing and is ready to be handed to the operations and support group that will run and maintain it going forward. The project is entering its closure phase and resources are already being released. Before closing, what should the project manager ensure?
choices: The warranty period and defect-liability terms with the vendor are fully documented.
Operations has the training, run-books, support processes, and system access needed to run it.
All project team members have logged their final timesheets and been formally released.
The go-live announcement has been distributed to all affected end users.
questions.explanation: Best: B — operational readiness (training, run-books, support processes, access) is what lets the receiving group actually run and sustain the product. Closest miss — A: warranty terms matter for transition but don't make operations able to run it. Also plausible — C: timesheets are administrative closure; D: an announcement is communication, not operational capability.
questions.task: Plan and manage closure or transitions

questions.question: As an agile product initiative completes its final increment, the project manager wants future teams to benefit from what this team learned about an unfamiliar toolchain and a difficult regulator. The team will disband within days, and the knowledge lives mostly in people's heads. What should the project manager do?
choices: Keep the team's private retrospective notes in the team's chat channel for reference.
Brief the incoming project manager verbally during a single handover meeting.
Capture lessons learned and add them to the organization's searchable knowledge repository.
Present a summary of the successes at the closing steering-committee review.
questions.explanation: Best: C — codifying lessons into the organization's searchable knowledge repository makes them discoverable and reusable by future teams. Closest miss — B: a verbal handover reaches one successor and isn't retained or searchable. Also plausible — A: chat notes are siloed and undiscoverable; D: a steering review celebrates but doesn't transfer usable lessons.

questions.question: A software-integration project engaged a fixed-price vendor, and the final deliverable has now been received. The sponsor wants the contract closed by the end of the week. However, one outstanding change request and a disputed invoice from the vendor both remain unresolved. What should the project manager do?
choices: Confirm deliverables were accepted and settle the open change and invoice disputes before closing.
Close the contract now to meet the deadline and resolve open items in post-closure negotiation.
Pay the disputed invoice in full to clear the account and expedite formal closure.
Escalate both open items to the sponsor and let procurement decide when to close.
questions.explanation: Best: A — procurement closure requires confirming deliverable acceptance and settling open claims and disputes before the contract is formally closed. Closest miss — D: procurement is rightly involved, but the PM should first drive resolution rather than defer the timing decision. Also plausible — B: closing over unresolved obligations forfeits leverage; C: paying a disputed invoice concedes without basis.
questions.task: Plan and manage procurement and closure

questions.question: At closure, a capital project still has unspent budget, and its management and contingency reserves were never drawn. A workstream lead proposes using the remaining money to add several nice-to-have enhancements before the financial books are closed. What should the project manager do?
choices: Approve the proposed enhancements since the funds are already allocated to the project.
Retain the funds in the project account to cover any post-closure warranty issues.
Release the unused funds and reserves to the organization per financial governance.
Transfer the surplus to the operations team to fund first-year product support.
questions.explanation: Best: C — unused budget and undrawn reserves return to the organization at closure per financial governance; anything more is new scope. Closest miss — B: holding funds for warranty sounds prudent, but post-closure support funding is a governance decision, not the PM retaining project money. Also plausible — A: enhancements are unapproved gold-plating; D: redirecting closed-project funds is a portfolio/governance call, not the PM's.

questions.question: Six weeks after a customer-loyalty app went live, the sponsor asks the project manager to confirm that the initiative is delivering the projected revenue lift and retention gains that justified its funding. The project team is already disbanding and the operating group is taking over. What should be ensured?
choices: The app's post-launch defect rate remains within the agreed operational support SLA.
A final project report records that all deliverables were completed and accepted.
Adoption dashboards show login and feature-usage volumes climbing steadily since launch.
An accountable owner and a benefits-measurement plan are assigned to track results over time.
questions.explanation: Best: D — benefits typically realize after the project ends, so ensure an accountable owner and a measurement plan carry benefit tracking beyond closure. Closest miss — C: adoption metrics are leading indicators, and a snapshot is not sustained measurement of the target benefits. Also plausible — A: defect/SLA is operational quality, not benefit; B: deliverable completion is output, not outcome.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. What is the simple payback period?
choices: About 3.3 years
3.0 years
2.0 years
About 2.6 years
questions.explanation: Best: cumulative inflows reach $350,000 by end of year 2, leaving $150,000 of the $500,000 to recover; year 3 brings $250,000, so payback = 2 + 150,000/250,000 = 2.6 years. Closest miss — B: 3.0 rounds up to the end of year 3 instead of interpolating within it. Also plausible — C and A misplace the crossover year.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. What is the total net (undiscounted) benefit over the four years?
questions.explanation: Best: total inflows = 150+200+250+300 = $900,000; net of the $500,000 cost = $400,000. Closest miss — A: $900,000 is the gross inflow before subtracting the investment. Also plausible — C is the cost itself, and D is a single year.

questions.question: Refer to the scenario. Which measure best supports a go/no-go decision that accounts for the time value of money?
choices: Total undiscounted benefit, because a larger sum is always preferable.
Simple payback, because recovering the cost faster is always better.
Net present value, because it discounts each future inflow to today's value.
Accounting ROI, because it is easy to compute and widely understood.
questions.explanation: Best: NPV discounts future cash flows to present value, so it is the measure that accounts for the time value of money in a go/no-go decision. Closest miss — B: payback is useful for liquidity/risk and is genuinely informative, but it ignores cash flows after the payback point and the discount rate. Also plausible — A and D ignore timing and the cost of capital entirely.

questions.question: A digital-banking program has handed its new fraud-detection platform to operations; the outputs were formally accepted. The sponsor now stresses that the business case promised measurable reductions in fraud losses. The PM wants to protect benefits realization after handover, distinct from output acceptance. Which TWO actions best protect realized benefits?
choices: Confirm a benefits owner in operations is accountable for tracking the fraud-loss KPIs against the business-case targets over the realization period
Obtain the operations team's formal sign-off that the delivered platform meets the documented acceptance criteria
Archive the project artifacts, release the team, and close the contract now that deliverables are accepted
Schedule a lessons-learned retrospective with the project team to capture what went well during delivery
Ensure the transition includes the measurement mechanisms, baselines, and review cadence needed to sustain and evidence benefits after go-live
questions.explanation: Best: Benefits realization typically occurs after project close, so it must be owned and measured in operations — assigning an accountable benefits owner to track the KPIs against targets (A) and transitioning the measurement mechanisms, baselines, and review cadence (E) are what actually protect realized value. Closest miss — B: output acceptance sign-off confirms the deliverable meets spec but says nothing about whether fraud losses actually fall — it is exactly the output-vs-outcome distinction the stem draws. Also plausible — C: archiving and closing addresses administrative closure, not sustained benefits; D: lessons learned improves future projects but does not secure this program's benefits.
questions.task: Plan and manage project/phase closure or transitions

questions.question: A steering committee overseeing three parallel workstreams complains that status reports arrive in inconsistent formats at irregular intervals, so members cannot compare progress or trust the underlying data. Confidence in the program is eroding, and one member has questioned whether reporting is under control. What should the project manager do to restore that confidence?
choices: Immediately send a consolidated one-off report to reassure the committee members.
Assign a program analyst to compile all reports into a uniform layout.
Agree a standard format, content, and fixed cadence with the committee, then apply it.
Add more metrics and detail to each report so members have full information.
questions.explanation: Best: inconsistent, unpredictable reporting is a communications-standard gap, so agreeing a common format, content, and fixed cadence with the committee and applying it rebuilds trust at the source. Closest miss - B: assigning an analyst to compile reports improves uniformity but does not settle agreed content or cadence with the committee. Also plausible - A: a one-off consolidated report reassures briefly; D: adding metrics gives more data, not more consistency.

questions.question: Kicking off a two-week internal tooling change staffed by a single developer with minimal risk, the project manager finds the PMO's standard template mandates a full change control board, weekly steering reviews, and a formal risk register. Applying all of it would cost more effort than the work itself. Which approach best fits the situation while respecting governance?
choices: Follow the full PMO template to remain compliant with organizational standards.
Propose a tailored, lighter governance approach and secure the PMO's agreement first.
Apply a lightweight process now and notify the PMO later if questioned.
Keep only the risk register, dropping the board and reviews unilaterally.
questions.explanation: Best: governance should be tailored to size and risk, so proposing a lighter approach and securing the PMO's agreement right-sizes the process legitimately. Closest miss - D: keeping only the risk register is sensible tailoring but done unilaterally, without the PMO sanction that keeps it compliant. Also plausible - A: following the full template is safe but wasteful for a two-week low-risk change; C: acting first and notifying later risks a governance exception.

questions.question: Leadership proposes letting an AI system automatically approve low-risk change requests without human review, expecting faster delivery. The project manager supports speed but is accountable for the integrity of the change process. Before enabling the capability, what should the project manager most ensure is in place?
choices: Ensure the AI is trained on the organization's full history of change decisions.
Ensure the change control board periodically reviews the AI's approvals for accuracy.
Ensure every low-risk change is logged so the team can trace it.
Ensure clear, auditable low-risk criteria, human accountability, and escalation for exceptions.
questions.explanation: Best: delegating approvals to an AI is legitimate only when clear, auditable low-risk criteria, human accountability, and escalation for exceptions are defined, which bounds and governs the automation. Closest miss - B: having the board review AI approvals is a valuable control but reacts after the fact rather than setting the criteria and accountability that authorize delegation. Also plausible - A: good training data helps accuracy, not governance; C: logging supports traceability but not decision authority.

questions.question: A program's compliance register lists more than forty mandatory security, safety, and contractual obligations, but assurance capacity this quarter is limited. Four representative items carry these non-compliance impact and lapse-likelihood ratings: W (impact 5, likelihood 2), X (impact 4, likelihood 4), Y (impact 2, likelihood 5), Z (impact 3, likelihood 2). How should the project manager allocate the limited assurance effort?
choices: Meet the highest-impact obligations first, starting with W.
Address the obligations most likely to lapse first, starting with Y.
Prioritize assurance by exposure, focusing first on X, while still meeting all obligations.
Treat all obligations equally and spread assurance effort uniformly across the register.
questions.explanation: Best: all obligations must be met, but with limited capacity assurance effort should be prioritized by exposure (impact x likelihood), and X scores highest at 16 versus W 10, Y 10, and Z 6. Closest miss - D: treating all obligations equally reflects their mandatory nature but, given limited capacity, spreads effort too thin to protect the highest-exposure risks. Also plausible - A: ranking by impact alone elevates W; B: ranking by likelihood alone elevates Y.

questions.question: A medical-device project must operate within strict regulatory limits, and the project manager wants early warning of any drift toward non-compliance rather than discovering breaches after periodic audits. The compliance environment is stable but unforgiving of violations. Which approach best provides that early warning before a violation actually occurs?
choices: Increase the frequency of formal compliance audits to catch issues sooner.
Define leading indicators and thresholds that flag drift toward non-compliance.
Require the compliance officer's sign-off at each phase gate before proceeding.
Log every past non-compliance event and analyze the trends afterward.
questions.explanation: Best: catching drift before a violation requires leading indicators with thresholds that flag movement toward non-compliance while it can still be corrected. Closest miss - C: compliance sign-off at each phase gate is proactive but periodic, leaving blind spots between gates where drift can occur. Also plausible - A: more frequent audits still detect issues after they happen; D: trend analysis of past events is inherently backward-looking.

questions.question: Reviewing environments midway through execution, the project manager discovers the team has been copying live customer records into an unsecured test system. This may breach both the client's data-protection clause and applicable privacy law, and the copies have been accumulating for weeks. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Contain the exposure, assess its scope and impact, and engage the privacy function.
Notify the client and regulator immediately that a data breach has occurred.
Direct the team to delete the copied records from the test system at once.
Add a control requiring anonymized data in test environments going forward.
questions.explanation: Best: the priority is to stop the ongoing exposure while assessing its scope and impact and engaging the privacy or compliance function, which both contains harm and informs required next steps. Closest miss - C: deleting the copied records addresses the exposure but may destroy evidence and precedes any assessment of what was breached. Also plausible - B: external notification may be required once scope is confirmed, not before; D: an anonymization control prevents recurrence but ignores the active exposure.

questions.question: An external auditor will soon test whether a fintech project meets its regulatory obligations, and the project manager wants the project positioned to demonstrate compliance convincingly rather than scrambling during the audit. Several teams contributed to the controls over many months. What best positions the project to demonstrate its compliance to the auditor?
choices: A narrative summarizing how the team believes it satisfied each obligation.
A recent internal audit report stating no major issues were found.
The full set of project plans showing intended compliance controls.
A maintained compliance register mapping each obligation to its control and evidence.
questions.explanation: Best: auditors test evidence against each obligation, so a maintained compliance register mapping every obligation to its control and supporting evidence positions the project to prove compliance directly. Closest miss - B: a clean internal audit report adds assurance but is a single summary, not obligation-level traceability to evidence. Also plausible - A: a narrative asserts compliance without proof; C: plans show intended controls, not evidence they operated.

questions.question: A new ESG disclosure regulation takes effect that appears to apply to the project's product line and would require carbon and supply-chain data the team does not currently collect. The team assumes existing reporting already satisfies it, and adding the disclosures could jeopardize the committed launch date. What should the project manager do?
choices: Accept the team's view that current reporting suffices and launch on schedule.
Add the new carbon and supply-chain disclosures immediately, accepting the launch slip.
Confirm applicability and the disclosure gap with compliance, then take the trade-off to governance.
Ask legal whether launch can proceed and defer the sustainability disclosures until afterward.
questions.explanation: Best: applicability is uncertain and the team is assuming, so confirming the rule's scope and the disclosure gap with compliance and then bringing the schedule trade-off to governance is the responsible sequence. Closest miss - D: a legal read is useful, but pairing it with deferring the disclosures presumes non-applicability at launch and skips quantifying the gap. Also plausible - A: accepting the assumption risks a breach; B: adding disclosures immediately over-commits before scope is confirmed.

questions.question: On a predictive building-automation project, a stakeholder formally requests switching to a low-carbon concrete mix they call essential to the client's public net-zero pledge. The change would raise material cost about six percent and add two weeks to the schedule; the current mix already meets code. How should the project manager best handle the request?
choices: Reject it as gold-plating since the current mix already meets code.
Evaluate it through change control, weighing ESG value against cost and schedule impact.
Approve the low-carbon mix immediately given the client's public net-zero commitment.
Defer the decision until the client confirms in writing that net-zero applies.
questions.explanation: Best: a formally requested change with real ESG value and cost and schedule impact belongs in change control, where its value is weighed against impact for a governed decision. Closest miss - D: confirming the net-zero commitment applies is reasonable diligence, but it defers the judgment instead of running the value-versus-impact trade-off. Also plausible - A: rejecting it as gold-plating dismisses legitimate ESG value; C: approving it immediately skips governed impact analysis.

questions.question: A change control board has approved adding multi-currency capability to an e-commerce platform partway through delivery. The project manager wants to implement the approved change correctly so that scope, plans, and stakeholders stay aligned. What should the project manager do to implement it correctly?
choices: Direct the team to begin building the multi-currency capability right away.
Update the requirements documentation and inform the development team of the new scope.
Communicate the approved change to affected stakeholders and record it in the change log.
Update the affected baselines and plans, then communicate and direct the work.
questions.explanation: Best: implementing an approved change correctly means updating the affected scope, schedule, and cost baselines and plans, then communicating and directing the work so controls stay aligned. Closest miss - C: communicating the change and logging it is necessary but incomplete without updating the baselines and plans that govern execution. Also plausible - A: starting to build immediately skips the baseline and plan updates; B: revising requirements alone updates one artifact, not the full baseline set.

questions.question: Midway through a consumer-fintech project, a regulator publishes a new rule adding mandatory data-consent requirements that take effect before the planned launch. The PM learns of it from a compliance bulletin. What are the TWO most appropriate first responses?
choices: Immediately implement the perceived requirements in the product without analysis to be safe before launch
Assess the impact of the new requirements on scope, schedule, cost, and risk, and engage compliance/legal to interpret the obligations
Log the regulatory change and route it through integrated change control so any baseline changes are formally evaluated and approved
Absorb the changes quietly within the team's slack and avoid alarming the sponsor or steering committee
Request a scope exclusion from the sponsor so the mandatory requirements can be deferred to a later release
questions.explanation: Best: B compliance-driven change is still a change: first understand it, then govern it. Assessing impact across scope/schedule/cost/risk with legal and compliance interpreting the obligation (B) provides the facts, and logging it into integrated change control ensures baseline impacts are formally evaluated and approved (C). Closest miss — A: implementing an un-analyzed interpretation "to be safe" risks building the wrong thing, gold-plating, or missing the actual legal requirement — analysis must precede action. Also plausible — D: hiding a mandatory regulatory change from governance is a compliance and transparency failure; E: mandatory regulatory requirements generally cannot simply be excluded or deferred past their effective date.
questions.task: Evaluate and address external business environment changes

questions.question: Facing a governance review, a cost analyst proposes quietly shifting the cost baseline to absorb an unfavorable variance, arguing that several small approved changes loosely justify the adjustment and no one will notice. The project manager must respond. What should the project manager do?
choices: Allow the adjustment only up to the value of the approved changes.
Report the analyst to leadership for proposing to falsify project data.
Decline the change and re-baseline only through approved, documented change control.
Leave the baseline unchanged and simply explain the variance in the next report.
questions.explanation: Best: any baseline change must go through authorized change control, so declining the quiet adjustment and re-baselining only the approved changes with documented authorization preserves integrity and reflects legitimate changes. Closest miss - D: leaving the baseline unchanged and explaining the variance is honest but forgoes properly incorporating the genuinely approved changes. Also plausible - A: capping the adjustment to approved value still rationalizes an unauthorized edit; B: reporting the analyst punishes a suggestion before addressing the process.

questions.question: Midway through a fintech product's release, a compliance lead asks the team to pull a mandatory ESG carbon-disclosure feature into the next two-week iteration. Doing so would displace a revenue-analytics story the sponsor ranked highest for this release. The regulation's deadline is three iterations away, and both items are sized similarly. How should the team decide what to load into the iteration?
choices: Reprioritize the backlog with the product owner, weighing regulatory deadline, value, and displaced work.
Load the ESG feature now because mandatory compliance outranks the discretionary revenue story.
Keep the sponsor's revenue story and schedule the ESG feature in a later iteration before the deadline.
Split both features into thinner slices so partial versions of each fit the iteration.
questions.explanation: Best: A — mid-release scope changes belong in product-owner-led backlog refinement using a weighted view (deadline slack, value, displaced work), not a reflexive swap; three iterations of slack means 'now' isn't forced. Closest miss — C: deferring the ESG feature is feasible given the slack, but it pre-decides the outcome before the weighted refinement. Also plausible — B: compliance is mandatory yet the deadline isn't imminent; D: slicing may help but doesn't settle prioritization.

questions.question: A hybrid data-platform program receives change-board approval to add a data-residency requirement. The approval authorized the scope but did not assess delivery impact. The current increment already carries committed work with a firm regulator demonstration date. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Incorporate the approved change into the current increment immediately, since it is already authorized.
Assess the change's impact on the committed increment's capacity and demo date, then schedule it.
Defer the change to the next increment to protect the committed regulator demonstration.
Ask the change board to trim other committed scope to make room now.
questions.explanation: Best: B — change-board approval authorizes the scope but not its scheduling; the PM must assess capacity and demo-date impact before slotting it. Closest miss — C: protecting the demo is reasonable, but deferral should follow the impact assessment, not precede it. Also plausible — A: authorized, yet absorbing it blindly endangers the committed demo; D: renegotiating scope may follow once impact is known.

questions.question: On a lean four-person analytics initiative, a stakeholder argues that because no formal change control board exists, no one is authorized to approve any scope change, and requests should be frozen until a board is chartered. Changes so far have been small and infrequent. What is the best response?
choices: Charter a formal change control board so change authority is unambiguous before proceeding.
Freeze all change requests until governance for approvals is formally established.
Tailor a lightweight change process with a named approver appropriate to the project's size.
Let the sponsor personally approve each change request as it arises.
questions.explanation: Best: C — change control is tailored to context; a small project needs a right-sized, documented process with a clear approver, not a heavyweight board or a freeze. Closest miss — D: a single approver is close, but naming the sponsor ad hoc lacks the defined criteria and logging a tailored process provides. Also plausible — A: a full CCB is disproportionate; B: freezing halts value unnecessarily.

questions.question: A shared staging environment fails, and three squads immediately flag themselves as blocked in the stand-up. Reviewing their boards, the delivery lead notices several in-progress stories don't actually depend on staging and could proceed. Restoring the environment may take a day. What should the delivery lead do first?
choices: Escalate the outage to infrastructure as a program-level blocker for all three squads.
Have all squads switch to unrelated backlog items until staging is restored.
Ask each squad to log the outage as a risk and continue as planned.
Confirm which work truly depends on staging before focusing impediment effort.
questions.explanation: Best: D — triage first to separate genuinely blocked work from work that can continue, so escalation and effort target real impediments. Closest miss — A: escalating the outage is needed, but flagging it as blocking all three squads overstates impact before triage. Also plausible — B: redirecting everyone wastes unblocked capacity; C: logging a present issue as a risk misclassifies it and delays action.

questions.question: Across a distributed program, several impediments have been escalated to leadership, but the teams cannot tell which ones are actively being worked, which are waiting, and which are stuck. Frustration is rising as duplicate escalations appear. What should the program manager do first?
choices: Create a shared impediment board showing each blocker's owner and current status.
Hold a daily leadership call to verbally update teams on escalated impediments.
Ask team leads to stop re-escalating until leadership responds to open items.
Assign each open impediment to a leadership sponsor for resolution.
questions.explanation: Best: A — a shared, visible impediment board with owner and status gives the continuous transparency the teams lack and stops duplicate escalations at the source. Closest miss — D: assigning owners is part of the fix, but without visible status teams still can't see progress. Also plausible — B: verbal updates aren't persistent or transparent; C: suppressing re-escalation treats a symptom of the visibility gap.

questions.question: For five consecutive iterations, a team has stalled waiting on the same manual security-access approval, each time improvising a workaround that costs roughly a day. The workaround succeeds but the delay recurs every cycle, and the team treats it as normal. What is the most effective way to address this recurring impediment?
choices: Add a one-day buffer each iteration to absorb the recurring approval delay.
Address the systemic cause by streamlining or automating the manual approval step.
Escalate the delay to management each time it blocks the iteration.
Document the workaround so the team can apply it faster next time.
questions.explanation: Best: B — the identical blocker recurring for five iterations points to a systemic process bottleneck; automating or streamlining the manual approval removes it at the source. Closest miss — D: standardizing the workaround cuts waste but leaves the root cause and the daily loss intact. Also plausible — A: buffering hides the waste; C: repeated escalation manages instances, not the systemic step.

questions.question: A program manager notices impediments are resolved individually but there is no way to confirm they stay resolved, and new ones surface late, only after they hurt delivery. She wants both durable resolution and earlier detection. Which approach best achieves both?
choices: Review all closed impediments at each release to confirm none have recurred.
Add impediment identification as a standing agenda item in every stand-up.
Run a monitored impediment board reviewing new and previously closed items regularly.
Require every team member to raise blockers immediately through a shared channel.
questions.explanation: Best: C — a monitored board reviewed on a cadence serves both aims: it surfaces new impediments early and re-checks closed ones for regression. Closest miss — B: stand-up attention catches new impediments but doesn't verify closed ones stay resolved. Also plausible — A: release-time review is too infrequent for early detection; D: an open channel aids raising but lacks systematic review of closed items.

questions.question: A component-supplier delay that the team had identified and for which it had prepared a contingency plan — qualifying an alternate supplier — has now occurred; the primary supplier confirms a six-week slip. The trigger condition the team defined has been met. What should the project manager do?
choices: Reassess the risk register to determine whether the delay changes other risk ratings.
Escalate the supplier delay to the sponsor and request a schedule extension.
Analyze whether the six-week slip exceeds the project's schedule tolerance before acting.
Execute the prepared contingency plan by activating the qualified alternate supplier.
questions.explanation: Best: D — the defined trigger has fired and a contingency response was pre-planned and ready, so the PM should execute it and then update records. Closest miss — C: confirming schedule tolerance is prudent, but the response was planned for exactly this trigger, so acting now beats re-analyzing. Also plausible — A: reassessment follows execution; B: escalation/extension is a fallback if the contingency proves insufficient.

questions.question: An open issue — intermittent authentication failures — requires input from operations, security, and an external vendor to resolve. It has sat unresolved for two weeks because each group assumes another is leading, and no one is coordinating the parties. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Assign one accountable owner to drive the issue and coordinate the parties.
Schedule a joint working session with operations, security, and the vendor to diagnose it.
Escalate the stalled issue to the steering committee for direction.
Break the issue into three parts and route one to each group.
questions.explanation: Best: A — the issue is stalled specifically because no one owns it; assigning a single accountable owner to coordinate the three parties is the direct fix, after which working sessions follow. Closest miss — B: a joint session is valuable and likely the owner's first act, but without ownership the coordination gap persists. Also plausible — C: escalation is premature before ownership; D: splitting the issue loses the cross-cutting coordination it needs.

questions.question: A sensitivity (tornado) diagram ranks how much each variable moves project NPV. Which variable should quantitative risk analysis and response focus on FIRST?
choices: Material cost — it has the widest swing, so NPV is most sensitive to it.
Interest rate — it appears at the top axis of the chart.
Scope volume — because scope is always the top project risk.
All four equally, since each variable appears on the chart.
questions.explanation: Best: the tornado is sorted by impact, and Material cost has the widest bar, so NPV is most sensitive to it — the first place to focus analysis and response. Closest miss — C: scope is often a major risk in general, but this chart shows Material cost, not scope volume, as the largest driver here. Also plausible — B confuses chart position with magnitude, and D ignores the ranking the diagram exists to show.

questions.question: At the initiation of a high-uncertainty R&D project, the sponsor asks how the team will handle risks consistently rather than reacting case by case. No agreed method yet exists for how risks will be identified, assessed, prioritized, and owned. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Begin identifying risks immediately and capture each one in the project risk register.
Set aside a management reserve sized to the project's overall uncertainty.
Develop a risk management plan setting how risks are identified, assessed, and owned.
Schedule recurring risk reviews across the entire project life cycle.
questions.explanation: Best: C — the sponsor is asking for a consistent method; the risk management plan defines how risks are identified, assessed, prioritized, and owned, and it frames identification, reserves, and reviews. Closest miss — A: identifying risks matters but, before the method is agreed, yields inconsistent results the plan should govern. Also plausible — B: reserves follow analysis; D: recurring reviews are one element of the plan, not a substitute.

questions.question: On a distributed program, identified risks are scattered — some in meeting minutes, some in email threads, some only in individual team members' memory. Nothing is consolidated, so risks are forgotten and duplicated. The project manager wants a reliable single source for tracking them. What should the project manager do?
choices: Ask each contributor to email their known risks to the project manager weekly.
Add a risk-review segment to the weekly status meeting agenda.
Assign owners to the most significant risks currently known.
Consolidate all identified risks into a single maintained risk register.
questions.explanation: Best: D — a single maintained risk register is the authoritative source that stops loss and duplication and underpins the other actions. Closest miss — B: a recurring review helps update risks but presumes a consolidated list to review. Also plausible — A: weekly emails leave information fragmented; C: assigning owners matters but only after risks are captured in one place.

questions.question: A team can actively manage only a few of its many risks. Four candidates are quantified: R1 — 70% probability, $40,000 impact; R2 — 20%, $260,000; R3 — 60%, $90,000; R4 — 15%, $50,000. The team prioritizes by expected exposure while noting worst-case severity. Which risk should receive active response planning first?
choices: R3, whose expected exposure of $54,000 is the highest of the four.
R2, whose $260,000 worst-case impact is by far the most severe.
R1, whose 70% probability makes it the most likely to occur.
R4, a low-exposure item worth clearing quickly to reduce the count.
questions.explanation: Best: A — prioritizing by expected exposure (probability × impact) ranks R3 highest at $54,000, marginally above R2's $52,000, directing scarce response capacity where it does most good. Closest miss — B: R2's severe worst case is a real concern and nearly ties, but on the stated basis it ranks just below R3. Also plausible — C: R1's exposure is only $28,000; D: R4's is lowest at $7,500.

questions.question: A construction program faces a low-probability but financially severe threat: failure of a specialized tunneling machine during a critical bore, which would trigger large third-party and delay liabilities the owner cannot absorb. The failure cannot be prevented and mitigation would be prohibitively expensive. Which risk response strategy is most appropriate?
choices: Mitigate the threat by adding preventive maintenance and redundant machine components.
Transfer the threat through insurance and a contract shifting liability to a specialist.
Accept the threat and fund a contingency reserve sized to the potential loss.
Avoid the threat by redesigning the bore to eliminate the specialized machine.
questions.explanation: Best: B — for a low-probability, high-financial-severity threat that can't be prevented and is too costly to mitigate, transferring the financial consequence via insurance and a liability-shifting contract fits. Closest miss — C: accepting with a reserve is defensible, but the stem says the owner cannot absorb the liability, so transfer is better. Also plausible — A: mitigation is stated to be prohibitively expensive; D: mid-program redesign to avoid may be infeasible and sacrifices the method's benefits.

questions.question: A program identifies an opportunity: if an early pilot group adopts a new low-energy processing tool, the organization could lock in measurable energy-cost and emissions reductions across the rollout, helping meet a corporate carbon target. The savings are not guaranteed — they depend on the pilot proving the tool at scale. How should the team respond to this opportunity?
choices: Accept the opportunity and capture the savings only if the pilot happens to succeed.
Share the opportunity with the tool vendor through a joint benefits arrangement.
Enhance the opportunity by resourcing the pilot to raise its chance of proving savings.
Exploit the opportunity by mandating organization-wide tool adoption immediately.
questions.explanation: Best: C — the benefit is probabilistic and hinges on the pilot proving out, so enhancing (investing to raise the probability the opportunity occurs) is the fitting positive-risk response. Closest miss — D: exploiting by mandating org-wide adoption before the pilot proves the tool discards the pilot's risk-reducing value and could lock in an unproven tool. Also plausible — A: passive acceptance forgoes actionable upside; B: sharing suits a partner better placed to capture value, not this case.

questions.question: Eight months into a two-year program, significant conditions have shifted — a key regulation changed and two vendors merged — yet the risk register has not been touched since the kickoff workshop. Delivery is currently on track, and the team is fully loaded with feature work. What should the project manager do?
choices: Leave the register as is while delivery is on track, revisiting it if problems appear.
Add the two new events to the risk register and continue with current work.
Schedule a full risk re-identification workshop at the next major milestone.
Reassess risks now to re-identify, re-rate, and retire them given changed conditions.
questions.explanation: Best: D — risk management is iterative; material environmental shifts warrant reassessing now to re-identify, re-rate, and retire risks rather than waiting for problems. Closest miss — C: a scheduled workshop is sound practice, but deferring to the next milestone leaves the register stale while conditions have already changed. Also plausible — A: waiting for problems is reactive despite being on track; B: adding only the two obvious events skips re-rating existing risks and finding others.

questions.question: A quantitative risk analysis update on a regional water-utility upgrade shows the expected monetary value of remaining threats has risen from $300,000 to $780,000, while only $250,000 of contingency reserve remains. The steering sponsor has not seen the new figures. Delivery pressure is high and descoping is unpopular. What should the project manager do next?
choices: Present the updated risk exposure, response options, and reserve shortfall to the sponsor/governance body; reassess the contingency requirement and obtain any funding or baseline authorization through the applicable process.
Mitigate the highest-EMV threats first to pull exposure within the remaining reserve.
Submit a management-reserve change request for the full funding gap immediately.
Rebaseline the schedule to defer threat-bearing work until reserves recover.
questions.explanation: Best: the exposure has been re-quantified and now exceeds both the contingency reserve and the PM's authority, so the PM surfaces the reforecast and options to governance and reassesses the contingency requirement, letting the authorized body decide on funding or baseline change. Closest miss — B: mitigating the highest-EMV threats is sound and should continue, but a jump well beyond the reserve is unlikely to be closed by mitigation alone and still leaves governance uninformed of a material change. Also plausible — C names a fixed management-reserve amount without options or analysis, and D defers threat-bearing work rather than resolving the exposure.
questions.task: Protect value: reserves and sponsor escalation

questions.question: A distributed mobile-banking squad delivers a working increment every two weeks but rolls straight into the next iteration each time. Defects and rework are climbing and morale is slipping, yet the team has no regular forum to examine how it actually works together. As the agile-minded project lead, what should you do first?
choices: Add a quality gate requiring sign-off before each iteration can close.
Facilitate regular retrospectives so the team inspects and improves its process.
Commission an external process audit to identify the sources of rework.
Introduce defect-density metrics on the iteration dashboard for visibility.
questions.explanation: Best: the missing practice is team self-inspection; facilitating regular retrospectives lets the team examine its way of working and own the improvements. Closest miss — D: dashboard metrics add visibility but not the reflective forum that turns insight into change. Also plausible — A: a gate imposes control rather than building improvement; C: an external audit removes team ownership and is heavier than needed.

questions.question: On a multi-phase government ERP rollout, the team diligently records lessons in a register at every phase gate, yet the same integration and testing mistakes reappear phase after phase. The register is well maintained but rarely consulted once entries are written. What should the project manager do?
choices: Restructure the lessons register with better tags so entries are easier to search.
Circulate the register to all team members and ask them to read it regularly.
Assign owners to high-impact lessons and build their actions into phase planning.
Schedule a single lessons-learned review for the whole program at project end.
questions.explanation: Best: recurrence persists because lessons are recorded but never actioned, so assigning owners and embedding their actions into upcoming phase planning closes the loop. Closest miss — D: a review helps, but end-of-project timing cannot prevent the recurring mistakes in the remaining phases. Also plausible — A: better tags aid retrieval, not follow-through; B: circulation without accountability rarely changes behavior.

questions.question: A retrospective on a facilities program finds the capital-estimating template compares chillers on purchase price alone, omitting energy and end-of-life disposal costs — the category behind repeated overruns. Option 1 costs $180,000 to buy, $22,000 per year to run for 10 years, and $15,000 to dispose. Option 2 costs $240,000 to buy, $14,000 per year for 10 years, and $10,000 to dispose. On a whole-life basis, which is cheaper and by how much?
choices: Option 1 is cheaper by $60,000.
Option 2 is cheaper by $25,000.
Option 2 is cheaper by $80,000.
Option 1 is cheaper by $55,000.
questions.explanation: Best: whole-life cost = capital + ten years' operating + disposal, giving Option 1 $415,000 and Option 2 $390,000, so Option 2 is cheaper by $25,000. Closest miss — A: compares purchase price only ($60,000), the exact omission the retrospective flagged. Also plausible — C: counts operating savings only ($80,000); D: adds capital and disposal but omits operating ($55,000).

questions.question: The chart shows cumulative net cash flow for two candidate projects; funding covers only one. Project Q recovers its cost sooner, but Project P has the higher cumulative value by year 5. The organization's stated priority is long-term value. Which should the PM recommend, and why?
choices: Project Q, because recovering cash sooner frees capital earlier.
Project Q, because a shorter payback period is always the safer financial choice.
Project P, because it aligns with the stated long-term-value priority despite its later payback.
Whichever the sponsor prefers, since both eventually turn positive.
questions.explanation: Best: with long-term value the stated priority, Project P — higher cumulative value by year 5 — fits, even though it breaks even later. Closest miss — A: Q's earlier payback is a real benefit (liquidity, lower exposure), but it optimizes speed of recovery, not the long-term value the organization said it wants. Also plausible — B overstates payback as 'always' safest, and D abdicates the PM's duty to tie the recommendation to the stated criterion.

questions.question: During a retrospective, a product team concludes that a mandatory three-signature approval before every release adds no value and delays each deployment by days. The approval is defined in the organization's governance standard and owned by the PMO. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Remove the redundant sign-offs immediately, since the team agreed they add no value.
Propose a streamlined approval to the PMO with evidence and pilot it.
Log the finding in the retrospective actions and continue with current approvals.
Escalate to the sponsor to have the governance standard waived for this project.
questions.explanation: Best: the step is genuine waste but is owned by the PMO under a governance standard, so the PM tailors it by bringing evidence to the owner and piloting an agreed change. Closest miss — D: escalating can work but bypasses the process owner and seeks a waiver instead of an evidence-based, reusable improvement. Also plausible — A: unilateral removal ignores governance authority; C: logging without acting forgoes a clear efficiency gain.

questions.question: A new case-management system will replace the tool that 600 support-center agents use every day, and the project manager anticipates that different teams and shifts will vary widely in how ready they are to adopt it. Before designing the rollout approach, what should the project manager do first?
choices: Conduct a change-impact and readiness assessment across the affected groups.
Build a comprehensive training curriculum covering every feature of the new system.
Schedule the go-live for a low-volume period to limit operational disruption.
Appoint change champions within each team to promote the new system.
questions.explanation: Best: with readiness varying across many groups, the PM first understands who is affected and how ready they are, so a change-impact and readiness assessment can shape training, timing, and support. Closest miss — D: champions help adoption but should be targeted using the assessment findings. Also plausible — B: full training is premature before needs are known; C: timing helps but presumes the rollout design.

questions.question: A logistics company is deploying an automated sortation system in the same warehouse where manual operations must keep running until cutover. Leadership is concerned the switch could disrupt daily shipments during the transition. What should the project manager do?
choices: Accelerate the deployment to shorten the window of potential disruption.
Add contingency budget to cover losses if shipments are delayed during cutover.
Develop a transition plan with phased cutover, parallel running, and back-out.
Tell customers that short delays may occur during the transition period.
questions.explanation: Best: because operations continue through the switch, the PM manages transition risk with a plan providing phasing, parallel running, and a back-out path. Closest miss — A: shortening the window can help, but a compressed cutover raises the chance of a disruptive failure with no fallback. Also plausible — B: budget covers losses, not the disruption; D: customer messaging manages expectations, not the operational risk.

questions.question: A hospital is standardizing its clinical documentation process across sites. Nurses at several sites are resisting, and interviews reveal the resistance comes from not understanding why the change is needed or what problem it solves. Training on the new forms is already scheduled. What should the project manager do?
choices: Expand the scheduled training so staff become fully proficient with the new forms.
Ask site managers to enforce the new process once training is complete.
Offer recognition to early adopters to build momentum for the change.
Communicate the change's rationale and expected benefits to the affected staff.
questions.explanation: Best: the interviews show the barrier is awareness — staff do not understand why — so the PM communicates the rationale and benefits before proficiency or enforcement can help. Closest miss — A: training builds ability but does not answer the 'why' driving the resistance. Also plausible — B: enforcement without buy-in can harden resistance; C: recognition reinforces adoption but does not close the awareness gap.

questions.question: Two months after a sales organization adopted a new CRM workflow, dashboards show representatives increasingly reverting to spreadsheets and side channels to manage their pipeline. Adoption had been strong at launch. What should the project manager do?
choices: Engage users to find what blocks sustained use, then reinforce adoption.
Re-run the original CRM training for all sales reps to refresh their skills.
Restrict access to the legacy spreadsheets so reps must use the CRM.
Report the declining adoption to the sponsor and request an enforcement mandate.
questions.explanation: Best: sustained adoption is slipping, so the PM investigates the barriers to continued use and applies targeted reinforcement — the sustainment work of change. Closest miss — C: removing the fallback can compel use but, without addressing why reps left, tends to breed new workarounds. Also plausible — B: retraining assumes an unevidenced skill gap; D: an enforcement mandate skips diagnosis of the cause.
