questions.question: Midway through a supply-chain transformation, the executive who sponsored it retires and a successor takes over the function, signaling a shift toward margin protection over the original growth agenda. The project's business case was built on growth. What should the project manager do?
choices: Continue executing the approved scope, since the business case was formally baselined.
Meet the new sponsor to grasp priorities, then reassess the business case.
Pause the project until the new executive issues a revised strategic direction.
Propose scope changes that align the project with margin protection right away.
questions.explanation: Best: a new sponsor with different priorities is a material change, so the PM first understands the new direction, then reassesses whether the business case and options still hold before altering anything. Closest miss — D: realigning to margin is likely needed, but proposing specific scope changes before confirming intent is premature. Also plausible — A: executing a possibly-misaligned baseline risks wasted value; C: a full pause overreacts and halts value.
questions.task: Respond to strategic and sponsor change

questions.question: Halfway through building a customer analytics platform, a new data-privacy law takes effect in the project's principal market, imposing consent and data-retention rules the current design does not meet. The team is mid-sprint on unrelated features. What should the project manager do first?
choices: Assess the law's impact on scope and design, engaging legal on required changes.
Add the consent and retention requirements to the product backlog for a future sprint.
Halt all development until the platform is redesigned for full legal compliance.
Continue the current sprint and address privacy once release scope is finalized.
questions.explanation: Best: a new mandatory law is a compliance-affecting external change, so the PM first assesses its impact on scope and design with legal to define what must change and how urgently. Closest miss — B: backlogging the requirements is a reasonable mechanism, but doing so before assessing exposure and deadline risks non-compliance. Also plausible — C: halting all work overreacts before impact is known; D: deferring assumes time the assessment has not confirmed.

questions.question: A five-year defense-adjacent modernization program operates in an environment where technology, supplier markets, and geopolitical conditions all shift unpredictably. The sponsor asks how external-environment scanning should be handled across the program's life. Which approach is most appropriate?
choices: Perform a thorough environmental scan at initiation and revisit it if a crisis hits.
Delegate environmental monitoring entirely to the enterprise risk-management function.
Scan the environment continuously and feed changes into risk and planning reviews.
Commission an annual external-environment report from a specialist consultancy.
questions.explanation: Best: in a volatile, long-running environment, scanning must be continuous and tied to the program's risk and planning cycles so emerging shifts actually change decisions. Closest miss — D: an annual specialist report adds rigor but its cadence lags fast-moving change. Also plausible — A: one-time-plus-crisis scanning is reactive; B: fully delegating to ERM detaches the program from signals affecting its own scope.

questions.question: While a consumer-appliance project is in design, a newly commercialized low-energy component reaches the market. It would render the project's planned high-efficiency feature obsolete against tightening energy regulations, yet it would also make a second, greener feature far cheaper to deliver. What should the project manager do?
choices: Adopt the new component immediately to capture the cost saving on the second feature.
Reject the change to protect the current design baseline and schedule.
Assess business-case and benefit impact, then take options through change control.
Escalate to the sponsor to decide whether to cancel the now-obsolete feature.
questions.explanation: Best: the new technology is both a regulatory threat and a value opportunity, so the PM evaluates both against the business case and benefits and takes integrated options through change control. Closest miss — A: adopting at once captures savings but skips impact analysis and governance for a change with regulatory implications. Also plausible — B: protecting the baseline ignores a compliance threat and a real value gain; D: escalating only the obsolete feature handles the threat, not the linked opportunity, and precedes analysis.
questions.task: External change to scope and value (sustainability)

questions.question: A fintech firm is nine months into building a lending product when a regulatory ruling bars its core credit-scoring method in the product's primary market, and most projected benefits depended on that market. Substantial budget has already been spent. What should the project manager do?
choices: Complete the build as scoped so the sunk investment is not wasted.
Recommend cancelling the project immediately in light of the ruling.
Redesign the scoring method to comply and continue toward the original launch.
Reassess the business case with the sponsor, weighing pivots against remaining spend.
questions.explanation: Best: the ruling breaks the business case, so the PM disregards sunk cost and reassesses with the sponsor which forward option — redesign, alternate market, or cancellation — best returns value for the remaining spend. Closest miss — B: cancellation may be the outcome, but recommending it before evaluating viable pivots is premature. Also plausible — A: finishing to honor sunk cost delivers an unusable product; C: redesign should be chosen only if it restores the business case.
